entries.question: Ari has searched their library this turn with [Bog Glider]. During their end step, Nico casts [Mission Briefing]. Can they use it to cast [Archive Trap] from their graveyard for free?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Nico can cast Archive Trap from the graveyard using Mission Briefing and may pay its {0} alternative cost (noting the alternative only applies if Ari is an opponent).
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can cast Archive Trap from their graveyard and pay its alternative cost of {0}, provided Ari is Nico's opponent.

Why it works:

1. Mission Briefing grants permission, not a cost change. Mission Briefing says you surveil 2, then choose an instant or sorcery card in your graveyard and "You may cast it this turn." That's permission to cast the card from the graveyard; it doesn't alter what Archive Trap costs. As the Mission Briefing ruling notes, Mission Briefing doesn't change when you can cast the chosen card — Archive Trap is an instant, so Nico can cast it right away during Ari's end step (or any other time this turn they'd have priority).

2. Archive Trap's alternative cost still applies. Archive Trap reads "If an opponent searched their library this turn, you may pay {0} rather than pay this spell's mana cost." An alternative cost is a cost you may pay instead of the spell's mana cost (rules 118.9, 118.9a), and an object's ability that lets a player pay an alternative cost functions while that object is on the stack — and, by extension, applies when it's cast from anywhere, including the graveyard (rule 113.6d). Nico announces the intent to pay the {0} alternative cost when proposing the spell (rule 601.2b).

3. The condition is met. Bog Glider's activated ability says "Search your library for a Mercenary permanent card..." — it contains the word "search," which is exactly what Archive Trap's ruling requires. Another Archive Trap ruling confirms it doesn't matter whether the searching player actually found a card, so it's irrelevant if Ari declined to find anything (Bog Glider's own ruling allows declining to find).

4. No conflict of alternative costs. Only one alternative cost can be applied to a spell (rules 118.9a, 601.2b), but Mission Briefing isn't an alternative cost — it's a casting permission — so paying Archive Trap's {0} is legal. Note {0} is technically a cost being paid, not "casting without paying its mana cost"; Archive Trap's mana cost and mana value remain {3}{U}{U} and 5, so any cost-increasing effect would apply on top of the {0} (per the Archive Trap rulings). Nico may also simply pay {3}{U}{U} instead if they prefer.

5. Aftermath: because Nico cast Archive Trap via Mission Briefing, when Archive Trap would be put into Nico's graveyard on resolution it's exiled instead.

Multiplayer note: Archive Trap only cares that "an opponent" of Nico searched this turn, and the Archive Trap ruling states the opponent you target doesn't have to be the opponent who searched. So at a table of three or more, Ari's Bog Glider search turns on the alternative cost even if Nico targets a different opponent for the mill 13. In a two-player game, Ari is necessarily the target. The one requirement in either case is that Ari be an opponent of Nico's — if Ari were Nico's teammate, the alternative cost would not be available.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Bog Glider's search resolved earlier in this same turn, before Mission Briefing resolved, as stated. If the search happened on a previous turn instead, the {0} alternative cost would not be available and Nico would have to pay {3}{U}{U}.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Mission Briefing allows Nico to cast Archive Trap from their graveyard, without any other restrictions on how it's cast. Nico can choose to pay the alternative cost of {0}.

entries.question: In a game of Two-Headed Giant, Antonio activates the last loyalty ability of [Chandra, Hope's Beacon] with X=1. Could they target both Nico and Noah?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: in Two-Headed Giant Nico and Noah are separate players and both can be targeted and dealt the ability's damage.
entries.answer:
Yes. Chandra, Hope's Beacon's −X ability says it deals X damage to "each of up to two targets," so Antonio may choose Nico and Noah as the two targets, and each of them is dealt 1 damage (the damage isn't divided — each target takes the full X).

Why this works in Two-Headed Giant: even though Nico and Noah share a life total as teammates, they are still two separate players and therefore two separate legal targets. Two-Headed Giant is played with two teams of two players each [810.1], and apart from life total and poison counters a team's resources are not shared [810.5]. Damage happens to each player individually, and the result is then applied to the team's shared life total [810.9]. So Chandra, Hope's Beacon dealing 1 damage to Nico and 1 damage to Noah results in their team's shared life total dropping by 2 total.

A couple of practical notes: the X in the −X cost is chosen as the ability is activated, so with X=1 Antonio pays 1 loyalty from Chandra, Hope's Beacon (leaving 4 if it entered this turn at 5). Antonio isn't restricted to opponents either — "any target" choices could include himself, his teammate, creatures, or planeswalkers; targeting both members of the opposing team is simply one legal choice.

This answer is specific to the Two-Headed Giant variant described in the rules provided (two teams of two).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Each member of a team is a separate player and is targeted independently.

entries.question: Avalyn has no cards in their library and controls a [Keranos, God of Storms]. What happens at the beginning of their draw step?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: no card is drawn so Keranos' abilities don't trigger and Avalyn loses before the next time a player would receive priority.
entries.answer:
Avalyn loses the game. At the beginning of their draw step Avalyn is required to draw a card from an empty library; they draw the remaining cards (here, none) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority [104.3c]. Concretely, the attempted draw from an empty library is recorded, and when state-based actions are next checked — immediately before any player gets priority in that draw step — Avalyn loses [704.5b].

Keranos, God of Storms does not save them and does not trigger. Keranos, God of Storms says "Reveal the first card you draw on each of your turns," and its triggered abilities key off revealing a land or nonland card drawn this way. Since no card is actually drawn, there is nothing to reveal, so the trigger event never occurs and neither ability triggers — an ability triggers only if its trigger event actually happens [603.2g]. In particular, the land-reveal trigger that would "draw a card" [Keranos, God of Storms ruling #1] never happens, so it can't refill anything, and the nonland-reveal trigger dealing 3 damage to any target also never happens.

Note that Keranos, God of Storms' abilities function on the battlefield whether or not devotion to blue and red is seven or more [Keranos, God of Storms ruling #2], so devotion is irrelevant here — the ability simply has no trigger event.

Two players vs. more: the rules provided say only that the player who attempted the draw loses [704.5b], so in a two-player game the opponent wins by default, and at a multiplayer table only Avalyn leaves the game while the others play on. The context provided doesn't include the specific multiplayer rules for a player leaving the game, so treat that last point as the general application of 704.5b rather than a detailed multiplayer ruling.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Avalyn can't draw a card, so no card is revealed and neither trigger triggers. Avalyn loses the game before they would next get priority.

entries.question: Abdullah casts [Telemin Performance] targeting Nico. In response, Nico casts [Veil of Summer]. Abdullah responds with their own Veil of Summer. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Abdullah's Veil resolves first, then Nico's, and Telemin Performance fails to resolve because its target is illegal (Nico has hexproof).
entries.answer:
Telemin Performance fizzles. Nico ends up safe, both players get their Veil of Summer effects, and Telemin Performance is removed from the stack and put into Abdullah's graveyard without doing anything.

How it plays out, top down (the stack resolves last-in, first-out; each spell cast in response to another resolves first) [117.7, 405.2, 405.5, 608.1]:

1. **Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves first.** Abdullah draws a card only if an *opponent* cast a blue or black spell this turn. Abdullah's own Telemin Performance doesn't count, and Nico's Veil of Summer is green, so in a two-player game Abdullah draws nothing (unless Nico cast some other blue or black spell earlier this turn). Abdullah's spells can't be countered this turn, and Abdullah and Abdullah's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black. None of this protects Telemin Performance's target — Abdullah's Veil of Summer only grants hexproof to Abdullah and Abdullah's own permanents, and Veil of Summer does not counter anything (Nico's Veil of Summer is unaffected and stays on the stack) [Veil of Summer].

2. **Nico's Veil of Summer resolves next.** Nico draws a card, because an opponent (Abdullah) cast a blue spell this turn — Telemin Performance is blue. Nico and Nico's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn, meaning Nico can't be the target of blue or black spells or abilities Nico's opponents control [Veil of Summer, 702.11d]. Note that rule 702.11d is written for permanents; Veil of Summer's own text explicitly extends the protection to the player as well, and card text wins over the general framing.

3. **Telemin Performance tries to resolve last, and doesn't.** On resolution the game rechecks targets. Nico, its only target, now has hexproof from blue, and Telemin Performance is a blue spell controlled by Nico's opponent, so Nico is an illegal target. Since every instance of "target" is illegal, Telemin Performance doesn't resolve; it's removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard [608.2b]. Nico reveals nothing, mills nothing, and Abdullah steals no creature. This is not a counter, so Abdullah's "spells you control can't be countered" from their own Veil of Summer doesn't save it [Veil of Summer].

Assumed timing: Telemin Performance is a sorcery, so it was cast in Abdullah's main phase with an empty stack, then Nico's Veil of Summer, then Abdullah's Veil of Summer on top. If instead Abdullah's Veil of Summer had somehow resolved before Nico's was cast, nothing changes for Telemin Performance — Nico's hexproof from blue still applies before Telemin Performance resolves.

Multiplayer difference: with more than two players, the only change is the card draws. Abdullah would draw a card if *any* opponent (not just Nico) had cast a blue or black spell this turn. Nico still draws off Telemin Performance being blue, and Telemin Performance still fizzles because it targeted Nico specifically.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves first. Then Nico's resolves and draws them a card. Then Telemin Performance tries to resolve and fails, since it has an illegal target.

(Abdullah's Veil of Summer didn't accomplish anything useful.)

entries.question: Athena controls [Teferi, Time Raveler] and Nicholas flashes in [The Wandering Emperor] on Athena's turn. Can Nicholas activate its abilities this turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Nicholas cannot cast The Wandering Emperor on Athena's turn due to Teferi, Time Raveler's restriction.
entries.answer:
Nicholas can't flash in The Wandering Emperor at all while Athena controls Teferi, Time Raveler — so the scenario as described can't legally happen. Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability says "Each opponent can cast spells only any time they could cast a sorcery," and that restriction beats the permission granted by flash. Flash is a static ability meaning "You may play this card any time you could cast an instant" [702.8a], but when one effect grants permission and another says it can't happen, the restrictive effect wins [101.2]; the Teferi, Time Raveler ruling confirms this even against another flash-granting effect. So Nicholas may only cast The Wandering Emperor during his own main phase with an empty stack, when he has priority [117.1a].

If The Wandering Emperor got onto the battlefield during Athena's turn some other way (an effect that puts her onto the battlefield rather than casting her — Teferi, Time Raveler only restricts casting spells, not activating abilities): then yes, Nicholas could activate one of her loyalty abilities during Athena's turn. Her own text reads "As long as The Wandering Emperor entered this turn, you may activate her loyalty abilities any time you could cast an instant," which overrides the normal sorcery-speed timing for loyalty abilities. Per The Wandering Emperor's ruling, he still gets only one loyalty activation that turn.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading "flashes in" as Nicholas trying to cast The Wandering Emperor for her mana cost {2}{W}{W} using flash during Athena's turn. If instead she was already on the battlefield from a previous turn, Teferi, Time Raveler is irrelevant to her abilities, but she also wouldn't have "entered this turn," so Nicholas would be limited to activating a loyalty ability at sorcery speed on his own turn.

Multiplayer: no difference. Teferi, Time Raveler's restriction applies to "each opponent," so it locks down every opponent at the table the same way it locks down Nicholas in a two-player game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nicholas cannot cast The Wandering Emperor on Athena's turn due to Teferi, Time Raveler's effect.

entries.question: In a Two-Headed Giant game, how much life does each team begin the game with?
entries.reason: The candidate states each team starts with 30 life, which matches the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
Each team begins a Two-Headed Giant game with 30 life. That total is a shared team life total, not 20 per player: the team's life total starts at 30 and both teammates draw from and contribute to that single number [810.4]. This is an explicit exception to the normal starting life total of 20 that each player has in a regular game [103.4a].

Because Two-Headed Giant is itself a multiplayer variant (two teams of two players), the "per team" framing is the whole point here — there is no per-player life total to track. The same 30-life figure applies regardless of how many teams are seated at the table.

entries.question: Aldo casts [Lumithread Field] for its morph cost. If Nico wants to counter it with [Spell Burst], what is the mana value of the Lumithread Field on the stack?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that a face-down morph spell has no mana cost and therefore a mana value of 0, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
The face-down Lumithread Field on the stack has mana value 0, so Nico must cast Spell Burst with X=0 — paying just {U} (plus {3} more if Nico wants buyback).

Why: casting a card using its morph ability turns it face down and it becomes a 2/2 face-down creature spell with no text, no name, no subtypes, and **no mana cost**; those are its copiable characteristics while face down [702.37a] [702.37c] [708.2a]. The mana value of an object with no mana cost is 0 [202.3a]. Aldo pays {3} to cast it that way, but that's an alternative cost being paid — it is not the spell's mana cost and does not set its mana value, so the mana value is 0, not 3 (and not 2, which is the mana value of the face-up {1}{W} Lumithread Field). The {1}{W} printed as Lumithread Field's morph cost is what Aldo would pay later to turn it face up; it likewise has no effect on the face-down spell's mana value.

So Spell Burst's instruction "Counter target spell with mana value X" is satisfied only with X=0. Per the Spell Burst ruling, the value chosen for X determines Spell Burst's own mana value, so Spell Burst on the stack will have mana value 0 as well (relevant if someone else wants to counter it with another Spell Burst). Total cost for Nico: {U}, or {3}{U} with buyback — the {U} is a colored symbol and is never reduced or replaced by the X choice.

One timing note: this holds only while Lumithread Field is still a face-down spell on the stack. If Aldo's spell had already resolved and the permanent were turned face up, the object would have its printed {1}{W} mana cost and mana value 2 — but a permanent isn't a spell and can't be targeted by Spell Burst at all.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. A morphed spell is a 2/2 creature with no mana cost. Since the spell has no mana cost, its mana value is 0.

entries.question: Alexis would like to choose colorless for [Regicide]. Can they?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Alexis cannot choose colorless because colorless is not one of the five colors and thus isn't a legal choice for Regicide's draft ability.
entries.answer:
No. When Regicide's draft ability asks each of the three players to choose a color, "colorless" isn't a legal choice — a player asked to choose a color must pick one of the five colors: white, blue, black, red, or green [105.4]. "Multicolored" is likewise not a color [105.4], and there are exactly five colors in the game [105.1].

So Alexis must name one of white, blue, black, red, or green when Regicide is drafted, and the three colors chosen (by the player to Alexis's right, by Alexis, and by the player to Alexis's left) must all be different from one another [Regicide ruling #6].

A related point that may be what's behind the question: even if Alexis could somehow have "colorless" in the mix, it wouldn't help — Regicide can't target colorless creatures [Regicide ruling #1]. A colorless object simply has no color [105.2c], so it can never be "one or more of the colors chosen." Conversely, Regicide's target may have extra colors beyond those chosen, as long as it's at least one of the chosen colors [Regicide ruling #3].

On player count: Regicide's draft ability inherently references the players to your right and left at the draft table, so it assumes a draft pod rather than a two-player game; regardless of how many players are seated, the restriction to the five colors is the same for each chooser.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Colorless is not a color.

entries.question: Alfonso controls [Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass] equipped with [Glaive of the Guildpact] and no Gates. Does it have vigilance and menace?
entries.reason: Both conclude the Glaive's static ability unconditionally grants vigilance and menace while only the +1/+0 depends on the number of Gates, so the candidate reaches the same ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes. Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass has both vigilance and menace, even though Alfonso controls no Gates. Its power and toughness remain 5/2, since the +1/+0 "for each Gate you control" adds +0/+0 with zero Gates.

Why: Glaive of the Guildpact's static ability reads "Equipped creature gets +1/+0 for each Gate you control and has vigilance and menace." That's one static ability that is simply true while Glaive of the Guildpact is attached, with no condition on controlling Gates for the keyword-granting part [604.1]. The Glaive of the Guildpact ruling states this explicitly: the equipped creature has vigilance and menace even if you control no Gates [Glaive of the Guildpact ruling #1].

The two parts of that ability are applied in different layers, which is why they don't depend on each other: granting vigilance and menace happens in layer 6 (ability-adding effects) [613.1f], while the +1/+0 per Gate is a power/toughness modification applied in layer 7c [613.4c]. With zero Gates the layer 7c modification is +0/+0, so Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass stays 5/2 — but the layer 6 grant is unaffected by that count.

Practical upshot: Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass can attack without tapping (vigilance) and can't be blocked except by two or more creatures (menace).

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since nothing here references opponents or a defending player choice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The only thing that Gates affect is how much Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass's power is increased.

entries.question: Ainsley casts [Tandem Takedown], granting their two [Devoted Hero] +1/+0. Can each Devoted Hero deal damage to a different one of Nolan's creatures?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude "No" and state Tandem Takedown specifies a single damage target (one "another target"), so both Devoted Heroes must deal their damage to that same single permanent.
entries.answer:
No. Tandem Takedown has only one damage target, so both Devoted Hero must deal their damage to the same single creature, planeswalker, or battle — you can't split them between two of Nolan's creatures.

Why: Tandem Takedown reads "Up to two target creatures you control each get +1/+0 until end of turn. They each deal damage equal to their power to another target creature, planeswalker, or battle." The word "target" appears twice: once for "up to two target creatures you control" (that instance lets you pick both Devoted Hero, since it asks for two different legal targets and the same object can't be chosen twice for one instance of "target"), and once for the singular "another target creature, planeswalker, or battle." That second instance defines exactly one object, so there is no second damage recipient to choose [115.3] [601.2c]. Targets are locked in as the spell is cast, and the number of targets doesn't change afterward [601.2c].

Result on resolution: each Devoted Hero becomes 2/2 (1/2 plus +1/+0), and each deals 2 damage to that one chosen permanent, for 4 damage total to it. Note that the damage target must be "another" permanent — it can't be either of the two Devoted Hero you targeted with the first part.

If, as Tandem Takedown resolves, that single damage target has become illegal, nothing deals or is dealt damage [Tandem Takedown ruling #1]. If instead one Devoted Hero has become an illegal target, the other still gets +1/+0 and deals damage equal to its power [Tandem Takedown ruling #2].

This works identically whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — Tandem Takedown's damage target isn't limited to a single opponent's permanents, but it's still just one target, so you can't spread it across creatures controlled by two different opponents either.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Tandem Takedown specifies that they each deal damage to another target creature, meaning one single other creature.

entries.question: Aaden has 3 [Witch's Familiar] in their graveyard and casts [Izoni, Thousand-Eyed]. After it enters the battlefield but before its trigger resolves, Nyla activates [Sentinel Totem] to exile all cards from Aaden's graveyard. When Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's ability resolves, how many tokens will be created?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion (zero tokens) because Izoni's undergrowth ability counts creature cards in the graveyard when it resolves and Sentinel Totem emptied Aaden's graveyard before that resolution.
entries.answer:
Zero tokens.

Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's undergrowth trigger counts the creature cards in Aaden's graveyard only once, at the moment the ability actually resolves and its effect is applied — not when Izoni, Thousand-Eyed entered the battlefield and not when the trigger went on the stack [608.2h]. Because Nyla's Sentinel Totem ability resolved first and exiled all graveyards, Aaden's graveyard contains zero creature cards when the undergrowth trigger resolves, so it creates no Insect tokens. The three Witch's Familiar cards are in exile, a different zone, and no longer count.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as Nyla activating and resolving Sentinel Totem's {T}, Exile this artifact ability while Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's trigger is still on the stack. If instead the undergrowth trigger had already resolved before Sentinel Totem's ability resolved, Aaden would have gotten 3 Insect tokens (one per Witch's Familiar), and exiling the graveyard afterward would not remove them.

What Aaden can still do: after Sentinel Totem's ability resolves but before the undergrowth trigger resolves, Aaden can activate Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's {B}{G}, Sacrifice another creature ability in response; that is explicitly allowed and each sacrifice that puts a creature *card* into the graveyard raises the token count [Izoni, Thousand-Eyed ruling #2]. Sacrificing creature tokens won't help, since tokens cease to exist and never count for undergrowth [Izoni, Thousand-Eyed ruling #3].

Player count doesn't change this. Sentinel Totem exiles all graveyards, so whether the table is two players or more, Aaden's graveyard is empty when the undergrowth ability is applied.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. The number of tokens to create is determined when the ability resolves, by which point the graveyard has no creatures in it.

entries.question: Atlas casts [Piracy] and would like to tap all of Nicole's lands but not cast any spells. Can Atlas do this?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Piracy only restricts how that mana can be spent and does not force spending it, so Atlas can tap Nicole’s lands and leave the mana unused.
entries.answer:
Yes. Piracy lets Atlas tap lands Atlas doesn't control for mana, and nothing in Piracy or the mana rules forces Atlas to actually spend that mana. Atlas can tap every one of Nicole's lands and simply let the mana sit unused.

Why:

- Piracy reads "Until end of turn, you may tap lands you don't control for mana. Spend this mana only to cast spells." That second sentence is a spending *restriction*, not a requirement to spend. Rule [106.6] describes exactly this kind of effect: some effects that produce mana restrict how that mana can be spent. A restriction limits what the mana may legally pay for; it never obligates the player to find something to pay for.
- The mana Atlas produces from Nicole's lands goes into Atlas's mana pool, where it can be spent immediately or stay there as unspent mana ([106.4]). Since Atlas casts nothing, it stays unspent.
- Atlas's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and Atlas is said to lose that mana ([106.4]). There is no penalty stated in the provided rules for losing unspent mana.

So the practical effect is that Nicole's lands are tapped (and unavailable to her until they untap), and Atlas gains nothing but the tapping. Note that the mana can only be spent to cast spells — not, for example, to activate abilities — but again, Atlas isn't required to spend it at all.

Timing note: Atlas must do the tapping while Piracy's effect is still active, i.e., during this turn, and at a time Atlas has priority (or while casting a spell/activating an ability). Tapping all of Nicole's lands at, say, the end step still works; the mana simply drains when that step ends.

Multiplayer: Piracy says "lands you don't control," so with more than two players Atlas may tap any opponent's lands, not just Nicole's — the answer above is otherwise identical. The rules provided here contain no multiplayer-specific text, so nothing changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game for this interaction.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Piracy creates a restriction on what Atlas must spend the mana on, but does not prevent them from not spending the mana.

entries.question: Annie controls [Heliod, Sun-Crowned] and casts [Essence Feed]. Can they choose to put Heliod, Sun-Crowned's +1/+1 counter on one of the tokens created by Essence Feed?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Heliod's triggered ability goes on the stack after Essence Feed finishes resolving (so the tokens exist) and thus can target one of those tokens.
entries.answer:
Yes. Annie may put the +1/+1 counter on one of the Eldrazi Spawn tokens Essence Feed creates.

Why: Heliod, Sun-Crowned's ability ("Whenever you gain life, put a +1/+1 counter on target creature or enchantment you control") triggers the moment Annie gains the 3 life, but a triggered ability isn't put onto the stack at that instant. It waits and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3], and state-based actions/triggers are handled right before that priority is granted [117.5]. No player gets priority in the middle of Essence Feed resolving — Annie follows the spell's instructions in the order written (target player loses 3 life; Annie gains 3 life and creates the three 0/1 colorless Eldrazi Spawn tokens) and only then does the spell finish [608.2c].

Since targets for a triggered ability are chosen as the ability is put on the stack [115.1d, 603.3d], by that time the three Eldrazi Spawn tokens are already on the battlefield under Annie's control, so each of them is a legal "target creature or enchantment you control." Annie could also choose Heliod, Sun-Crowned itself (Heliod, Sun-Crowned can be the target of its own triggered ability) or any other creature or enchantment they control.

A couple of notes: the 3 life from Essence Feed is a single life-gaining event, so Heliod, Sun-Crowned's ability triggers only once — one counter, one target. And in a game with more than two players, the only difference is that Annie picks which player Essence Feed's "target player loses 3 life" hits; the life gain, the tokens, and the targeting of Heliod, Sun-Crowned's trigger work exactly the same.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Annie creates the tokens, then gains life as part of the resolution of Essence Feed. After Essence Feed has resolved, Heliod, Sun-Crowned's trigger will be put on the stack. At that point Annie can choose a token as their target.

entries.question: Aleah casts [Clash of Titans], can Aleah choose Nixon's [Storm Crow] for both targets?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: "another" prevents the same creature from being chosen for both targets.
entries.answer:
No. Aleah must choose two different creatures; Nixon's Storm Crow can only be one of the two targets of Clash of Titans.

Why: Clash of Titans reads "Target creature fights another target creature." It does use the word "target" twice, and rules 115.3 and 601.2c say that when a spell uses "target" in multiple places the same object may be chosen once for each instance  or the targeting criteria are met. That last part is the catch here: the second instance's targeting criteria is "another target creature," and "another" means a creature other than the one already chosen for the first instance. Nixon's Storm Crow therefore doesn't fit the criteria for the second target if it was already chosen as the first, so the choice is illegal and Aleah would have to pick a different legal creature (or the spell can't be cast at all if Nixon's Storm Crow is the only creature on the battlefield).

What Aleah can do: per the Clash of Titans ruling, both targets may be creatures controlled by the same player, so Aleah may have Nixon's Storm Crow fight a second creature Nixon controls. On resolution each deals damage equal to its power to the other (Nixon's Storm Crow deals 1 and has 2 toughness), and per the other Clash of Titans ruling, if either target is illegal as Clash of Titans tries to resolve, neither creature deals or is dealt damage (608.2c covers following the spell's instructions on resolution).

This answer is the same at a two-player table and in multiplayer \u2014 the "another" restriction is about the objects chosen, not about who controls them.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The word "another" here retains its normal English meaning, and means that both targets cannot be the same creature.

entries.question: Alejandro controls [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider] and two [Blight Mamba]s. If Alejandro deals combat damage with both Blight Mambas, how many poison counters will Nico get?

entries.answer:
Nico gets 4 poison counters.

Why: each Blight Mamba is a 1/1 with infect. Damage dealt to a player by a source with infect doesn't cause life loss; instead it causes that source's controller to give the player that many poison counters [120.3b] [702.90b]. So each Blight Mamba's 1 combat damage would have Alejandro give Nico 1 poison counter.

Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider's first ability then applies: if Alejandro would put one or more counters on a permanent or player, he puts twice that many instead. Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider cares about who is putting the counters, not who receives them [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider ruling #2], and it's Alejandro (the controller of each Blight Mamba) who is putting the poison counters on Nico. Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider's halving ability doesn't apply, since Nico isn't the one putting the counters on. So each Blight Mamba's 1 poison counter becomes 2, for 4 total. (Whether you treat the two Blight Mambas as one combined event or two separate ones, the math is the same: 2 doubled to 4, or 1 doubled to 2 twice.)

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both Blight Mambas actually connected with Nico in the combat damage step (unblocked or otherwise dealing their damage to Nico) and that Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider was already on the battlefield when that damage was dealt. If Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider weren't on the battlefield at the moment the counters are given, Nico would get only 2. Also, if either Blight Mamba's damage were prevented, that Blight Mamba would give no poison counters at all [Blight Mamba ruling #1].

Relevance: a player with ten or more poison counters loses the game as a state-based action [Blight Mamba ruling #4], so this is 4 of the 10 Nico needs.

Multiplayer note: nothing changes in a game with more than two players — only the player who was dealt the combat damage (Nico) receives the poison counters, and each Blight Mamba would need to have dealt its damage to Nico specifically for the full 4.

entries.answer_gold: Two damage will be dealt to Nico and they will get four poison counters. ([702.164c], [702.90b])

entries.question: Andre casts [Abrupt Decay] targeting Nico's 5/5 Horse creature token, then responds by targeting it with [Arcane Denial]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Arcane Denial can't counter Abrupt Decay (Decay still resolves and destroys the token) and Arcane Denial's delayed draw effects still occur on the next upkeep.
entries.answer:
Abrupt Decay is not countered — it resolves and destroys the 5/5 Horse token — but Arcane Denial's other effects still happen (the card draws at the next upkeep).

Step by step:

1. **Abrupt Decay is a legal target for Arcane Denial.** Abrupt Decay's "This spell can't be countered" is an ability that functions while it's on the stack [113.6g], but it doesn't stop a counterspell from targeting it. Arcane Denial can legally target it [Abrupt Decay ruling #2].

2. **Arcane Denial resolves first** (it was cast in response, so it's on top of the stack). Its "Counter target spell" instruction simply doesn't happen: when an effect says something happens and another effect says it can't, the "can't" wins [101.2], and the impossible part of the instruction is ignored while the rest of the spell does as much as it can [101.3, 609.3, Abrupt Decay ruling #2].

3. **The rest of Arcane Denial still applies.** It sets up delayed triggered abilities for the beginning of the next turn's upkeep [603.7a]: the controller of the targeted spell (Andre, who cast Abrupt Decay) may draw up to two cards, and the controller of Arcane Denial draws a card. Andre chooses 0, 1, or 2 when that ability resolves, not before [Arcane Denial ruling #1]. If Nico cast Arcane Denial, Nico gets the one-card draw and Andre gets the up-to-two draw; if Andre cast Arcane Denial himself, both triggers belong to Andre (one card plus up to two).

4. **Abrupt Decay then resolves** and destroys the Horse token. A token that isn't a copy of another object has mana value 0 [Abrupt Decay ruling #1], so despite being a 5/5 the Horse is a nonland permanent with mana value 3 or less and is a legal target. It's destroyed.

Assumption on timing: I read "responds" as Arcane Denial being cast while Abrupt Decay is still on the stack, so Arcane Denial resolves first. If Arcane Denial were somehow cast after Abrupt Decay had already resolved, it would have no legal spell to target at all and couldn't be cast that way — but the outcome for the Horse token is the same either way.

Nothing here depends on the number of players: the effects only involve the two named players, so the result is identical in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table (the upkeep draws simply happen at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep, whoever's turn that is).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Arcane Denial resolves but can't counter Abrupt Decay. During Nico's upkeep, Andre draws one to three cards, based on their choice.

entries.question: Arabella controls [Yixlid Jailer] and casts [Ever After] targeting [Dearly Departed] and [Fugitive Wizard]. Will Fugitive Wizard enter with a +1/+1 counter?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line — Fugitive Wizard does not get a +1/+1 counter — aligning with the reference that Dearly Departed has no graveyard ability (and also correctly notes the simultaneous return issue).
entries.answer:
No — Fugitive Wizard enters with no +1/+1 counter, for two independent reasons.

**1. Yixlid Jailer turns off Dearly Departed's graveyard ability.** Dearly Departed's ability is one that states the zone it functions in ("As long as this creature is in your graveyard..."), so it's an ability that would normally work from the graveyard rather than the battlefield [113.6b]. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," an ability-removing continuous effect applied in layer 6 [113.10, 613.1f]. While Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield, Dearly Departed in Arabella's graveyard simply has no abilities at all, so there is nothing to give Fugitive Wizard an extra counter.

**2. Even without Yixlid Jailer, Dearly Departed isn't in the graveyard at the relevant moment.** Ever After returns both target creature cards to the battlefield simultaneously as it resolves. So at the instant Fugitive Wizard enters, Dearly Departed is entering the battlefield too, not sitting in the graveyard, and its "as long as this creature is in your graveyard" condition isn't met.

A couple of side notes: Ever After makes Fugitive Wizard a black Zombie *in addition to* its other colors and types, so it's still a Human Wizard — the Human requirement of Dearly Departed's ability would have been satisfied; the problem is purely that the ability isn't active. And Ever After goes on the bottom of its owner's library rather than to the graveyard, which doesn't change anything here.

If instead Ever After had targeted only Fugitive Wizard and left Dearly Departed in the graveyard, the answer would still be no while Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield — Dearly Departed would have lost its ability. Remove or destroy Yixlid Jailer first, and then a Human creature entering under Arabella's control while Dearly Departed sits in her graveyard would get the counter.

The rules relied on here don't depend on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

entries.answer_gold: No. Dearly Departed has no abilities while in the graveyard.

entries.question: Nicholas controls [Solitary Confinement]. Addilyn attacks with [Ranger of Eos] and casts [Skullcrack] targeting themselves. Does Nicholas lose life?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Skullcrack's "damage can't be prevented" overrides Solitary Confinement so Nicholas will lose life (assuming Skullcrack resolves before the damage is dealt).
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Skullcrack resolves before combat damage is dealt, Nicholas takes Ranger of Eos's 3 combat damage and loses 3 life. Solitary Confinement's "Prevent all damage that would be dealt to you" still tries to apply, but Skullcrack's "Damage can't be prevented this turn" overrides it, so nothing is actually prevented [615.12] [101.2] [Skullcrack ruling #2].

Why:

- Skullcrack's second sentence is a global, non-targeted effect: it shuts off damage prevention for the whole turn for everyone, not just for the player it targets. That's why Addilyn can target themselves with the damage portion and still turn off Nicholas's protection — Solitary Confinement gives Nicholas shroud, so Nicholas can't be the target of Skullcrack, but Skullcrack doesn't need to target Nicholas to strip prevention.
- A "can't" effect beats an effect that allows or directs something to happen [101.2]. Solitary Confinement says damage is prevented; Skullcrack says damage can't be prevented. Skullcrack wins.
- Solitary Confinement's prevention effect isn't countered or removed — it still "applies" to the damage, it just prevents nothing [615.12] [Skullcrack ruling #2]. Solitary Confinement itself remains on the battlefield.
- So Ranger of Eos's 3 combat damage (it's a 3/2) is dealt to Nicholas in full if it's unblocked, and damage dealt to a player reduces that player's life total. (The provided rules don't include the numbered rule stating that damage causes life loss, but nothing in the provided material stops it here.) Note also that Skullcrack's own 3 damage goes to Addilyn, who chose to be the target — Nicholas takes nothing from that part.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Skullcrack resolved before the combat damage step (for example, cast in the declare blockers step). If instead Skullcrack resolved after combat damage was already dealt, that earlier damage would already have been prevented by Solitary Confinement and Nicholas would have lost no life from Ranger of Eos; Skullcrack would only affect damage dealt for the remainder of the turn.

Player count: the rules provided here aren't specific to two players, and nothing changes with more players — except that in a multiplayer game Ranger of Eos must actually be attacking Nicholas (or a planeswalker/battle Nicholas controls) for Nicholas to be dealt that combat damage, and Skullcrack's prevention shutoff applies to everyone at the table for the turn.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Skullcrack says that damage can't be prevented, so Solitary Confinement doesn't prevent it.

entries.question: Armani casts [Hangarback Walker] with X = 3. Can Neriah counter it with [Thoughtbind]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that with X=3 Hangarback Walker has mana value 6 on the stack, so Thoughtbind (which targets spells with mana value 4 or less) cannot target it.
entries.answer:
No. With X = 3, Hangarback Walker's mana value on the stack is 6, which is more than 4, so Thoughtbind can't legally target it.

Why: Hangarback Walker's mana cost is {X}{X}, and both X's must be the same number [Hangarback Walker ruling #2]. Armani announces X = 3 as part of casting the spell, and while the spell is on the stack each {X} equals that announced value [107.3a]. Mana value is the total amount of mana in the mana cost regardless of color [202.3], and for an object with {X} in its mana cost, X counts as the chosen number while the object is on the stack [202.3e]. So on the stack Hangarback Walker costs {3}{3} = {6} generic, giving a mana value of 6. (Note that in any other zone -- hand, graveyard, battlefield -- X is treated as 0, so Hangarback Walker's mana value there is 0 [202.3e]; that doesn't help Neriah, because Thoughtbind checks the spell while it's on the stack.)

Thoughtbind reads "Counter target spell with mana value 4 or less," so Hangarback Walker at mana value 6 is not a legal target and Neriah simply can't cast Thoughtbind targeting it. Neriah could only counter Hangarback Walker this way if Armani had chosen X = 0, 1, or 2 (mana values 0, 2, and 4).

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players: mana value and legal targeting work the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The mana value of a spell is determined by adding together the symbols in the upper right corner of the card. The mana value of Hangarback Walker on the stack is 6.

entries.question: Avery casts [Sram's Expertise]. As it resolves, they would like tap the tokens it created to cast [Collective Effort] escalated twice. Can they?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: the Servos exist and can be tapped to pay Collective Effort's escalate additional costs while Sram's Expertise resolves, so the spell can be cast for free with escalates paid.
entries.answer:
Yes. Avery can tap two of the Servo tokens Sram's Expertise just created to pay Collective Effort's escalate cost twice, choosing three modes total, and still cast Collective Effort for free.

Why it works:

1. Order of effects. Sram's Expertise's controller follows its instructions in the order written ([608.2c]), so the three 1/1 Servo tokens are created first, and only then does Avery get the option to cast a spell with mana value 3 or less from hand without paying its mana cost. The Servos are already on the battlefield and untapped when Collective Effort is cast.

2. Casting during resolution. Because Sram's Expertise specifically allows Avery to cast a spell during its resolution, Avery casts Collective Effort by following the normal casting steps (rules 601.2a–i), except that no player gets priority after it's cast; Collective Effort goes on top of the stack above the still-resolving Sram's Expertise ([608.2g]).

3. "Without paying its mana cost" is an alternative cost ([118.9d]), and Collective Effort's mana cost is {1}{W}{W}, mana value 3, so it's a legal choice. Per the Sram's Expertise ruling, casting a card without paying its mana cost means you can't also use some other alternative cost, but you may still pay additional costs.

4. Escalate is an additional cost, not an alternative one. "Escalate—Tap an untapped creature you control" means "For each mode you choose beyond the first as you cast this spell, you pay an additional [cost]," and it follows the rules for additional costs in 601.2f–h ([702.120a]). Additional costs and cost increases still apply on top of an alternative cost ([118.9d]). Avery announces the modes chosen and the intent to pay the escalate costs as part of announcing Collective Effort ([601.2b]).

5. Summoning sickness doesn't matter. Escalate's cost is "tap an untapped creature you control" — it is not the {T} symbol in an ability of the tokens themselves. Per the Collective Effort ruling, you can tap any untapped creature you control for escalate, including one you haven't controlled continuously since the beginning of the turn, so freshly created Servo tokens are legal.

So Avery taps two Servos, picks three modes on Collective Effort (or two modes with one escalate payment if they prefer), pays no mana at all, and Collective Effort resolves before Sram's Expertise finishes and goes to the graveyard.

Player count doesn't change any of this; the only difference at a multiplayer table is that the third mode ("Put a +1/+1 counter on each creature target player controls") gives Avery more players to choose among as the target.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The instructions of a resolving spell are carried out in the order written, so the tokens will be on the battlefield at that time. Tapping creatures for escalate is an additional cost. ([702.120a]) Avery may still pay an additional cost for Collective Effort while casting it for the alternative cost given to it by Sram's Expertise.

entries.question: Nikolas controls [Mindcrank]. Ari casts [Vampiric Tutor]. Will the card Ari put on top of their library get milled?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Mindcrank triggers during Vampiric Tutor's resolution and will mill the tutored card when that trigger later resolves.
entries.answer:
Yes — the card Ari put on top with Vampiric Tutor gets milled (Ari mills 2 cards: the tutored card and the one beneath it).

Why: Vampiric Tutor's text resolves in the order written — Ari searches, shuffles and puts the chosen card on top, and only then loses 2 life. So by the time the life loss happens, the tutored card is already sitting on top of Ari's library. Nikolas's Mindcrank triggers on "whenever an opponent loses life," and Ari is Nikolas's opponent, so the trigger condition is met during Vampiric Tutor's resolution.

Nothing happens the moment a trigger condition is met [603.2]; triggered abilities can trigger while a spell is resolving, but they wait [117.2a]. Mindcrank's ability is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority — which is after Vampiric Tutor has finished resolving [603.3, 117.5]. When the Mindcrank trigger then resolves, Ari mills 2 cards off the top of their library, and the top card is the tutored card.

A note on timing: this assumes the normal resolution order printed on Vampiric Tutor (shuffle and place on top first, life loss second) — that's the only legal order for a single resolving spell, and the shuffle-and-put-on-top is a single action [Vampiric Tutor ruling #1]. If some other effect caused Ari to lose the 2 life before the card was placed (it can't here), the mill would happen off a different library configuration and the tutored card would be safe.

If Ari wants to keep the card, they'd need a response between Vampiric Tutor's resolution and the Mindcrank trigger's resolution (e.g., drawing the card in that window), since players get priority with the Mindcrank trigger on the stack [117.5].

Multiplayer: the answer is the same. Mindcrank checks life loss by "an opponent" of Nikolas, so it triggers for Ari and for any other opponent of Nikolas who loses life, and each such player mills that many cards; it would not trigger off Nikolas's own life loss.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Mindcrank triggers during the resolution of Vampiric Tutor and will be put onto the stack after Vampiric Tutor finishes resolving. (Ari can cast an instant before the trigger resolves.)

entries.question: Does Nicole have a chance to cast [Surgical Extraction] after Addison has drawn for turn but before they have a chance to cast a sorcery?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — after the draw occurs the draw step grants priority, so Nicole can cast an instant like Surgical Extraction before Addison can cast sorceries.
entries.answer:
Yes. Addison's draw for turn is a turn-based action at the start of the draw step [504.1], and after it happens the active player (Addison) gets priority during the draw step [504.2]. Once Addison passes priority, Nicole receives priority while still in the draw step — before Addison's precombat main phase ever begins — and since Surgical Extraction is an instant she can cast it right there.

A few supporting points:

- The draw step is not one of the no-priority steps. Only the untap step and certain cleanup steps end without any player receiving priority [500.3]; the draw step explicitly grants priority [504.2].
- Addison cannot cast a sorcery during the draw step at all — sorcery timing requires a main phase — so Nicole's window in the draw step is comfortably "after the draw, before any sorcery." Even in Addison's precombat main phase, Addison would have to cast the sorcery and Nicole would then get priority with it on the stack, but the draw-step window comes first.
- To cast Surgical Extraction Nicole pays {B/P}, which is one black mana or 2 life; she chooses which as she casts it, and she can't choose the 2 life if she's at 1 life or less [Surgical Extraction ruling #1, Surgical Extraction ruling #5]. She also needs a legal target: a card in a graveyard that isn't a basic land card.

Multiplayer note: the same is true with more than two players, but priority passes in turn order, so any players seated between Addison and Nicole get priority (and could respond) before Nicole does. The specific turn-order priority rule (rule 117) wasn't included in the context provided here, so treat that ordering detail as a general expectation rather than something quoted; the guarantee that Nicole eventually gets a draw-step window follows from [504.2] and [500.3].

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Players receive priority in the draw step after a card has been drawn.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Frogtosser Banneret]. Will it affect the cost of [Knowledge Exploitation]?

Yes. Knowledge Exploitation is a Kindred Sorcery — Rogue, so it's a Rogue spell, and Frogtosser Banneret reduces its total cost by {1}.

Why: kindred is a card type that lets a noncreature card have creature types (its subtypes are drawn from the same list as creature subtypes) [308.1] [308.2]. Knowledge Exploitation's type line "Kindred Sorcery — Rogue" therefore makes it a Rogue spell on the stack even though it isn't a creature spell, which is exactly what Frogtosser Banneret's ability keys off of.

Resulting costs (only the generic portion shrinks; the colored symbols are untouched):
- Normal cost {5}{U}{U} becomes {4}{U}{U}.
- Prowl cost {3}{U} becomes {2}{U}. Frogtosser Banneret reduces the total cost regardless of whether you paid an alternative cost such as prowl [Frogtosser Banneret ruling #2].

Note that Knowledge Exploitation is only a Rogue, not also a Goblin, so it gets the single {1} reduction, not {2} [Frogtosser Banneret ruling #1].

One caution about the free spell: when Knowledge Exploitation resolves and you cast the found instant or sorcery from the opponent's library without paying its mana cost, Frogtosser Banneret's reduction is irrelevant there unless that card is itself a Goblin or Rogue spell — and even then you're paying no mana cost, so there's nothing to reduce [Knowledge Exploitation ruling #2].

entries.question: Amir casts [Archon of Cruelty], and before it resolves Norah casts [Surge of Salvation]. What happens when the Archon resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Archon enters the battlefield but its ETB trigger has no legal target due to Surge of Salvation (hexproof) and therefore does nothing, so Amir doesn't draw or gain life.
entries.answer:
Archon of Cruelty still resolves and enters the battlefield as a 6/6 flier — Surge of Salvation doesn't counter it. What changes is the enters-the-battlefield trigger: if Norah is Amir's only opponent, that trigger has no legal target and is simply removed from the stack, so nobody sacrifices, discards, or loses life, and Amir draws no card and gains no life.

Why: Surge of Salvation gives Norah (the player) and her permanents hexproof until end of turn. Hexproof on a player means "You can't be the target of spells or abilities your opponents control" [702.11c]. I'm assuming Surge of Salvation resolved while Archon of Cruelty was still on the stack, which is the normal outcome when it's cast in response.

Archon of Cruelty's triggered ability says "target opponent sacrifices a creature or planeswalker of their choice, discards a card, and loses 3 life. You draw a card and gain 3 life." It triggers when Archon of Cruelty enters, and its target is chosen when the ability is put on the stack, using the same targeting process as casting a spell [603.3d, 601.2c]. Amir controls that ability, so Norah — an opponent of Amir with hexproof — can't be chosen [702.11c]. If no legal target can be chosen, the ability is removed from the stack and none of it happens, including the "You draw a card and gain 3 life" part, since the whole ability does nothing [603.3d]. All of the ability's actions are a single package taken in the listed order, so removing the ability removes all of them [Archon of Cruelty ruling #1].

Two players vs. multiplayer: with only Amir and Norah, the trigger fizzles off the stack as described. At a bigger table, Amir simply targets some other opponent who doesn't have hexproof, and that opponent sacrifices a creature or planeswalker of their choice, discards, and loses 3 life while Amir draws and gains 3 life. Only if every opponent is untargetable does the trigger get removed [603.3d, 702.11c].

Also note for the rest of the turn: Surge of Salvation prevents all damage black and/or red sources would deal to creatures Norah controls this turn, and Archon of Cruelty is black — so if it attacks or fights Norah's creatures later this turn, that damage to her creatures is prevented (damage to Norah herself is not prevented). Its "or attacks" trigger would also need a legal target while Norah has hexproof.

If instead the timing were reversed — Surge of Salvation somehow resolving only after Amir had already put the trigger on the stack with Norah as its target — the trigger would already have a target, but Norah would then be an illegal target on resolution and the ability would do nothing anyway.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Archon of Cruelty's ability triggers but is not placed onto the stack, since there are no legal targets for it. Amir will not draw a card or gain life.

entries.question: Adelynn controls [Clockwork Beast] which has one +1/+0 counter on it. They want to activate its ability with X = 8. Can they?

entries.answer:
Yes — Adelynn can activate Clockwork Beast's ability with X = 8, but it will only ever add six counters.

Why the activation is legal: X is a placeholder whose value the controller chooses and announces as part of activating the ability, and nothing on Clockwork Beast caps the value of X itself [107.3a][601.2b]. So Adelynn announces X = 8, pays the activation cost of {8} (eight generic mana, payable with any colors and/or colorless) and {T} (tapping Clockwork Beast), during their own upkeep as the ability requires.

What happens on resolution: the ability says "Put up to X +1/+0 counters on this creature. This ability can't cause the total number of +1/+0 counters on this creature to be greater than seven." Clockwork Beast has one +1/+0 counter, so at most six more can go on. Adelynn chooses a number from 0 up to X when the ability resolves [608.2d][Clockwork Beast ruling #5]; if they choose 8, the "can't" clause on the card overrides the "put" instruction and only six counters are placed, bringing the total to seven [101.2][609.3][Clockwork Beast ruling #4]. Note this is Clockwork Beast's own printed restriction doing the work — it limits only this ability, so other spells or abilities could still push it above seven +1/+0 counters.

Practical upshot: paying X = 8 wastes 2 mana; X = 6 achieves exactly the same result at the lowest cost.

Number of players doesn't matter here — this is entirely a choice by Clockwork Beast's controller during their own upkeep, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

entries.question: Naomi has 7 life and controls two [Death's Shadow]s. Angelo uses [Ajani Unyielding] to exile one of the Death's Shadows. What happens next?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Naomi gains 6 life from the exiled Death's Shadow and then the remaining Death's Shadow is put into her graveyard by state-based actions.
entries.answer:
Naomi gains 6 life (going to 13), and then her other Death's Shadow is put into her graveyard as a state-based action.

Step by step:

1. Before the ability resolves, Naomi is at 7 life, so each Death's Shadow gets -7/-7 and is a 6/6 (13/13 base, minus her life total) [Death's Shadow].
2. Ajani Unyielding's −2 ability exiles one Death's Shadow, then its controller gains life equal to its power. Even though a Death's Shadow that isn't on the battlefield is 13/13 [Death's Shadow ruling #2], the life gained uses the power of the creature as it last existed on the battlefield [Ajani Unyielding ruling #1], i.e. 6. This matches the last-known-information rule for objects that have left the public zone the effect expected them in [608.2h]. So Naomi — the exiled Death's Shadow's controller, not Angelo — gains 6 life and goes to 13.
3. The value of X for the surviving Death's Shadow isn't locked in; it tracks Naomi's current life total [Death's Shadow ruling #4]. At 13 life, that Death's Shadow gets -13/-13 and becomes 0/0.
4. Nothing happens mid-resolution; state-based actions are only checked the next time a player would receive priority, which is after Ajani Unyielding's ability finishes resolving [117.5, 704.3]. At that check, a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard, and regeneration can't save it [704.5f]. Naomi's remaining Death's Shadow dies.

So Angelo effectively kills both: one via exile, one via the life gain.

Player-count note: this plays out identically at two players or in multiplayer, because Ajani Unyielding's −2 gives the life to the exiled creature's controller (Naomi) regardless of who controls Ajani Unyielding or how many opponents there are. The one variant to watch is Two-Headed Giant, where "your life total" is your team's life total for Death's Shadow [Death's Shadow ruling #3]. Also, if Naomi's life total had been negative, X would be treated as 0 [Death's Shadow ruling #1].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Death's Shadow is a 6/6 when it gets exiled, so Naomi gains 6 life. Before Angelo receives priority again, state-based actions are checked, and the game sees that the remaining Death's Shadow now has 0 toughness, and it will be put into Naomi's graveyard.
