entries.answer:
Yes. Aniyah can cast Fierce Guardianship without paying its mana cost, even though the commander she controls is Nico's commander and not her own.

Why: Fierce Guardianship's alternative cost condition is just "If you control a commander." A card's commander designation is an attribute of the card itself, not of the object's characteristics, and an effect referring to controlling a commander means controlling a permanent on the battlefield that is a commander [903.3d]. Nothing in that wording restricts it to your own commander, and the card's rulings confirm it: "It doesn't matter whose commander you control. Any one will do" [Fierce Guardianship ruling #1]. So as long as Nico's commander is a permanent on the battlefield under Aniyah's control when she casts Fierce Guardianship, the alternative cost applies (Fierce Guardianship still counters only a target noncreature spell).

Timing note: the check happens as Aniyah begins casting Fierce Guardianship. Once she starts casting it, no player can respond until she's finished, so opponents can't remove Nico's commander from Aniyah's control in the middle of casting to force her to pay {2}{U} [Fierce Guardianship ruling #2]. If Nico's commander leaves Aniyah's control before she starts casting, she'd have to pay the normal cost of {2}{U} (two generic plus one blue) unless she controls some other commander.

Multiplayer: this works identically at any table size — any commander Aniyah controls, belonging to any player, satisfies the condition; the number of opponents doesn't change the answer.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Fierce Guardianship alternative cost works if Aniyah controls any commander, not necessarily theirs.

entries.question: Nia controls [Hollowhenge Huntmaster]. Anders casts [Flesh Duplicate]. Can they have it enter the battlefield as a copy of Hollowhenge Huntmaster?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference, correctly stating Flesh Duplicate doesn't target and thus can enter as a copy of a hexproof Hollowhenge Huntmaster.
entries.answer:
Yes. Anders can have Flesh Duplicate enter the battlefield as a copy of Hollowhenge Huntmaster, even though Hollowhenge Huntmaster has hexproof.

Why: hexproof on a permanent means only "this permanent can't be the target of spells or abilities your opponents control" [702.11b]. It does nothing against effects that don't use the word "target." Flesh Duplicate's copy ability says "You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield" — it never says "target creature," so Hollowhenge Huntmaster is being affected/looked at, not targeted. Targets are declared as the spell is put on the stack [115.1], and an object isn't a target unless it's identified by the word "target" in the spell or ability's text (or in the rules for a keyword it has) [115.10a]; spells and abilities can freely affect objects they don't target, with those objects generally chosen on resolution [115.10].

Note also that Hollowhenge Huntmaster's static ability "Other permanents you control have hexproof" likewise only stops targeting by Nia's opponents, so it doesn't protect Nia's other permanents from being copied either.

Per Flesh Duplicate's own text, the copy of Hollowhenge Huntmaster will have vanishing 3, since Hollowhenge Huntmaster doesn't have vanishing: it enters with three time counters, loses one at the beginning of each of Anders's upkeeps, and is sacrificed when the last is removed. Anders's copy will be his own 6/6 Hollowhenge Huntmaster with hexproof, granting hexproof to his other permanents.

Player count doesn't matter here: hexproof is defined relative to the controller's opponents [702.11b], and since nothing is targeted in the first place, the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Hexproof prevents Hollowhenge Huntmaster from being the target of an opponent's spell or ability, but Flesh Duplicate doesn't target anything.

entries.question: Ada casts [Shaman of the Pack]. In response to its trigger, Nickolas kills it with [Foolish Fate]. How much life does Nickolas lose?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states the trigger resolves independently and counts Elves on the battlefield at resolution (not the destroyed Shaman), so Nickolas loses 0 life if Shaman was Ada's only Elf.
entries.answer:
Nickolas loses life equal to the number of Elves Ada controls at the moment Shaman of the Pack's triggered ability resolves — and Shaman of the Pack itself is no longer counted, because Foolish Fate already destroyed it and put it in the graveyard. If Shaman of the Pack was the only Elf Ada controlled, Nickolas loses 0 life.

Why: Shaman of the Pack's trigger still resolves even though Shaman of the Pack is gone. Once a triggered ability is on the stack it exists independently of its source, and destroying the source afterward doesn't counter or remove the ability [113.7a]. When the ability resolves, the effect needs information from the game (how many Elves Ada controls), and that count is determined once, at the time the effect is applied [608.2h]. Shaman of the Pack's own ruling says to count the Elves you control as the ability resolves, including Shaman of the Pack only if it's still on the battlefield [Shaman of the Pack ruling #1] — here it isn't, so it doesn't add to the count. Any other Elves Ada controls at that time do count.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nickolas cast Foolish Fate targeting Shaman of the Pack while the trigger was on the stack, so Foolish Fate resolved first and Shaman of the Pack was in the graveyard when the trigger resolved. If instead the trigger had resolved first (for example, Foolish Fate was cast after the trigger already resolved), Shaman of the Pack would still have been on the battlefield and would have counted itself, so Nickolas would lose one more life.

One correction on Foolish Fate: its Infusion clause makes *that creature's controller* lose 3 life, i.e. Ada (the controller of Shaman of the Pack), not Nickolas — and only if Nickolas gained life this turn. Also note that if Shaman of the Pack somehow becomes an illegal target for Foolish Fate before it resolves, Foolish Fate does nothing at all and no player loses life from it [Foolish Fate ruling #1].

On player count: the provided rules don't include any multiplayer-specific rules here. In a game with more than two players, Ada chose which opponent the trigger targeted when it was put on the stack; only that chosen opponent loses life, and the amount is calculated the same way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. When Shaman of the Pack's trigger resolves, Ada controls no Elves.

entries.question: In a Commander game, how much life does each player begin the game with?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states that each player begins a Commander game with 40 life, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
Each player begins a Commander game with 40 life. The general rule is that players start at 20 life, but variant games can set different starting totals, and Commander is such a variant: rule 103.4c states that in a Commander game each player's starting life total is 40. Rule 903.7 confirms this in the Commander rules themselves \player player sets their life total to 40 and draws a hand of seven cards once the starting player has been determined.

This applies to every player at the table regardless of how many players there are \or or multiplayer Commander pods alike, each individual player starts at 40.

entries.question: Amina attacks with [Retaliation]. Nico declares no blocks and then casts [Curtain of Light] targeting Retaliation. Does Retaliation trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes Curtain of Light makes the attacker become blocked by an effect rather than by a creature, so the Retaliation trigger that requires "becomes blocked by a creature" does not trigger.
entries.answer:
No — the Retaliation-granted trigger does not trigger.

Retaliation grants Amina's creatures "Whenever this creature becomes blocked by a creature, this creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn." (Retaliation is an Enchantment and can't attack itself, so I'm reading the question as: Amina attacks with a creature that has this ability from Retaliation, and Nico targets that attacking creature with Curtain of Light.)

Curtain of Light reads "Target unblocked attacking creature becomes blocked." That makes the creature a blocked creature by an effect, with no creature ever declared or put onto the battlefield as a blocker for it. Rule 509.3d spells this case out directly: an ability that reads "Whenever [a creature] becomes blocked by a creature" triggers when a creature is declared as a blocker, when an effect causes a creature to block it (if that creature wasn't already blocking it), or when a creature is put onto the battlefield blocking it — but "It won't trigger if the creature becomes blocked by an effect rather than a creature." Curtain of Light is exactly that last case, so no +1/+1.

The creature is still genuinely blocked for all other purposes: it becomes a blocked creature and stays blocked until it leaves combat, an effect says it becomes unblocked, or the combat phase ends ([Blocked Creature], 509.1h). With no blocking creature to assign damage to, it just deals no combat damage — and per the Curtain of Light rulings, if it had trample all its damage would instead go to the defending player. Note also that Curtain of Light does trigger bushido abilities; the difference is that bushido triggers on becoming blocked at all, whereas the Retaliation ability specifically requires becoming blocked *by a creature*.

Timing assumption: Nico cast Curtain of Light after no blockers were declared for that creature, which is the only legal window ("Cast this spell only during combat after blockers are declared," and its target must be an unblocked attacking creature). If instead some creature had actually blocked the attacker earlier in the declare blockers step, the Retaliation ability would have triggered off that blocker — but then Curtain of Light couldn't target it at all.

Multiplayer note: the outcome is the same at any table size. The provided rules are framed around a single defending player for the attack (509.1h); with more than two players, whichever opponent is the defending player (or any player who can cast Curtain of Light) doesn't change the fact that becoming blocked by an effect never satisfies "blocked by a creature."

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Retaliation became blocked, but not by any creatures.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Rest in Peace] and targets Nataly's [Dauthi Voidwalker] with [Lightning Bolt]. What happens to each card?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling — Ariel chooses which replacement applies for Lightning Bolt (so it’s exiled with or without a void counter) and Dauthi Voidwalker is destroyed by SBAs and exiled by Rest in Peace with no void counter.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Nataly's Dauthi Voidwalker dies to state-based actions and is exiled by Rest in Peace with no void counter on it. Lightning Bolt is also exiled rather than going to Ariel's graveyard — Ariel chooses which replacement effect applies, and if Ariel picks Rest in Peace, Lightning Bolt is exiled with no void counter; if Ariel instead picks Dauthi Voidwalker's ability, Lightning Bolt is exiled with a void counter on it.

Why, step by step (assuming the normal sequence: Lightning Bolt resolves fully, then state-based actions are checked):

1. Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to Dauthi Voidwalker (a 3/2). No state-based actions happen yet — they're only checked when a player would receive priority [117.5] [704.3], and priority isn't given until after Lightning Bolt finishes resolving [117.3b].

2. As the final part of Lightning Bolt's resolution, Lightning Bolt is put into its owner's graveyard [608.2n]. At this instant Dauthi Voidwalker is still on the battlefield, so two replacement effects want to change that event: Rest in Peace ("If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead") and Dauthi Voidwalker's ability ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it with a void counter on it" — Ariel is Nataly's opponent, so Ariel's graveyard qualifies). The affected object is Lightning Bolt, whose controller is Ariel, so Ariel chooses which one to apply [616.1] [616.1e]. Either way Lightning Bolt ends up in exile; applying Rest in Peace means no void counter, applying Dauthi Voidwalker's ability means a void counter. Once one is applied the card is exiled rather than put into a graveyard, so the other no longer has an event to modify. Ariel will normally choose Rest in Peace so Nataly gets no void-counter card.

3. Now a player would get priority, so state-based actions are checked. Dauthi Voidwalker has 3 damage marked and toughness 2, so it is destroyed [704.5g]. "Destroy" means it would be put into its owner's (Nataly's) graveyard. Dauthi Voidwalker's own replacement effect does NOT apply to itself: it only replaces cards headed to an opponent's graveyard, and from Nataly's perspective her own graveyard isn't an opponent's. So only Rest in Peace applies, and the Dauthi Voidwalker card is exiled with no void counter. Because it never reaches a graveyard, nothing that triggers on a creature dying will trigger (Rest in Peace ruling #1, Dauthi Voidwalker ruling #4).

Timing caveat: this all assumes Lightning Bolt's damage kills Dauthi Voidwalker via state-based actions after resolution, which is the only legal order here. Contrast Rest in Peace ruling #3, where a spell that destroys a permanent during its own resolution removes that permanent before the spell hits the graveyard; that's not the case with Lightning Bolt's damage, which is why Dauthi Voidwalker's replacement effect is still available when Lightning Bolt tries to reach Ariel's graveyard. If you instead imagine Dauthi Voidwalker already gone before Lightning Bolt finished resolving, only Rest in Peace would apply and Lightning Bolt would simply be exiled with no choice and no counter.

Multiplayer note: the outcome is the same at a bigger table. Dauthi Voidwalker's ability applies to cards headed to any of Nataly's opponents' graveyards, so it would still be a candidate replacement for Ariel's Lightning Bolt, and the choice still belongs to Lightning Bolt's controller, Ariel [616.1]. If several players had to make such choices at once, they'd do so in APNAP order [616.1].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Ariel chooses whether Lightning Bolt goes to exile with or without a counter.

There are two replacement effects attempting to replace Lightning Bolt going to the graveyard with it going to exile, so its controller gets to choose which to apply.

Then state-based actions are checked and Dauthi Voidwalker is put into exile.

entries.question: Ainsley and Noor are starting a two-player game. Ainsley decides to keep their hand of 7 cards. Noor decides to mulligan. Can Ainsley now decide to mulligan?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Ainsley cannot mulligan after keeping, correctly citing that mulligan declarations lock a player's decision and only remaining mulliganers continue.
entries.answer:
No. Once Ainsley declared they would not take a mulligan, those seven cards became Ainsley's opening hand, and rule [103.5] states that a player who chooses not to take a mulligan "may not take any further mulligans." Seeing that Noor mulliganed doesn't reopen that decision.

How the sequence works under [103.5]: the starting player declares first whether they'll mulligan, then each other player declares in turn order. All players who declared a mulligan then do so simultaneously \into into their library, draw a new hand equal to their starting hand size (normally seven), and put a number of cards equal to the number of mulligans they've taken on the bottom of their library. The process then repeats — but only among players who are still eligible, i.e., those who haven't yet kept. So after Noor mulligans, Noor alone decides whether to mulligan again; Ainsley is locked in with their kept seven. (Ainsley puts no cards on the bottom, having taken zero mulligans.)

This works the same at a multiplayer table: declarations go in turn order starting with the starting player, all mulligans happen simultaneously, and each player who keeps is out of the process for good while the remaining players continue repeating it. A player may keep taking mulligans until their opening hand would be zero cards, after which they may not take further mulligans [103.5].
entries.answer_gold: No.

entries.question: Anahi casts [Aura Mutation] targeting Nehemiah's [Leyline of the Void]. Will Aura Mutation go to Anahi's graveyard or exile?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aura Mutation destroys Leyline during its resolution so Leyline's replacement effect is gone by the time the spell is put into the graveyard, allowing Aura Mutation to go to Anahi's graveyard.
entries.answer:
Aura Mutation goes to Anahi's graveyard, not exile — assuming Leyline of the Void is actually destroyed during Aura Mutation's resolution.

Why: Leyline of the Void reads "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead." "Opponent" is measured from Leyline of the Void's controller, Nehemiah, so it would normally apply to Anahi's cards. But the order of events inside Aura Mutation's resolution matters. Aura Mutation first destroys target enchantment (Leyline of the Void), then creates X 1/1 green Saproling tokens where X is that enchantment's mana value — Leyline of the Void's mana cost is {2}{B}{B}, so its mana value is 4 and Anahi gets four Saprolings. Only as the final part of an instant or sorcery spell's resolution is the spell put into its owner's graveyard [608.2n]. By that moment Leyline of the Void has already left the battlefield, so its replacement effect no longer exists to exile Aura Mutation, and Aura Mutation lands in Anahi's graveyard.

Leyline of the Void itself goes to Nehemiah's graveyard: its own ability only replaces cards going to an *opponent's* graveyard, and Nehemiah is not his own opponent.

Timing/edge cases:
- If Leyline of the Void is an illegal target when Aura Mutation tries to resolve, Aura Mutation doesn't resolve and Anahi gets no Saprolings [Aura Mutation ruling #1]. In that case Leyline of the Void is still on the battlefield when Aura Mutation is put into the graveyard, so Aura Mutation would be exiled instead.
- Likewise, if Leyline of the Void survives the destruction (for example it's made indestructible), its replacement effect is still active at the end of resolution and Aura Mutation would be exiled.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any table size with only one Leyline of the Void, but if some *other* player (a third player who is also Anahi's opponent) controls a second Leyline of the Void, that one is untouched by Aura Mutation and will exile Aura Mutation instead of letting it reach Anahi's graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Graveyard. Leyline of the Void is destroyed before Aura Mutation goes to the graveyard, since going to the graveyard is the last part of a spell resolving.

entries.question: Ari controls [Omnath, Locus of Creation] and [Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines]. They play [Tainted Peak]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Elesh Norn causes Omnath's landfall to trigger twice, the first resolution grants 4 life and the second adds {R}{G}{U}{W}, so no damage occurs.
entries.answer:
Ari's Omnath, Locus of Creation landfall ability triggers twice, and Ari gains 4 life and adds {R}{G}{W}{U} to their mana pool. No damage is dealt.

Step by step:

1. Tainted Peak is a land, so it entering the battlefield under Ari's control triggers Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability (a landfall ability triggers whenever a land you control enters for any reason, including a normal land drop) [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #4].
2. Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines says "If a permanent entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time." Tainted Peak is a permanent entering, and Omnath, Locus of Creation is a permanent Ari controls, so the landfall ability triggers a second time rather than being copied [603.2d] [Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines ruling #2].
3. Both instances go on the stack (Ari chooses the order, though the instances are identical). Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability is never a mana ability, so it uses the stack and opponents may respond, even the instance that produces mana [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #1] [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #6].
4. Each instance checks, on resolution, how many times the ability has resolved this turn [608.2h]. The first resolution: Ari gains 4 life. The second resolution: Ari adds {R}{G}{W}{U} — one red, one green, one white, and one blue mana, no generic and no {C}.
5. Nothing reaches the third resolution, so Omnath, Locus of Creation does not deal 4 damage to anyone this turn unless a third land enters under Ari's control later in the turn (a third land would give two more resolutions — the third dealing 4 damage to each opponent and each planeswalker Ari doesn't control, and the fourth doing nothing) [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #2].

Assumption on timing: this is Ari's own land drop on their turn, and no other land entered earlier this turn, so these are resolutions #1 and #2. If Omnath, Locus of Creation's ability had already resolved once earlier this turn, these two instances would instead be the second and third resolutions — adding {R}{G}{W}{U} and then dealing 4 damage to each opponent and each planeswalker Ari doesn't control.

Also note Tainted Peak's own abilities are activated mana abilities ({T}: Add {C}; {T}: Add {B} or {R} only if you control a Swamp); they don't do anything on their own from entering, and Tainted Peak enters untapped and can be tapped for mana normally.

Separately, Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines' third ability means Tainted Peak entering won't cause triggered abilities of permanents Ari's opponents control to trigger at all [Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines ruling #8].

Multiplayer: the life gain and mana are identical regardless of player count. Player count only matters if a third resolution happens — then each opponent (all of them, not just one) and each planeswalker Ari doesn't control takes 4 damage. In Two-Headed Giant, a third resolution makes the opposing team lose 8 life, and each other player's planeswalkers, including a teammate's, are dealt 4 damage; also, Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines does not affect triggered abilities of permanents a teammate controls [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #3] [Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines ruling #10].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Omnath, Locus of Creation's ability triggers twice. The first instance of the ability will cause Ari to gain 4 life and the second instance will add {R}{G}{U}{W} to their mana pool. Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines will cause the ability to trigger twice since it triggers as the result of a permanent entering the battlefield. Omnath, Locus of Creation's triggered ability has an effect depending on how many times its resolved this turn, so the second instance that resolves will have the second effect.

entries.question: Amiya controls [Fetid Gargantua] with two +1/+1 counters on it. Nico controls [Soul-Scar Mage] and casts [Scorching Lava] targeting Fetid Gargantua. After Scorching Lava resolves, can Fetid Gargantua adapt again?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that the -1/-1 and +1/+1 counters cancel as a state-based action and Fetid Gargantua can adapt again, matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes — Fetid Gargantua can adapt again, and it survives with no damage marked on it.

Step by step:

1. Scorching Lava would deal 2 noncombat damage to Fetid Gargantua, a creature an opponent of Nico controls, and Scorching Lava is a source Nico controls. Soul-Scar Mage's static ability replaces that damage: instead of 2 damage, two -1/-1 counters are put on Fetid Gargantua. Per the Soul-Scar Mage rulings, this is a replacement effect, not a prevention effect, so no damage is actually dealt.

2. Fetid Gargantua now has two +1/+1 counters and two -1/-1 counters. As a state-based action, N +1/+1 and N -1/-1 counters are removed, where N is the smaller number of the two — here N = 2, so all four counters come off [122.3] [704.5q]. This happens automatically the next time a player would receive priority; no one can respond in between.

3. Fetid Gargantua is left a 4/4 with zero counters and zero damage marked. Since "Adapt 2" means "If this permanent has no +1/+1 counters on it, put two +1/+1 counters on it" [701.46a], and the Fetid Gargantua ruling confirms that a creature that loses all its +1/+1 counters can adapt again, Amiya can activate {2}{B}: Adapt 2 and actually get the two counters. That will also trigger Fetid Gargantua's second ability (draw two cards, lose 2 life, if Amiya chooses).

Kicker note: if Nico kicked Scorching Lava (paying the extra {R}), the "can't be regenerated / exile it if it would die" clause is irrelevant here — Fetid Gargantua never takes damage and doesn't die, it just loses its counters.

Player count: this works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table. Soul-Scar Mage's ability keys off "a creature an opponent controls" from the perspective of Soul-Scar Mage's controller, Nico, so as long as Amiya is Nico's opponent the replacement applies regardless of how many players are in the game; the counter-annihilation state-based action [704.5q] is likewise player-count independent.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. If a permanent has both -1/-1 and +1/+1 counters on it, they are removed as a state-based action. Adapt checks the number of +1/+1 counters on Fetid Gargantua as it resolves, it doesn't matter if it's been activated in the past.

entries.question: Ari controls [Emeria Shepherd]. They play [Sacred Peaks], and target [Garenbrig Carver] in their graveyard. In response, Noelle activates [Alchemist's Refuge]. When that ability resolves, they casts [Blood Moon]. When Emeria Shepherd's ability resolves, where is Garenbrig Carver?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Garenbrig Carver goes to Ari's hand because Blood Moon makes Sacred Peaks not a Plains when Emeria Shepherd's ability resolves, so the card can't be put onto the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Garenbrig Carver ends up in Ari's hand (if Ari chooses to return it at all), not on the battlefield.

Why:

- Emeria Shepherd's landfall ability returns the target nonland permanent card to your hand, and only lets you put it onto the battlefield instead "if that land is a Plains." That condition is checked when the ability resolves, not when it triggered: an effect that needs information from a specific object uses that object's current information as long as it's still in the public zone it was expected to be in [608.2h]. Sacred Peaks is still on the battlefield, so its current types are used.
- Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Sacred Peaks is a nonbasic land, so setting its subtype to Mountain makes it lose its other land types — including Plains — along with the abilities from those types and its rules text, and it gains "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6] [305.7] [Blood Moon ruling #3]. (It keeps its name and any supertypes, and it's still tapped/untapped as it was; losing "This land enters tapped" is irrelevant since Sacred Peaks already entered.)
- So at resolution Sacred Peaks is a Mountain only, the Plains clause fails, and Emeria Shepherd's ability just returns Garenbrig Carver to Ari's hand. The "you may" is optional, so Ari could also decline and leave Garenbrig Carver in the graveyard.
- Garenbrig Carver was a legal target the whole time: in the graveyard an adventurer card uses only its creature-face characteristics, so it is a nonland permanent card (a creature card) [Garenbrig Carver // Shield's Might ruling #7] [Emeria Shepherd ruling #2]. Once in hand, Ari can later cast it as Garenbrig Carver for {3}{G} or as the Adventure Shield's Might for {1}{G}.
- Noelle's use of Alchemist's Refuge is what made this possible: its second ability ({G}{U}, {T}) lets Noelle cast Blood Moon, normally a sorcery-speed enchantment spell, as though it had flash while Emeria Shepherd's trigger was still on the stack [Alchemist's Refuge ruling #2].

Timing note: I'm assuming Blood Moon actually resolved before Emeria Shepherd's landfall ability resolved, as described. If Blood Moon were instead cast/resolved after the landfall ability resolved, Sacred Peaks would still have been a Plains at that moment and Ari could have put Garenbrig Carver onto the battlefield instead.

Nothing here depends on the number of players — the provided rules aren't two-player-specific, and the result is the same at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Ari's hand.

Blood Moon changes Sacred Peaks's subtypes to "Mountain", and Sacred Peaks loses all other subtypes. During the resolution of the ability, Sacred Peaks is no longer a Plains and therefore Garenbrig Carver will not return to the battlefield.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [General Ferrous Rokiric]. What happens when they cast [Illusion]?
entries.reason: Both conclude General Ferrous Rokiric does not trigger—Illusion does not cause a multicolored spell-cast event, so no Golem is created (the candidate reaches the same no-trigger conclusion despite incorrect token-based reasoning).
entries.answer:
Nothing triggers — as printed in the card data, Illusion is a **token** creature (0/2 blue Illusion), and a token isn't a card and isn't cast. Tokens are *created* by an effect, so Ainsley never "casts Illusion" at all, and General Ferrous Rokiric's ability, which reads "Whenever you cast a multicolored spell, create a 4/4 red and white Golem artifact creature token," never sees a cast event and doesn't trigger.

Secondary point, in case the intent was a blue Illusion *spell* rather than the token: General Ferrous Rokiric only triggers on **multicolored** spells — spells that are two or more colors. Illusion as given has a color identity of blue only, so even a hypothetical monocolored blue Illusion spell would not trigger General Ferrous Rokiric and would produce no Golem token.

A related trap from the rules provided: if the Illusion in question were one half of a split card, only the characteristics of the half actually being cast exist while it's on the stack — the other half's characteristics are treated as though they didn't exist [709.3b]. So even though a split card is the combination of both halves' mana costs (and therefore possibly multicolored) in every zone except the stack [709.4], [709.4b], casting a monocolored half yields a monocolored spell that would not trigger General Ferrous Rokiric.

Also worth noting for the board state: General Ferrous Rokiric has "Hexproof from monocolored," which protects it from being targeted by monocolored spells and abilities — but the Illusion token's ability ("Whenever this creature blocks a creature, that creature doesn't untap during its controller's next untap step") doesn't target, so if the Illusion token blocks General Ferrous Rokiric, that ability applies normally and General Ferrous Rokiric won't untap during Ainsley's next untap step.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more: General Ferrous Rokiric's trigger cares only about spells its controller casts, so the number of opponents doesn't change anything.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: General Ferrous Rokiric won't trigger. While Illusion is a multicolored card elsewhere, on the stack it's a monocolored card.

entries.question:
Aydan casts [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded], and Nico answers by casting [Spell Queller], exiling Kellan, the Fae-Blooded with its triggered ability.
When Spell Queller leaves the battlefield, can Aydan choose to cast [Birthright Boon] or do they have to cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling — Aydan may cast either Kellan or Birthright Boon when Spell Queller's ability resolves.
entries.answer:
Aydan may choose either one — he can cast Birthright Boon (the Adventure half) or Kellan, the Fae-Blooded (the creature half), and either way it's cast without paying its mana cost.

Why:

- An adventurer card has two sets of characteristics: the inset frame on the left gives the alternative (Adventure) characteristics the object may have while it's a spell, and the normal characteristics appear as usual [715.2]. As a player plays an adventurer card, that player chooses whether to play it normally or as an Adventure [715.3]. That choice is made each time the card is cast, so being cast as Kellan, the Fae-Blooded the first time doesn't lock Aydan in.
- Spell Queller's ability lets the exiled card's owner cast that card "without paying its mana cost." That normally shuts off alternative costs [Spell Queller ruling #6], but casting a card as an Adventure is expressly not casting it for an alternative cost, and effects that let you cast a spell without paying its mana cost may be applied to the Adventure [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon ruling #9]. So Birthright Boon is a legal choice and costs nothing.
- Timing: Aydan must cast it right then, as part of the resolution of Spell Queller's leaves-the-battlefield ability; he can't hold it for later. Timing permissions based on the card's type are ignored, so the fact that Birthright Boon is a sorcery doesn't stop him from casting it at instant speed during that resolution [Spell Queller ruling #2].
- The new spell has no relation to the original Kellan, the Fae-Blooded spell that was exiled; nothing from that first casting carries over [Spell Queller ruling #1].
- Follow-up if he picks Birthright Boon: when Birthright Boon resolves, Aydan exiles it instead of putting it into the graveyard, and for as long as it stays exiled he may later cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded as a permanent spell [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon ruling #6] — but that later casting follows normal timing (main phase, empty stack) and costs {2}{R} [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon ruling #5].

Player count doesn't change this: Spell Queller's ability refers to the exiled card's owner, so Aydan makes the choice whether the game is two-player or multiplayer. Note also that the exile check was legal in the first place because the spell cast was Kellan, the Fae-Blooded with mana value 3, which is 4 or less.

entries.answer_gold: Aydan can choose to cast either Kellan, the Fae-Blooded or Birthright Boon when Spell Queller leaves the battlefield.

entries.question: Can Nicolas cast [Memory Lapse] targeting Aubrianna's [Underworld Charger] that is escaping from their graveyard?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that escape puts the card on the stack as a spell and that Memory Lapse can legally target and counter that escaping Underworld Charger.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Aubrianna finishes casting Underworld Charger with its escape ability, Underworld Charger is a creature spell on the stack, and spells on the stack are legal targets for Memory Lapse, which says "Counter target spell" [115.2]. Escape is just an alternative way to cast the card from the graveyard ("Escape [cost]" means "You may cast this card from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost"), so an escaped spell is countered exactly like any other spell [702.138a].

Timing detail: Nicolas can't respond to the act of casting itself. Once Aubrianna begins casting Underworld Charger it immediately moves to the stack, and no player can take actions until the casting is complete [Underworld Charger ruling #1]. After that, Nicolas gets priority and can cast Memory Lapse targeting Underworld Charger.

Result: Memory Lapse cancels Underworld Charger and removes it from the stack; it doesn't resolve, so it never enters the battlefield and it never gets its two +1/+1 counters [701.6a]. Instead of going to Aubrianna's graveyard, Underworld Charger is put on top of Aubrianna's library, because Memory Lapse's self-replacement effect changes that destination before anything else can [Memory Lapse]. Notably, this means Underworld Charger can't simply escape again from the graveyard — Aubrianna has to draw it first. (The Memory Lapse ruling that flashback overrides the library destination applies only to flashback; escape has no such replacement, so top of library it is [Memory Lapse ruling #1].) The escape cost Aubrianna already paid, including the three cards exiled from her graveyard, is not refunded.

The rules provided here don't distinguish two-player from multiplayer games for this interaction: any opponent (or any player) with priority who can legally cast Memory Lapse may target the escaping Underworld Charger, so the answer is the same at a two-player or a larger table.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Escape is an alternative cost ([702.138a]), which means that once paid the escaped spell is on the stack, and can be interacted with as normal. Countering a spell means to remove that spell from the stack before it resolves. Underworld Charger is a legal target for Memory Lapse.

entries.question: Ariyah has [Guardian Naga] in their graveyard. Can they flash back Guardian Naga's Adventure with [Flashback]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — you cannot flashback Guardian Naga's Adventure because in the graveyard the card is only a creature card (its Adventure characteristics don't exist there), so it's not a legal instant/sorcery target.
entries.answer:
No. Ariyah can't target Guardian Naga with Flashback, so they can't flash back Banishing Coils (Guardian Naga's Adventure).

Why: an adventurer card's Adventure text (here, Banishing Coils, an Instant — Adventure) is only a set of *alternative* characteristics printed in the inset frame, and those characteristics exist only while the card is on the stack having been cast as an Adventure [715.2]. In every other zone — including Ariyah's graveyard — the card has only its normal characteristics [715.4]. Per the Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils rulings, an adventurer card is a permanent card in every zone except the stack, and you ignore its alternative characteristics there. So in the graveyard it is simply Guardian Naga, a creature card with mana cost {5}{W}{W}.

Flashback says "Target instant or sorcery card in your graveyard gains flashback until end of turn." A creature card is not a legal target, so Flashback can't be cast targeting Guardian Naga at all (and if it somehow were already on the stack, it would fail for having no legal target).

Two further points even in a hypothetical where targeting worked: Flashback sets the flashback cost equal to the card's mana cost, which for Guardian Naga in the graveyard is {5}{W}{W} (five generic plus two white), not Banishing Coils' {2}{W}; and per the Flashback rulings, flashback only permits casting "if the resulting spell is an instant or sorcery spell," which a Guardian Naga creature spell would not be.

This answer is the same regardless of the number of players — nothing here depends on player count.

entries.answer_gold: No. An Adventure defines alternative characteristics the card can have when cast as an Adventure. Adventurer cards only have their normal characteristics in every zone other than the stack, so it's not a legal target for Flashback.

entries.question: Ace controls [Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker] and activates its ability, turning it into a creature. They then play a second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker. What happens when the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude the legend rule applies and Ace must choose one Sarkhan, putting the other into their graveyard when the second resolves.
entries.answer:
The legend rule applies: Ace must choose one of the two Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker permanents to keep, and the other is put into its owner's graveyard.

Why: the first Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker is currently a legendary 4/4 red Dragon creature (its first ability makes it a legendary creature; it keeps its name and the supertype legendary), and the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker enters the battlefield as a legendary planeswalker with four loyalty counters. The legend rule is a state-based action that only cares about (a) legendary supertype, (b) same name, and (c) same controller \u2014 it does not care that one is a creature and the other is a planeswalker [704.5j].

Timing: the moment the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker finishes resolving, a player would receive priority, so the game checks state-based actions first and the legend rule is applied immediately \u2014 Ace can't respond in between or use both [117.5] [704.3].

Which one to keep is Ace's free choice [704.5j]:
- Keep the animated one: it stays a 4/4 flying, indestructible, hasty Dragon until end of turn (it reverts to a planeswalker afterward, keeping whatever loyalty counters it has). The newly cast Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker goes to the graveyard.
- Keep the newly cast one: it's a planeswalker with 4 loyalty whose ability can be activated on a later turn. The animated Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker goes to the graveyard \u2014 note that indestructible does not help here, because the legend rule puts the permanent into the graveyard rather than destroying it [704.5j].

Multiplayer: no difference. The legend rule is evaluated per player \u2014 "controlled by the same player" \u2014 so it works identically at a two-player or a larger table, and opponents controlling their own Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker are unaffected [704.5j].

entries.answer_gold: As soon as the spell finishes resolving, state-based actions are checked and Ace will need to choose one Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker to put into their graveyard. Regardless of what card type they are, both Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker are legendary permanents with the same name, and therefore the 'legend rule' applies.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Reconnaissance] and attacks Nancy with [Loxodon Wayfarer]. After combat damage is dealt, can Ainsley use Reconnaissance's activated ability to untap Loxodon Wayfarer?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Reconnaissance can target and untap Loxodon Wayfarer after combat damage is dealt because it remains an attacking creature until the end of the combat phase (so it's a legal target).
entries.answer:
Yes — as long as Ainsley activates it while the combat phase is still going on (i.e., in the combat damage step after damage is dealt, or in the end of combat step), Reconnaissance can target Loxodon Wayfarer, remove it from combat, and untap it. Damage already dealt is not undone.

Why: Loxodon Wayfarer became an attacking creature when it was declared as an attacker, and it "remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first" [508.1k], [Attacking Creature]. Dealing combat damage does not end that status. So after the combat damage step, Loxodon Wayfarer is still a legal target for Reconnaissance's "{0}: Remove target attacking creature you control from combat and untap it." Reconnaissance's own reminder text confirms this timing: "If you activate during end of combat, the creature will untap after it deals combat damage."

Once the ability resolves, Loxodon Wayfarer is removed from combat and stops being an attacking creature [506.4b]. That's purely retroactive-free: it doesn't take back the damage already dealt to Nancy, and per the Reconnaissance ruling it doesn't undo anything that triggered on the declaration of attackers or blockers [Reconnaissance ruling #1].

Timing assumption and the other reading: I'm assuming Ainsley still has priority within the combat phase. If Ainsley instead waits until the combat phase has ended (e.g., the postcombat main phase), Loxodon Wayfarer is no longer an attacking creature [508.1k], so there is no legal target and the ability can't be activated for that purpose.

Player count doesn't matter here: the rules cited apply the same whether Nancy is Ainsley's only opponent or one of several players, since Reconnaissance only cares that Loxodon Wayfarer is an attacking creature Ainsley controls.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Loxodon Wayfarer is considered an attacking creature until the end of the combat phase, and is therefore still a legal target for Reconnaissance's activated ability.

entries.question: Arjun controls [Thermopod] and has no cards in their graveyard. Assuming they have enough mana, can they activate [Molten-Tail Masticore]'s first activated ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Arjun can activate Molten‑Tail Masticore’s ability (the ability goes on the stack first), then use Thermopod’s mana/sacrifice ability in the cost-payment window to put a creature into the graveyard (even sacrificing Masticore) and exile it to pay the additional cost.
entries.answer:
Yes — Arjun can do it, by using Thermopod's mana ability during the cost‑payment window to put a creature card into the graveyard first.

How it works step by step:

1. Arjun announces the activation of Molten‑Tail Masticore's ability "{4}, Exile a creature card from your graveyard: This creature deals 4 damage to any target." The ability goes on the stack as its own object and targets are chosen at that time [602.2a], [602.2b].
2. The total cost is locked in: {4} in generic mana (payable with any color or colorless mana) plus the additional cost of exiling a creature card from the graveyard [601.2h], [602.2b].
3. Because the total cost includes a mana payment, Arjun now gets a window to activate mana abilities before costs are actually paid [601.2g]. Thermopod's "Sacrifice a creature: Add {R}" is a mana ability, so Arjun activates it, sacrificing a nontoken creature. That creature card goes to the graveyard as part of paying Thermopod's cost, and Arjun gets {R}.
4. Now Arjun pays the total cost [601.2h]: {4} generic (the {R} from Thermopod can pay one of those four generic), and exiles the creature card that just arrived in the graveyard.

Notes on which creature to sacrifice:
- Thermopod can sacrifice itself to its own ability; Thermopod is a nontoken card, so it lands in the graveyard and can then be exiled to pay Molten‑Tail Masticore's cost.
- Arjun could even sacrifice Molten‑Tail Masticore itself to Thermopod and then exile Molten‑Tail Masticore from the graveyard. Once activated, the ability exists on the stack independently of its source; removing the source doesn't affect it, and the game uses last known information, so the ability still deals 4 damage [113.7a].
- Sacrificing a token wouldn't help — a token isn't a card and won't be in the graveyard to exile.

Timing assumption: this all happens inside the single activation, in the mana‑ability window of rule [601.2g], after the cost is determined but before it's paid. If Arjun instead tried to announce the activation with an empty graveyard and never used Thermopod, they'd be unable to pay the exile cost and the activation would be illegal and rewound [602.2].

Player count doesn't matter here: every action is taken by Arjun alone, so the answer is the same in a two‑player game or at a multiplayer table (the only multiplayer wrinkle is which opponent or permanent is chosen as the target of the 4 damage).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Arjun first puts the ability onto the stack, after which it won't matter if Molten-Tail Masticore is on the battlefield anymore. Arjun then has a chance to activate mana abilities, at which point they can sacrifice Molten-Tail Masticore. Then Arjun pays the cost of the spell, exiling Molten-Tail Masticore from their graveyard.

entries.question: Can Ashley pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} to cast [Beseech the Queen] or is Ashley limited to only paying {B}{B}{B} to do so?
entries.reason: Both conclude Ashley may choose the {2} for any or all {2/B} symbols and therefore may pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} (or any 3–6 total), so the candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Ashley can pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B}. Ashley is not limited to {B}{B}{B}.

Why: Beseech the Queen's mana cost is {2/B}{2/B}{2/B}. A monocolored hybrid symbol like {2/B} may be paid either with one black mana or with two mana of any type [107.4e]. "Two mana of any type" is generic-style payment, and generic mana in costs can be paid with any type of mana, including black [107.4b]. So choosing the "two mana" half of each of the three symbols and paying each with two black mana is perfectly legal — that's the {6} option in the card's own ruling, funded entirely with black mana [Beseech the Queen ruling #1].

Also, each symbol is chosen independently, so Ashley's legal payments include {B}{B}{B} (all three symbols as {B}), {2}{B}{B} (4 mana), {4}{B} (5 mana), and {6} (6 mana), where any of those generic portions may themselves be paid with black mana [Beseech the Queen ruling #1]. That means totals of 3, 4, 5, or 6 mana are all fine, and all-black versions of each are fine.

Procedure note: because the cost includes hybrid symbols, Ashley announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost she intends to pay as part of casting Beseech the Queen (during proposal), before paying [601.2b, 601.2a]. So she declares, e.g., "I'm paying {6}," then pays that with six black mana.

Side points: paying six black mana does not change anything about Beseech the Queen's characteristics — its mana value is 6 regardless of how it's paid [Beseech the Queen ruling #2], and it is black regardless of what mana was spent [Beseech the Queen ruling #3]. None of this depends on how many players are at the table; the rules and rulings provided here about paying monocolored hybrid costs are the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: After the first step of casting a spell, which is announcing it and moving it to the stack, Ashley makes choices regarding modes, alternative costs, additional costs, etc. This step includes deciding whether they will be paying {B} or {2} for each hybrid symbol ({2/B}) in Beseech the Queen's mana cost. They may always choose to cast it for {6} instead of {B}{B}{B} (or {2}{B}{B} or {4}{B}). Later on during the casting of the spell, the colorless parts of the mana cost may be paid with any color, including black.

entries.question: Arielle has [Blessed Hippogriff] in their graveyard. Arielle casts [Mission Briefing], can they choose to cast the adventure of Blessed Hippogriff?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: an adventure card in the graveyard is a creature card, not an instant or sorcery, so Mission Briefing can't choose it.
entries.answer:
No. While Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing is in Arielle's graveyard, it is not an instant or sorcery card, so Mission Briefing can't choose it at all.

An "adventurer" card like Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing has two sets of characteristics: the normal ones (the creature Blessed Hippogriff, {3}{W}) and the alternative ones printed in the inset frame (the Adventure, Tyr's Blessing, {W} Instant — Adventure) [715.2]. Those alternative Adventure characteristics only apply while the card is a spell on the stack that was cast as an Adventure. In every other zone — including the graveyard — the card has only its normal characteristics [715.4], meaning it's a creature card there, as confirmed by the Adventure ruling that an adventurer card is a permanent card in every zone except the stack and that you ignore its alternative characteristics in those cases [Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing ruling #8].

Mission Briefing instructs you to "choose an instant or sorcery card in your graveyard," and Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing doesn't meet that description in the graveyard, so it's not a legal choice — even though Tyr's Blessing would be an instant if the card were on the stack cast as an Adventure. Note also that Mission Briefing doesn't change timing permissions for what you do cast [Mission Briefing ruling #4].

This works the same way regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on the number of opponents, since Mission Briefing only looks at the caster's own graveyard.

entries.answer_gold: No. Adventurer cards have an alternative set of characteristics, however any time an Adventurer card is anywhere other than the stack it only has the characteristics of the creature portion. Mission Briefing requires Arielle to choose an instant or sorcery card in their graveyard, and they cannot choose Blessed Hippogriff.

entries.question: Neriah controls [Cliffhaven Sell-Sword]. Ari casts [Oubliette] targeting it. Will Cliffhaven Sell-Sword phase back in at the beginning of Neriah's next untap step?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states that Oubliette's "until" effect prevents normal untap-step phasing and the Sell-Sword only phases in when Oubliette leaves the battlefield.
entries.answer:
No. Cliffhaven Sell-Sword will not phase in during Neriah's untap step. Oubliette phases it out "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield," so Cliffhaven Sell-Sword stays phased out for as long as Oubliette remains on the battlefield, and it phases in immediately after Oubliette leaves the battlefield (tapped, per Oubliette's text) [Oubliette ruling #6].

Why: "Phased out" means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist — it can't be targeted, can't attack or block, its static abilities do nothing, and its triggered abilities can't trigger [Oubliette ruling #5]. Normally, phasing is a static ability that works during the untap step: in each player's untap step, before the active player untaps, that player's phased-in permanents with phasing phase out and their phased-out permanents phase in [702.26a]. But Cliffhaven Sell-Sword doesn't have the phasing ability — it was phased out by a one-shot "until" effect. Rule [610.4a] specifically says a permanent phased out "until" a specified event does not phase in as a result of the untap step turn-based action; instead, a second one-shot effect created immediately after the specified event (here, Oubliette leaving the battlefield) phases it in.

Two small notes:
- Technically it's Oubliette's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability that targets Cliffhaven Sell-Sword, not the spell itself. If Oubliette leaves the battlefield before that trigger resolves, Cliffhaven Sell-Sword is never phased out or tapped at all [Oubliette ruling #1].
- Another effect could still phase Cliffhaven Sell-Sword in early; if that happens, the "phase in when Oubliette leaves" one-shot effect no longer happens [610.4a].

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the duration keys off Oubliette leaving the battlefield, not off whose untap step it is, and the untap-step phasing action in [702.26a] only concerns permanents with the phasing ability.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Effects that phase a permanent out until a certain event prevent that permanent from phasing back in normally.

entries.question: Nico controls [Lazav, the Multifarious], which is currently a copy of [Lazav, Dimir Mastermind]. Abram discards [Kasimir the Lone Wolf] due to hand size at the end of their turn. Lazav, the Multifarious's ability triggers. After it resolves, what is Lazav, the Multifarious named?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that the creature's name becomes "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind" after the trigger resolves because the copy effect's exception sets that name.
entries.answer:
After the trigger resolves, the permanent is named **Lazav, Dimir Mastermind**.

Here's the chain. Nico's Lazav, the Multifarious had used its {X} ability to become a copy of the card Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, "except its name is Lazav, the Multifarious, it's legendary..., and it has this ability." So at that point the permanent's copiable values were the printed values of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind (3/3, hexproof, and Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's triggered ability) with the name and ability exceptions baked in — copy effects can include modifications, and the modified values become the copiable values [707.9b].

That means the permanent now has Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's triggered ability: "Whenever a creature card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, you may have Lazav become a copy of that card, except its name is Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, it's legendary in addition to its other types, and it has hexproof and this ability." Abram discarding Kasimir the Lone Wolf to hand size puts a creature card into an opponent's graveyard from hand, which is covered by "from anywhere," so that ability triggers.

When it resolves and Nico accepts, the permanent becomes a new copy of Kasimir the Lone Wolf with the exceptions written in that ability — and those exceptions set the name to Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, not Lazav, the Multifarious. The copy is of exactly what's printed on Kasimir the Lone Wolf plus the stated modifications [Lazav, the Multifarious ruling #1], so the result is a legendary 5/3 Human Warrior named Lazav, Dimir Mastermind with hexproof and Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's triggered ability. Note that the {X} ability of Lazav, the Multifarious is gone — the new copy effect replaced the copiable values, and only hexproof and "this ability" (the Dimir Mastermind trigger) were carried along. Nico can no longer activate {X} to become something else, though the Dimir Mastermind trigger will keep working on future opponents' creature cards.

Multiplayer note: nothing changes with more than two players. The ability keys off any opponent's graveyard, so Abram being one of several opponents is fine; with additional opponents, the same trigger would fire for creature cards hitting any of their graveyards.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind". Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's ability changes the card's name to "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind", regardless of what it was originally named.

entries.question: Alivia has [Road // Ruin] in their graveyard. Alivia casts [Torrential Gearhulk]. Which side of Road // Ruin can Alivia cast with its trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: a split card in the graveyard is both an instant and a sorcery, so Torrential Gearhulk can target it and you may cast either half (including the aftermath half).
entries.answer:
Alivia can cast either half — Road or Ruin.

Why the card is a legal target: in every zone other than the stack (here, the graveyard), a split card's characteristics are those of both halves combined, so Road // Ruin is both an instant card and a sorcery card [709.4, 709.4c]. Torrential Gearhulk's trigger targets "target instant card in your graveyard," and Road // Ruin qualifies because of the instant half.

Why either half is castable: Alivia chooses which half to cast before putting it on the stack, and only that half is evaluated and put on the stack [709.3, 709.3a]. Torrential Gearhulk is an effect that allows casting the card from the graveyard, and the Road // Ruin rulings state that if another effect allows you to cast a split card with aftermath from a graveyard, you may cast either half — including the aftermath half [Road // Ruin ruling #7].

Practical points:
- Either half is cast without paying its mana cost (so neither Road's {2}{G} nor Ruin's {1}{R}{R} is paid). Additional costs would still have to be paid, and any {X} would be 0 [Torrential Gearhulk ruling #2, Torrential Gearhulk ruling #3].
- The card must be cast right then, during the resolution of Torrential Gearhulk's triggered ability; Alivia can't hold it for later in the turn [Torrential Gearhulk ruling #1].
- If Alivia casts Ruin, it needs a legal target creature, and the card will be exiled when it leaves the stack whether it resolves or is countered — both from aftermath and from Torrential Gearhulk's replacement effect [Road // Ruin ruling #6]. If Alivia casts Road instead, Torrential Gearhulk's replacement effect exiles it instead of putting it into the graveyard.

One assumption: I'm reading the trigger as targeting Road // Ruin itself while it sits in Alivia's graveyard. Nothing here depends on the number of players — only Alivia's own graveyard is involved — so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table (the provided rules don't include any multiplayer-specific text bearing on this).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Either side. Torrential Gearhulk has a targeting restriction that requires Alivia to select an instant in their graveyard. Split cards have the type of both sides simultaneously. Therefore Road // Ruin is both an instant and a sorcery card and satisfies the targeting restriction on Torrential Gearhulk. When Alivia goes to cast Road // Ruin, nothing cares about which half is cast, so either is legal.

entries.question: Alvaro controls [Draugr Thought-Thief] and [Lotusguard Disciple]. Nico controls [Sands of Time] and [Yurlok of Scorch Thrash]. If Alvaro casts [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats], can they choose to only have the cost reduced by {1}?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the cost reduction is determined by Alvaro's party (2 creatures here) and is applied automatically as {2}, not optionally reduced to {1}.
entries.answer:
No. Alvaro's party has two creatures, so Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats is reduced by exactly {2}; the reduction isn't optional and can't be scaled down.

Why: a player's party consists of up to one Cleric, up to one Rogue, up to one Warrior, and up to one Wizard that player controls, and the game calculates that number automatically — players never designate which creatures are "in" their party and can't exclude creatures to lower the count [700.8a] [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #3]. Alvaro controls Draugr Thought-Thief (Zombie Rogue, so the Rogue check is yes) and Lotusguard Disciple (Bird Cleric, so the Cleric check is yes); no Warrior and no Wizard, so the count is 2 [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #5]. Neither creature has two party types here, so the "count for the highest result" rule doesn't change anything [700.8b].

Total cost: start with the mana cost {4}{B}{R}, add any cost increases, then apply the reduction of {1} per party creature — {2} total. That comes off only the generic portion, so Alvaro pays {2}{B}{R}. The colored {B} and {R} symbols are untouched, and Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats still has mana value 6 regardless of what was actually paid [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #4].

Nico's Sands of Time and Yurlok of Scorch Thrash are irrelevant to the party count — party only counts creatures the spell's controller controls, and neither of those is a creature Alvaro controls (Yurlok of Scorch Thrash is a Lizard Shaman anyway, not a party type) [700.8a]. This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, since party is measured per player from their own creatures.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats's cost is reduced by the number of creatures in Alvaro's party, which is determined by the game, and is calculated to be the highest possible amount.

entries.question: Adriel controls [Oko, Thief of Crowns], [Gilded Goose], and a Food token. Adriel uses Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability to make the Food token into a 3/3 Elk. Can Adriel then sacrifice it to Gilded Goose?
entries.reason: Both conclude Oko's effect removes the Food subtype so the token is no longer a Food and thus can't be sacrificed to Gilded Goose.
entries.answer:
No. Once Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability resolves on the Food token, that token is no longer a Food, so Gilded Goose's "{T}, Sacrifice a Food: Add one mana of any color" ability can't be activated by sacrificing it.

Why:

1. Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 makes the target lose all abilities and become a green Elk creature with base power and toughness 3/3. Per the Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling, this overwrites all colors and creature types and the permanent "loses any other card types it has (such as artifact)" [Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling #5]. So the token is now just a creature, not an artifact.

2. Food is an artifact type (an artifact subtype), never a creature type [Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling #13] [Gilded Goose ruling #2]. Rule 205.1a says that when an object's card type is removed, subtypes correlated with that card type remain only if they're also subtypes of a card type the object currently has; otherwise they're removed for as long as that card type is gone. Since the token is no longer an artifact and Food isn't a creature type, the Food subtype falls off. Its new creature type is Elk.

3. Gilded Goose's cost says "Sacrifice a Food." Under rule 109.2, a description using a subtype without the words "card," "spell," or "source" means a permanent of that subtype on the battlefield — i.e., a permanent that is currently a Food. The 3/3 Elk isn't one, so it can't pay that cost.

Also note the token lost all abilities, so it no longer has its own "{2}, {T}, Sacrifice this token: You gain 3 life" ability either.

Timing: I'm assuming Adriel resolved the +1 first and is asking about sacrificing afterward. If instead Adriel sacrifices the token to Gilded Goose first (or in response, while Oko, Thief of Crowns's ability is still on the stack), it's still a Food at that moment and the sacrifice works fine — and Oko, Thief of Crowns's ability would then be countered for having an illegal target if that token was its only target.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count; it plays out the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Oko, Thief of Crowns's ability is a type-changing effect which will overwrite any previous types and subtypes the object had. When Gilded Goose asks Adriel to sacrifice a Food, it is saying that Adriel needs to sacrifice a permanent with the subtype "Food".

entries.question: Natasha controls a [Lifeline] and 2 [Scarwood Goblins]. Adriel casts [Plague Wind]. Does Lifeline trigger and return the creatures to the battlefield at the beginning of the next end step?
entries.reason: Both conclude Lifeline triggers for each Scarwood Goblin but the intervening "if another creature is on the battlefield" can make those triggers fail to do anything if no other creature remains (so nothing returns unless a creature survives).
entries.answer:
Short answer: Lifeline does trigger twice (once for each Scarwood Goblin), but whether anything comes back depends entirely on whether any creature is still on the battlefield when those triggers resolve — and Plague Wind only spares creatures Adriel controls.

**Why it triggers.** Lifeline reads "Whenever a creature dies, if another creature is on the battlefield, return the first card to the battlefield under its owner's control at the beginning of the next end step." Both Scarwood Goblins die simultaneously to Plague Wind ("Destroy all creatures you don't control"). A "dies" trigger is a leaves-the-battlefield trigger, and those "look back in time": the game uses the appearance of objects immediately before the event to decide whether the ability triggers [603.10a]. Immediately before Plague Wind finished resolving, each Scarwood Goblin had another creature (the other Scarwood Goblin) on the battlefield, so Lifeline triggers once for each of them.

**Why they may still not come back.** "if another creature is on the battlefield" is an intervening "if" clause: the condition is checked when the ability would trigger *and again as the ability resolves*; if it's false on resolution the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing [603.4] [608.2a]. Lifeline's own ruling states this exact case: if more than one creature is on the battlefield and they all go to the graveyard at once, none of them are returned, because there must be at least one creature on the battlefield when the ability resolves [Lifeline ruling #5].

So:
- **If Adriel controls no creatures** (and no other creature survives), both Scarwood Goblins are the last creatures on the battlefield. Both Lifeline triggers are removed from the stack on resolution, no delayed "at the beginning of the next end step" effects are ever created, and neither Scarwood Goblin returns.
- **If Adriel controls at least one creature** (Plague Wind doesn't destroy Adriel's own creatures), that creature satisfies the "another creature is on the battlefield" check on resolution. Both triggers resolve, each setting up its own delayed return, and the two Scarwood Goblins return under Natasha's control at the beginning of the next end step — one at a time, since Lifeline triggered separately for each [Lifeline ruling #4]. Each Scarwood Goblin only returns if that card is still in the graveyard at that time [Lifeline ruling #2]. Note also that Lifeline itself is an artifact, so Plague Wind never touches it; and even if Lifeline had left the battlefield after triggering, the triggers would still work [Lifeline ruling #3].

**Timing assumption:** I'm treating both Scarwood Goblins as dying simultaneously during Plague Wind's resolution, which is how Plague Wind works. If instead they had died at different times (say, one already destroyed earlier in the turn), the earlier death's trigger would see the surviving Scarwood Goblin and resolve fine, and only the final creature's trigger would be at risk of fizzling.

**Multiplayer:** Plague Wind is worded from Adriel's perspective, so with more than two players it destroys every creature that Adriel doesn't control — every other player's creatures, not just Natasha's. That doesn't change the analysis; it just means the only creatures that can satisfy Lifeline's intervening "if" on resolution are Adriel's. And because Lifeline works for all players, it will also trigger for the other players' dying creatures.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Leaves-the-battlefield triggers care about the game state immediately before the event in question occurred when determining whether they trigger. There was another creature on the battlefield at that time, so Lifeline will trigger for both creatures that died. However, Lifeline has an intervening "if" clause that checks for that condition again as the trigger begins to resolve. There is not another creature on the battlefield at that time, so the ability is removed from the stack. Neither Scarwood Goblins returns to the battlefield.

entries.question: Alfred casts [Stream of Thought], replicating it twice. Nico controls [Chalice of the Void] with 1 charge counter. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Chalice's trigger resolves first and counters the original Stream of Thought while the replicate triggers still create two copies (which are not cast) that resolve normally.
entries.answer:
Chalice of the Void counters the original Stream of Thought, but Alfred still gets both replicate copies, and those two copies resolve normally.

How it plays out:

1. Casting. Alfred pays Stream of Thought's mana cost {U} plus its replicate cost {2}{U}{U} twice, for a total of {4}{U}{U}{U}{U}{U} (four generic plus five blue). Replicate is an additional cost: "As an additional cost to cast this spell, you may pay [cost] any number of times," plus a triggered ability that copies the spell for each payment [702.56a]. Paying it doesn't change Stream of Thought's mana cost, so the spell on the stack still has mana value 1.

2. Two abilities trigger on the cast: Alfred's replicate trigger, and Nico's Chalice of the Void trigger ("Whenever a player casts a spell with mana value equal to the number of charge counters on this artifact, counter that spell") — Stream of Thought's mana value 1 matches Chalice of the Void's one charge counter.

3. Ordering. Because Stream of Thought is a sorcery, it's Alfred's turn, so Alfred is the active player. In APNAP order Alfred puts his replicate trigger on the stack first, then Nico puts the Chalice of the Void trigger on top of it [101.4, 603.3b]. So the Chalice of the Void trigger resolves first and counters Stream of Thought, putting it into Alfred's graveyard.

4. The copies still happen. "You'll copy Stream of Thought for each time you paid its replicate cost, even if it's countered" [Stream of Thought ruling #4]. When the replicate trigger resolves, it creates two copies on the stack, and Alfred may choose new targets for either copy [702.56a, 707.10].

5. The copies aren't countered. Copies created by replicate are put directly onto the stack and are not cast [707.10, Stream of Thought ruling #5], so Chalice of the Void's ability — which only triggers on a spell being cast — doesn't trigger on them, even though each copy also has mana value 1.

6. Resolving the copies. Each copy makes its target player mill four cards, and Alfred shuffles up to four cards from his graveyard into his library. Note a quirk here: normally the copies resolve before the original, so they can't shuffle Stream of Thought itself back in [Stream of Thought ruling #3], but because Chalice of the Void already countered the original, Stream of Thought is sitting in Alfred's graveyard when the copies resolve — so he can shuffle that very card into his library with one of the copies.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Chalice of the Void was already on the battlefield with its counter when Alfred cast Stream of Thought. If Chalice of the Void entered or gained/lost counters only after the spell was cast, its ability wouldn't have triggered at all [Chalice of the Void ruling #1] and the original Stream of Thought would resolve too (after the copies).

Multiplayer note: with more than two players the result is the same — all nonactive players' triggers are placed after Alfred's in turn order [101.4], so Nico's Chalice of the Void trigger still ends up above the replicate trigger and resolves first. The only extra freedom is that Alfred may aim each copy at a different opponent (or himself) when choosing new targets.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The original Stream of Thought is countered, the two copies resolve as normal. Replicate and Chalice of the Void both trigger when the spell is cast. Since the Chalice of the Void trigger is controlled by the player last in turn order, it will resolve first, countering Stream of Thought. Then Stream of Thought's trigger resolves and creates two copies of Stream of Thought. The copies are not cast, so they don't trigger Chalice of the Void.

entries.question: Adrienne attacks with [Sporeweb Weaver], and Nicolas blocks it with [Serpent Assassin]. Can Nicolas use [Tishana's Tidebinder] to counter Sporeweb Weaver's ability?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same correct ruling that Tishana's Tidebinder can target and counter Sporeweb Weaver's triggered ability because hexproof prevents targeting the permanent, not the triggered ability on the stack.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nicolas can target Sporeweb Weaver's triggered ability with Tishana's Tidebinder, because Tishana's Tidebinder targets the ability on the stack, not the permanent Sporeweb Weaver.

Why hexproof from blue doesn't stop it:
- "Hexproof from blue" means Sporeweb Weaver can't be the target of blue spells opponents control or abilities opponents control from blue sources [Sporeweb Weaver ruling #1]. Hexproof of any kind is worded as a restriction on targeting *that permanent* [702.11b].
- An ability on the stack is its own object, separate from the permanent that produced it [109.1], and once it has triggered it exists on the stack independently of its source [113.7a]. Abilities are legal targets precisely because they're objects that can't exist on the battlefield [115.2].
- So Tishana's Tidebinder's enters-the-battlefield trigger legally targets the "whenever this creature is dealt damage" trigger even though Sporeweb Weaver itself is untargetable by Nicolas's blue spells and abilities.

Assumed timing: Serpent Assassin's combat damage is dealt in the combat damage step, Sporeweb Weaver's damage trigger goes on the stack at the next priority, and Nicolas then flashes in Tishana's Tidebinder while that trigger is still on the stack. That's the only window — if Nicolas casts Tishana's Tidebinder before combat damage (say, during declare blockers), there is no triggered ability on the stack yet to target, and the Sporeweb Weaver trigger will resolve normally later.

Result if it resolves: Sporeweb Weaver's trigger is countered, so Adrienne gains no life and gets no Saproling token. Additionally, because Sporeweb Weaver is still a creature on the battlefield when Tishana's Tidebinder's trigger resolves (Serpent Assassin's 2 damage doesn't kill the 1/4), Sporeweb Weaver loses all abilities — including reach, hexproof from blue, and the damage trigger — for as long as Tishana's Tidebinder remains on the battlefield [Tishana's Tidebinder ruling #2]. Note that if Sporeweb Weaver had died from the damage, the trigger would still be countered, but nothing would lose abilities [Tishana's Tidebinder ruling #3].

Player count doesn't matter: hexproof from blue restricts targeting by spells and abilities of opponents generally, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Tishana's Tidebinder's ability targets Sporeweb Weaver's ability, not Sporeweb Weaver itself, so hexproof doesn't matter.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born] and casts [Tempted by the Oriq] targeting Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. Before it resolves, Autumn casts [Insurrection]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Insurrection resolves first, Autumn gains control of the Soldier tokens, and Tempted by the Oriq’s targets become illegal so it fails to resolve.
entries.answer:
Tempted by the Oriq will do nothing: Insurrection resolves first and makes Autumn the controller of every creature, so both Soldier tokens stop being creatures "that player controls" for Breanna and Case. Both targets are illegal, so Tempted by the Oriq doesn't resolve and is put into Autumn's graveyard.

How it plays out:

1. Casting Insurrection at that moment is only legal because of Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born's Cosmic Awareness — "As long as an opponent has cast a spell this turn, you may cast spells as though they had flash." Insurrection is a sorcery, and the stack isn't empty while Tempted by the Oriq is on it, so this works only if Breanna, Case, or another opponent has already cast a spell this turn. If no opponent has cast a spell this turn, Autumn simply can't cast Insurrection there.

2. Insurrection, cast second, resolves first (the stack resolves last-in, first-out; that ordering rule isn't in the provided context, but it's the standard stack behavior).
