It untaps all creatures, Autumn gains control of all of them until end of turn, and they all gain haste — including Breanna's Soldier token and Case's Soldier token (Insurrection ruling: you untap all creatures, control all creatures, and give all creatures haste).

3. Tempted by the Oriq then tries to resolve. Its targeting requirement is "target creature or planeswalker that player controls with mana value 3 or less," checked again on resolution: a spell rechecks the legality of its targets, and changes to the game state (here, a change of controller) can make a target illegal; if every target for every instance of "target" is illegal, the spell doesn't resolve and goes to its owner's graveyard [608.2b]. Since Autumn now controls both Soldier tokens, neither is a creature Breanna controls or a creature Case controls, so both targets are illegal and Tempted by the Oriq is removed from the stack.

4. Net result: Autumn controls and can attack with both Soldier tokens this turn (they have haste from Insurrection), but Insurrection's control effect ends at end of turn, so the tokens go back to Breanna and Case during the cleanup step. Autumn loses out on Tempted by the Oriq's permanent theft — that spell's control-changing effect would have lasted indefinitely (Tempted by the Oriq ruling).

Assumed timing / the other order: I'm assuming Insurrection was cast while Tempted by the Oriq was still on the stack, as described. If instead Autumn had let Tempted by the Oriq resolve first and then cast Insurrection, Tempted by the Oriq would have taken both Soldier tokens indefinitely, and Insurrection's temporary control of them afterward would be redundant — Autumn would keep them permanently.

Partial-illegality note: [608.2b] only counters the spell if all targets are illegal. If, say, only Breanna's token had changed controllers and Case's had not, Tempted by the Oriq would still resolve and steal Case's token permanently.

Player count: this scenario already involves at least three players (Autumn plus opponents Breanna and Case), and Tempted by the Oriq targets once "for each opponent." In a two-player game there'd be only one target, and Insurrection making that single target illegal would likewise cause Tempted by the Oriq to be removed from the stack with no effect.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Insurrection resolves and Autumn gains control of all the Soldier tokens. Then Tempted by the Oriq begins to resolve, but its targets are now illegal, so it does not resolve and is removed from the stack.

entries.question: Amelia casts [Aminatou's Augury] exiling an artifact and an instant. Afterwards Amelia casts another Aminatou's Augury, which exiles an instant. Can they cast both instants?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling: each Aminatou's Augury creates a separate, self-linked permission for the cards it exiles, so Amelia may cast an instant from each.
entries.answer:
Yes — Amelia can cast both instants, one under each Aminatou's Augury.

Why: each Aminatou's Augury is a single ability that both exiles cards and then refers to "the exiled cards." An ability that both causes objects to be affected and refers back to those same objects is linked to itself [607.1, 607.1c], so each copy of Aminatou's Augury grants permission only for the cards that that particular Aminatou's Augury exiled. The "one spell of each nonland card type" allowance is therefore tracked separately per resolution — it is not a shared, once-per-turn cap.

So the first Aminatou's Augury lets Amelia cast one artifact and one instant from among its eight exiled cards; the second Aminatou's Augury independently lets Amelia cast one instant (and one of each other nonland type) from among its own exiled cards. Neither Aminatou's Augury's permission reaches the other's exiled pile.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both Aminatou's Augury spells are cast in the same turn. Each Aminatou's Augury's permission lasts only "until end of turn," so if the second Aminatou's Augury were cast on a later turn, the first Aminatou's Augury's instant would no longer be castable from exile and only the second instant could be cast. Also, normal timing rules still apply to the spells cast this way [Aminatou's Augury ruling: "You must follow the normal timing permissions and restrictions of each spell you cast"], though instants can be cast whenever Amelia has priority, and casting an exiled card moves it out of exile so it can't be cast again [Aminatou's Augury ruling: "Casting an exiled card causes it to leave exile. You can't cast it multiple times"].

Player count doesn't matter here: the provided rules contain nothing that changes this between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Each Aminatou's Augury creates a separate effect that applies to cards it exiled. Casting an instant off the first Aminatou's Augury doesn't preclude Amelia from casting an instant off the second one.

entries.question: Agustin casts [Seasoned Pyromancer] and has two other cards in hand, one of which is a land card. Nico controls [Leyline of the Void]. How many tokens are created?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes that Leyline of the Void exiles the discarded cards but Seasoned Pyromancer still sees them and only one nonland was discarded, so one token is created.
entries.answer:
One 1/1 red Elemental token.

How it plays out: Seasoned Pyromancer's enters-the-battlefield ability makes Agustin discard two cards, then draw two cards, then create a token for each nonland card discarded this way. Discarding means moving a card from its owner's hand to that player's graveyard [701.9a]. Agustin is an opponent of Nico, who controls Leyline of the Void, so its replacement effect ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead") applies: both discarded cards are exiled rather than reaching Agustin's graveyard.

Those cards were still discarded, and Seasoned Pyromancer's ability can still see them. Exile is a public zone, and although an object that changes zones is normally a new object with no memory of its past, an effect that moves an object to a public zone can still find that object [400.7j]. Leyline of the Void's own ruling confirms this: abilities that check whether a card was discarded still work, and spells or abilities that check the characteristics of the discarded card can find that card in exile [Leyline of the Void ruling #3].

Agustin discarded exactly two cards, one of which was a land card, so only one nonland card was discarded this way — one Elemental token. Agustin still draws two cards.

Multiplayer note: Leyline of the Void only replaces cards going to the graveyards of Nico's opponents, so the answer is the same at a two-player table or a bigger one, as long as Agustin is an opponent of Nico. If Agustin were Nico's teammate (or Nico himself), the cards would hit the graveyard normally and the token count would be unchanged anyway — still one.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One token is created. The cards discarded from hand can still be seen by Seasoned Pyromancer's effect even though going to the graveyard was replaced by going to exile.

entries.question: Aranza controls a [Welding Jar] enchanted by Nico's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Aranza's upkeep, Nico casts [Word of Seizing] to take control of the Welding Jar. What happens as the trigger resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aranza cannot sacrifice Welding Jar after Nico gains control, so the trigger's "unless" cost can't be paid and Aranza is dealt 2 damage.
entries.answer:
Aranza takes 2 damage from Curse Artifact. Because Word of Seizing has already resolved and Nico controls Welding Jar, Aranza cannot sacrifice Welding Jar when Curse Artifact's trigger resolves, so the "unless" clause fails and Curse Artifact deals 2 damage to Aranza.

Why:

- Curse Artifact's trigger reads "deals 2 damage to that player unless they sacrifice that artifact." Rule 118.12a says "[Do something] unless [a player does something else]" means the same as "[A player may do something else]. If [that player doesn't], [do something]." So the sacrifice is an optional cost Aranza may pay on resolution of the trigger; if it isn't paid, the damage happens (118.12).
- Rule 701.21a: a player can't sacrifice a permanent they don't control. Word of Seizing gave Nico control of Welding Jar until end of turn, so Aranza — the player the trigger is targeting for damage, since she was the enchanted artifact's controller at the beginning of her upkeep — has no legal way to pay. Nico is not offered the choice; only the player named by the trigger can pay it.
- Word of Seizing's split second (and [Word of Seizing ruling #6]) means that once Word of Seizing was on the stack, Aranza could only take mana abilities and certain special actions — she could not activate Welding Jar's "Sacrifice this artifact: Regenerate target artifact" ability in response. Also, casting Word of Seizing didn't alter Curse Artifact's already-triggered ability ([Word of Seizing ruling #5]); that trigger just resolves and, with the cost unpayable, deals the damage.

Timing assumption and the alternative: I'm assuming Nico cast Word of Seizing after Curse Artifact's ability triggered and that it resolved before the trigger did (which is the normal stack order). If Aranza had gotten priority before Word of Seizing was cast and sacrificed Welding Jar to its own regenerate ability, that still wouldn't help — Welding Jar would be in the graveyard, so she still couldn't pay the sacrifice cost on resolution and would still take 2 damage. The only way she avoids the damage is by still controlling Welding Jar when the trigger resolves and choosing to sacrifice it then.

Player count doesn't change anything here: the trigger's damage goes to the enchanted artifact's controller (Aranza) regardless of how many players are at the table, and only she may pay the sacrifice cost.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aranza is dealt 2 damage. Sacrificing the Welding Jar is a cost. If the cost isn't paid, the default action of dealing 2 damage to Aranza happens. Aranza cannot sacrifice a permanent that they don't control.

entries.question: Alina controls a [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle] and 5 [Mountain]s. They plays a 6th Mountain and target Nico with Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger. In response, Nico activates [Memorial to War], targeting the Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle. Will they be dealt 3 damage?
entries.reason: Both say the trigger on the stack still resolves and the condition is still met (destroying Valakut afterwards doesn’t stop the ability), so Nico can be dealt 3 damage.
entries.answer:
Yes — Nico still takes 3 damage (if Alina chooses to have the damage dealt), even though Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle is destroyed first.

Why:

1. Once a triggered ability is on the stack it exists independently of its source. Destroying or otherwise removing the source after that point doesn't affect the ability, and where the ability says the source does something ("you may have this land deal 3 damage to any target"), the game uses the source's last known information — the source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists [113.7a]. So Memorial to War destroying Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle in response does not counter or fizzle the trigger.

2. The intervening 'if' clause is still satisfied. Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's ability checks the condition twice: when the Mountain enters (Alina controlled 5 other Mountains, so it triggered) and again on resolution — it does nothing if Alina controls fewer than five Mountains other than the one that entered [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #4]. Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle is not itself a Mountain, so destroying it doesn't lower the Mountain count; Alina still controls the 5 other Mountains, and the condition is met. (Compare [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #2]: only a Mountain leaving the battlefield changes that count.)

3. Nico was targeted when the ability triggered; Alina decides whether to actually have the damage dealt as the ability resolves, since the ability says "you may" [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #1]. If Alina says yes, Nico is dealt 3 damage.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nico activated Memorial to War ({4}{R}, {T}, Sacrifice Memorial to War) while Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger was already on the stack, so Memorial to War's land-destruction resolves first. If instead Nico had somehow destroyed Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle before the 6th Mountain entered, the ability would never have triggered at all and no damage would occur.

Player count: nothing here changes with more than two players — Nico was chosen as the target when the ability triggered, and that target is unaffected by how many opponents are at the table. (The provided rules don't include any multiplayer-specific rule that would alter this.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Removing the source of an ability on the stack does not affect that ability.

entries.question: Arely equips [Barbed Batterfist] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Champion of the Flame becomes a 4/2 (1/1 +2/+2 from its ability +1/-1 from Barbed Batterfist) and does not die.
entries.answer:
No — Champion of the Flame does not die. With Barbed Batterfist attached, Champion of the Flame is a 4/2.

The math: Champion of the Flame is printed 1/1. Its own static ability gives it +2/+2 for each Aura and Equipment attached to it, and Barbed Batterfist is one Equipment attached to it, so that's +2/+2. Barbed Batterfist itself says the equipped creature gets +1/-1. Both are power/toughness modifications from static abilities, which apply together in layer 7c; they're cumulative and the order they're applied in doesn't matter (see [613.5], where multiple layer 7c effects simply add together). 1/1 + 2/+2 + 1/-1 = 4/2.

Since Champion of the Flame's toughness is 2 (greater than 0), the state-based action check that happens whenever a player would receive priority finds nothing to do to it ([704.3]). It only dies if it has 2 or more damage marked on it at that check — but a 1/1 Champion of the Flame with any damage marked would already have been destroyed before you equipped, so in the normal case there's no marked damage and it survives.

Timing note: I'm assuming Barbed Batterfist is attached with no damage already marked on Champion of the Flame. If Champion of the Flame somehow already had damage marked (for example, it was pumped earlier in the turn and took 2+ damage), attaching Barbed Batterfist raises its toughness to 2 but marked damage stays on it, and it would be destroyed at the next state-based action check if that damage is 2 or more ([704.3]).

The converse warning on Champion of the Flame's ruling matters later: if Barbed Batterfist is unattached, destroyed, or moved to another creature during the turn, Champion of the Flame drops back toward 1/1 and previously nonlethal marked damage can become lethal [Champion of the Flame ruling #1].

One aside on Barbed Batterfist: if it was equipping the 2/2 Rebel token it created, you can pay its equip cost of {1} (as a sorcery) to move it to Champion of the Flame; the Rebel token stays on the battlefield and returns to 2/2 [Barbed Batterfist ruling #1].

The provided rules here are not player-count dependent, so this answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, Champion of the Flame will be a 4/2 and not die. All continuous effects are applied instantly before state based actions are checked.

entries.question: Aviana controls a [Meng Huo's Horde] and a [Deathrite Shaman]. Nico controls a [Propaganda]. Can Aviana use Deathrite Shaman's ability to pay for the Meng Huo's Horde to attack?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude no — Propaganda's attack cost must be paid during declare attackers and Deathrite Shaman's targeted ability isn't a mana ability usable then (and any mana made earlier would have emptied).
entries.answer:
No. Aviana cannot use Deathrite Shaman's first ability to produce the mana for Propaganda's attack cost.

Why:

1. Propaganda's cost is an additional cost on the declaration of the attacker, paid during the declare attackers step at the moment attackers are declared, not an ability that can be activated later [Propaganda ruling #3][Propaganda ruling #4]. Attacking with Meng Huo's Horde while Nico's Propaganda is on the battlefield requires paying {2} (two generic mana, payable with mana of any color or colorless).

2. Declaring attackers is a turn-based action with a fixed sequence: the active player declares attackers and chooses optional costs [508.1g], the total cost is locked in [508.1h], the active player may then activate mana abilities [508.1i], and finally pays all costs — partial payment is not allowed [508.1j]. The only thing Aviana may do inside that window to make mana is activate a mana ability.

3. Deathrite Shaman's first ability ({T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color.) is not a mana ability, because it requires a target [605.1a][Deathrite Shaman ruling #2]. It uses the stack and can be responded to, so it cannot be activated during the mana-ability window in 508.1i.

4. Could Aviana just activate Deathrite Shaman earlier, in the beginning of combat step, and hold the mana? No — each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and that mana is lost [106.4]. Mana made during the beginning of combat step is gone before the declare attackers step begins [500.4]. And once the declare attackers step starts, the declaration happens as a turn-based action before anyone gets priority, so there is no chance to resolve a non-mana ability first.

So Aviana needs {2} from some other source (a real mana ability, a mana-producing land, etc.) to attack Nico with Meng Huo's Horde. Note that Deathrite Shaman's second and third abilities don't make mana at all, so they're irrelevant here.

Timing note: I'm assuming Aviana wants to activate Deathrite Shaman as part of, or immediately before, declaring attackers. If instead she activated it at some earlier point in the same step in which attackers are declared — which is impossible for the declare attackers step, since the declaration is the first thing that happens — the mana would still have to survive to the payment; mana made in any prior step is emptied.

Multiplayer: Propaganda reads "Creatures can't attack you...," so the {2} is owed only for creatures attacking Nico. In a two-player game that means every attack. With three or more players, Aviana can attack a different opponent (or a planeswalker/battle they control, if any) with Meng Huo's Horde and owe Propaganda nothing.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Propaganda imposes a cost on Meng Huo's Horde attacking, which must be paid as a part of declaring it as an attacker. Deathrite Shaman's ability is not a mana ability, so the last time it could be activated before attackers are declared is during the beginning of combat step. At the end of that step, the mana would empty from Aviana's mana pool.

entries.question: Amos casts [Rise from the Grave] targeting [Rhizome Lurcher] in their graveyard. Assuming there are no other cards in any graveyards, how many +1/+1 counters will Rhizome Lurcher enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Rhizome Lurcher enters with one +1/+1 counter because its replacement "enters with" ability counts the card itself as it enters the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Rhizome Lurcher enters the battlefield with one +1/+1 counter.

Why: Rhizome Lurcher's undergrowth ability reads "This creature enters with a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the number of creature cards in your graveyard." An "enters with..." ability is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield, and the number is determined as the permanent enters, using the game state at that moment [614.1c] [614.12]. At that moment Rhizome Lurcher itself is still counted — the card's own ruling states that if you return Rhizome Lurcher from your graveyard to the battlefield, its undergrowth ability counts itself [Rhizome Lurcher ruling #3]. Since the problem states no other cards are in any graveyard, the count is exactly 1, so Rhizome Lurcher enters as a 3/3 (2/2 plus one +1/+1 counter).

Rise from the Grave also makes Rhizome Lurcher a black Zombie in addition to its other colors and types; that doesn't change the counter count, and it only adds black and Zombie rather than overwriting Fungus Zombie or its green/black colors [Rise from the Grave ruling #3].

Assumption and multiplayer note: I'm assuming Rhizome Lurcher is in Amos's own graveyard (as the question says "their graveyard"). Rise from the Grave can target a creature card in *any* graveyard, which matters at a table with more than two players just as it does with two: if Rhizome Lurcher were instead coming out of an opponent's graveyard, "your graveyard" in the undergrowth ability would mean Amos's graveyard (Amos controls Rhizome Lurcher as it enters), Rhizome Lurcher would not be counting itself, and with no other cards anywhere it would enter with zero counters as a 2/2.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One. Rhizome Lurcher has a replacement effect that modifies how it will enter the battlefield. The game needs to know how Rhizome Lurcher will enter the battlefield, and must do that before it enters the battlefield. At that point it will be in the graveyard and will count itself.

entries.question: Ava controls [Undead Minotaur] enchanted with [Shade's Form]. Nico casts [Hour of Revelation] to destroy both Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form. Will Undead Minotaur return to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Shade's Form's "when enchanted creature dies" triggered ability sees the creature and aura immediately before they die, so the trigger goes on the stack and returns Undead Minotaur to the battlefield under Ava's control.
entries.answer:
Yes — Undead Minotaur returns to the battlefield under Ava's control.

Why: Shade's Form reads "When enchanted creature dies, return that card to the battlefield under your control." That is a leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability (its trigger condition is a permanent going from the battlefield to a graveyard), and leaves-the-battlefield abilities are one of the listed exceptions where the game "looks back in time" [603.10a]. Instead of checking what exists after the event, the game uses the existence of the ability and the appearance of the objects immediately before the event. Immediately before Hour of Revelation destroyed everything, Shade's Form was on the battlefield attached to Undead Minotaur, so the ability triggers even though Shade's Form is put into the graveyard at the exact same time as Undead Minotaur [603.10a], [603.1].

Sequence: Hour of Revelation resolves and destroys all nonland permanents simultaneously, including Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form. Shade's Form's trigger goes on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, and when it resolves, the Undead Minotaur card is returned from the graveyard to the battlefield under the control of the ability's controller — Ava, who controlled Shade's Form. Shade's Form itself stays in the graveyard; it does not come back attached, so the returned Undead Minotaur is a fresh 2/3 with no Aura on it and no {B} pump ability.

One timing caveat: this assumes Shade's Form was still attached to Undead Minotaur at the moment Hour of Revelation resolved. If Shade's Form had already left the battlefield beforehand (for example, destroyed by an earlier spell), it would not be there to trigger, and Undead Minotaur would simply stay in the graveyard.

Player count doesn't matter here — the rules provided contain nothing that treats this differently at a multiplayer table than in a two-player game; the trigger belongs to Ava as Shade's Form's controller regardless of who cast Hour of Revelation.

(Side note on the spell's cost, not affecting the outcome: Hour of Revelation costs {3}{W}{W}{W}, and its own text reduces it by {3} — the generic portion only — if there are ten or more nonland permanents on the battlefield, leaving {W}{W}{W}.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Shade's Form has a triggered ability that occurs when the enchanted permanent dies. For most triggers the game checks to see if they occur right after every event. However for "dies" triggers the game checks what the game state looked like right before they triggered to see if they trigger. In this case, checking right before Hour of Revelation resolved results in Shade's Form triggering and returning Undead Minotaur to the battlefield.

entries.question: Amara controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nehemiah casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
entries.reason: Both conclude Wayward Angel ends up a black 6/6 with no abilities because Humility sets it to a 1/1 and removes abilities while the threshold's +3/+3 and Muraganda Petroglyphs' +2/+2 still modify its P/T to 6/6.
entries.answer:
**Wayward Angel ends up as a black 6/6 Angel Horror creature with no abilities** (name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, mana value 6, still controlled by Amara).

Here's the layer-by-layer walkthrough, assuming the order stated in the question: Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield when Nehemiah's Humility resolved, so Humility has the later timestamp [613.7, 613.7a]. Wayward Angel's threshold ability is a single static ability whose effect has parts in several layers, and per [613.6] each part applies in its own layer — and once the effect starts applying, it keeps applying in the later layers even if the ability generating it gets removed along the way.

- **Layer 5 (color) [613.1e]:** Threshold is active (7+ cards in Amara's graveyard), so Wayward Angel "is black." This happens *before* Humility strips abilities in layer 6, so it sticks. Per [Wayward Angel ruling #1], Wayward Angel is black only, not white and black.
- **Layer 6 (abilities) [613.1f, 613.3]:** In timestamp order, Wayward Angel's threshold effect first grants trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature"; then Humility, with the later timestamp, removes *all* abilities from all creatures — flying, vigilance, trample, the upkeep trigger, and the threshold ability itself [Humility ruling #3]. Wayward Angel now has no abilities.
- **Layer 7b (setting P/T) [613.4, 613.4b]:** Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1.
- **Layer 7c (modifying P/T) [613.4c]:** Two effects apply, and they simply add together (order doesn't matter): the threshold effect's +3/+3 still applies under [613.6] even though the ability was removed in layer 6, and Muraganda Petroglyphs gives +2/+2 because, as of layer 6, Wayward Angel is a creature with no abilities. 1/1 + 3/+3 + 2/+2 = **6/6**.

Muraganda Petroglyphs itself is unaffected — it's an enchantment, not a creature, so Humility doesn't touch it, and its static ability keeps working. Note also that per [Muraganda Petroglyphs ruling #1] any text at all counts as an ability, which is exactly why the +2/+2 only turns on once Humility has scrubbed Wayward Angel clean.

Timing caveat: if instead Wayward Angel had entered the battlefield *after* Humility resolved (later timestamp), then in layer 6 Humility would apply first and the threshold effect second, leaving Wayward Angel with trample and the sacrifice trigger. It would then have abilities, Muraganda Petroglyphs would not apply, and it would be a black 4/4 (1/1 base +3/+3) with trample and the upkeep trigger.

Player count doesn't matter here: Humility says "all creatures" and Muraganda Petroglyphs says "creatures," so both apply regardless of controller, and the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Wayward Angel is a Black, 6/6 creature with no abilities. The rest of its characteristics remain the same as printed on the card. 
Wayward Angel's threshold ability changes both its color, abilities, and P/T. Therefore, it applies in layers 5, 6, and 7 with the appropriate parts applying in their appropriate layers, and the layers are applied in order. Similarly, Humility's effect is applied in layers 6 and 7, as appropriate. 
Applying layers in order:
- In layer 5, Wayward Angel becomes black. 
- In layer 6 there are two contending effects: Wayward Angel's ability giving it trample and an upkeep triggered ability, and Humility's ability removing all abilities from Wayward Angel. There is no dependency between the two, since Wayward Angel's ability has already started applying in a previous layer, and will continue to apply even if removed by Humility's ability. The effects are then applied in timestamp order with Wayward Angel's ability applying first, since it has an earlier timestamp. So in layer 6, Wayward Angel first gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature.", and then loses all abilities to Humility.
- In layer 7, P/T setting effects are applied first, so that Humility first turns Wayward Angel into a 1/1. Then effects modifying P/T are applied, of which there are two: Wayward Angel's own ability that, even though removed, continues to apply and gives it +3/+3, and Muraganda Petroglyphs's ability giving Wayward Angel +2/+2 since it now has no abilities. Wayward Angel's P/T is finally 6/6.

entries.question: Nayeli controls [Trinisphere]. Ainsley casts [Noxious Revival], paying 2 life for the Phyrexian mana. What is the total cost of the Noxious Revival?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final cost ({3} and 2 life) and correctly explains that Ainsley can choose to pay 2 life for the Phyrexian symbol and that Trinisphere then raises the mana component to three.
entries.answer:
Ainsley pays {3} (three generic mana) plus the 2 life. Because Ainsley chose to pay 2 life for the Phyrexian symbol, the mana component of Noxious Revival's cost is nothing, so Trinisphere raises it to three mana — and that added mana is generic, payable with any colors or colorless mana [107.4f].

Why, step by step:
- {G/P} is a Phyrexian mana symbol: it can be paid with one green mana or by paying 2 life [107.4f].
- Ainsley announces the choice to pay 2 life while proposing the spell (the same point at which modes and X are chosen), which is before the total cost is calculated [601.2b], [Noxious Revival ruling #3].
- The total cost is then determined: mana cost, plus additional costs and increases, minus reductions, and then effects that directly affect the total cost are applied and the cost is locked in [601.2f]. Trinisphere is applied last, after all increases and reductions, if the mana component is less than three mana [Trinisphere ruling #1].
- With 2 life chosen, Noxious Revival's mana component is zero mana, which is less than three, so Trinisphere makes it three mana. Locked-in total cost: {3} and 2 life.

Note the alternative choice: if Ainsley had instead announced paying {G} for the Phyrexian symbol, the mana component would be one green mana, and Trinisphere would bring it to three mana as {2}{G} — the green requirement stays, only generic mana is added. Ainsley cannot switch after the cost is locked in [601.2f].

Also note Noxious Revival's mana value stays 1 regardless of what Ainsley actually paid [Trinisphere ruling #1].

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; Trinisphere affects each spell cast by any player, including Nayeli's own, and nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: {3} and 2 life. While casting Noxious Revival, Ainsley chooses whether to pay life or mana for each Phyrexian mana symbol in the cost. Trinisphere is applied afterwards and increases the cost up to the minimum of 3 mana.

entries.question: Anakin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Maritime Guard] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Anakin casts [Clever Impersonator], choosing to copy the Mizzium Transreliquat and then choosing to copy the Animate Dead with its new copy ability as it enters the battlefield. They choose to enchant a [Balduvian Barbarians] in their graveyard. After Clever Impersonator's trigger resolves and returns the Balduvian Barbarians to the battlefield, Anakin activates the ability of the Clever Impersonator to turn it into a copy of Maritime Guard. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Clever Impersonator cannot enter as Animate Dead (so Balduvian Barbarians isn't returned) and instead enters as Sakashima, later able to become a copy of Maritime Guard.
entries.answer:
**The key step fails: Clever Impersonator cannot become a copy of Animate Dead, so Balduvian Barbarians is never returned. Clever Impersonator simply enters as a copy of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces (with Mizzium Transreliquat's {1}{U}{R} ability), and the later activation then makes it a permanent copy of Maritime Guard.**

Step by step:

**1. What Clever Impersonator copies.** Clever Impersonator's replacement ability lets it enter as a copy of any nonland permanent, and when the chosen permanent is itself a copy, Clever Impersonator enters as whatever that permanent is copying [Clever Impersonator ruling #5], [707.2]. Mizzium Transreliquat used its second ability, which does not wear off and leaves it a copy of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} ability [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #1], and the results of all copy effects are copied [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #4]. So Clever Impersonator enters as a legendary 3/1 Sakashima of a Thousand Faces that also has the {1}{U}{R} "become a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability" ability. (Mizzium Transreliquat could legally target Sakashima of a Thousand Faces in the first place only because Mycosynth Lattice makes every permanent an artifact.)

**2. The Sakashima choice is illegal.** Because Clever Impersonator enters as Sakashima of a Thousand Faces, Sakashima's own "as it enters" copy ability is active and can be applied [707.5], [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #1], [Clever Impersonator ruling #6]. But that ability reads "enter as a copy of **another creature you control**." Animate Dead is an Aura, and Mycosynth Lattice only makes permanents artifacts in addition to their other types — it does not make them creatures; an Aura would need something like March of the Machines to become a creature [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4]. Animate Dead is therefore an artifact enchantment Aura, not a creature, and is not a legal choice. Clever Impersonator stays a Sakashima of a Thousand Faces copy with the {1}{U}{R} ability. Note that if Anakin had wanted Animate Dead, Clever Impersonator's *own* ability ("any nonland permanent") could have chosen it — but that choice was spent on Mizzium Transreliquat.

**3. No Animate Dead trigger, no Balduvian Barbarians.** Since Clever Impersonator never becomes an Animate Dead, its enters-the-battlefield trigger never exists, nothing is enchanted, and Balduvian Barbarians stays in the graveyard.

**4. Legend rule.** Anakin now controls two permanents named Sakashima of a Thousand Faces (Mizzium Transreliquat and Clever Impersonator). Both copies include Sakashima's other ability, "The 'legend rule' doesn't apply to permanents you control," so neither is sacrificed [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #7].

**5. The activation on Maritime Guard.** Clever Impersonator has the {1}{U}{R} Mizzium Transreliquat ability, so it can target Maritime Guard — legal because Mycosynth Lattice makes Maritime Guard an artifact. Mycosynth Lattice's third ability lets Anakin pay the {U} and {R} with mana of any color (or colorless mana), though it removes no other restrictions on that mana [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1]. On resolution, Clever Impersonator permanently becomes a copy of Maritime Guard — a 1/3 Merfolk Soldier (an artifact and colorless because of Mycosynth Lattice) — except it keeps the {1}{U}{R} ability [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #1]. It loses Sakashima's copy ability and legend-rule ability. It does **not** get -1/-0: Animate Dead is attached to the original Maritime Guard, and non-copy effects, counters, and Auras aren't copied [707.2], [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #2], [Clever Impersonator ruling #10]. The original Maritime Guard, Animate Dead, and Mizzium Transreliquat-as-Sakashima are all unaffected.

**Timing note:** I'm assuming the Sakashima choice is attempted as Clever Impersonator enters (the only time it could be) and that the {1}{U}{R} activation happens afterward. If Anakin instead activated {1}{U}{R} on Maritime Guard while responding to something, the result is the same — the copy effect just applies at whatever point it resolves and doesn't wear off.

**Player count:** nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table; every effect involved affects only Anakin's own permanents or applies equally to everything on the battlefield.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. When Clever Impersonator enters the battlefield and copies Sakashima of a Thousand Faces, it then hard Sakashima of a Thousand Faces's ability to enter the battlefield as a copy of a creature, but it's attempting to copy an enchantment. This is illegal, since Sakashima of a Thousand Faces can only copy creatures, not enchantments.

entries.question: Amare casts [Insatiable Hemophage] targeting [Canal Monitor] to mutate unto it. Can Nico cast [Withering Boon] to counter Insatiable Hemophage?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — a spell cast for its mutate cost is still a creature spell and can be targeted and countered by Withering Boon.
entries.answer:
Yes. A mutating Insatiable Hemophage is still a creature spell, so Nico can target it with Withering Boon.

Why: mutate is a static ability that functions while the spell is on the stack; paying the mutate cost {2}{B} instead of Insatiable Hemophage's mana cost {3}{B} is just an alternative cost, and it makes the spell "a mutating creature spell" that targets a non-Human creature with the same owner — here, Canal Monitor [702.140a]. Nothing about that changes Insatiable Hemophage's card type: it is still a Creature spell on the stack. Withering Boon says "Counter target creature spell," and per its ruling a "creature spell" is any spell with the type Creature [Withering Boon ruling #2]. So Insatiable Hemophage is a legal target.

Costs for Nico: Withering Boon costs {1}{B} — one generic mana plus one black mana — and, as an additional cost to cast it, Nico must pay 3 life [Withering Boon ruling #1]. The life payment is part of casting, not part of resolution, so Nico pays it even if Withering Boon is later countered or its target becomes illegal.

If Withering Boon resolves and counters Insatiable Hemophage, Insatiable Hemophage never resolves, so it never mutates onto Canal Monitor and its "Whenever this creature mutates" ability never triggers — Canal Monitor is simply left alone as a 5/3 Lizard. Also note that Withering Boon targets the spell Insatiable Hemophage, not Canal Monitor; Canal Monitor being the mutate target is irrelevant to Withering Boon's legality.

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table — any opponent with priority can respond. The only multiplayer-specific note in the provided material concerns Insatiable Hemophage's mutate trigger in Two-Headed Giant (the opposing team loses twice X while you gain X) [Insatiable Hemophage ruling #1], and that trigger never happens at all if Withering Boon counters the spell.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes, Nico can use Withering Boon to counter Insatiable Hemophage if it was cast for the mutate cost. A spell that was cast for a mutate cost is still a creature spell and, therefore, can be countered by Withering Boon. ([702.140a])

entries.question: Amirah controls Azors Gateway with 4 different CMC cards exiled by it. They targets it with [Karn's Touch]. After that resolves, they activates [Azor's Gateway], and transforms it into [Sanctum of the Sun]. What are the characteristics of the new object after it has transformed?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Karn's Touch remains in effect after the transform, leaving Sanctum of the Sun as a legendary artifact land creature with P/T 2/2 and its mana ability until the effect ends.
entries.answer:
After the transform, the permanent is Sanctum of the Sun, and it is a **legendary artifact land creature** with power and toughness each equal to its mana value (2), so a 2/2, and it still has Sanctum of the Sun's "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total" ability. It is untapped (the transform ability untaps it as part of resolution).

Why:

1. **The Karn's Touch effect survives the transform.** Transforming does not create a new object, and any effects that applied to the permanent continue to apply to it [712.18]. Karn's Touch's effect is a continuous effect with a fixed duration — until end of turn [611.1] — so it keeps applying to the same permanent even though the face-up face is now Sanctum of the Sun.

2. **Types stack rather than replace.** Karn's Touch says the permanent "becomes an artifact creature." An effect that makes something an "artifact creature" lets the object retain all of its prior card types, supertypes, and subtypes [205.1b]. Sanctum of the Sun is printed as a Legendary Land, so with Karn's Touch applied it is a Legendary Artifact Land Creature. It gains no creature subtype (Karn's Touch grants none), and it keeps its land status and therefore its mana ability, which is still a mana ability that doesn't use the stack [Azor's Gateway // Sanctum of the Sun].

3. **Power/toughness.** Karn's Touch sets power and toughness each equal to the permanent's mana value [Karn's Touch]. The mana value of this double-faced card is 2 (from the front face Azor's Gateway's {2} cost — two generic mana, no colored or {C} symbols), so Sanctum of the Sun is a 2/2 while Karn's Touch's effect lasts. Note the provided context doesn't include the general rule text for how a back face derives its mana value; I'm relying on the card data listing this card at MV 2.

4. **Summoning sickness / activating the ability.** Once Karn's Touch resolved, Azor's Gateway was a creature, so its {T} ability — and later Sanctum of the Sun's {T} mana ability — can only be activated if Amirah has continuously controlled that permanent since the beginning of their most recent turn; it doesn't matter how long it has been a creature [Karn's Touch ruling #1]. I'm assuming Amirah met that condition when they activated Azor's Gateway; if the permanent had come under their control this turn, that activation wouldn't have been legal in the first place. I'm also assuming the card drawn and exiled by that activation had a fifth distinct mana value, which is what enabled the life gain, untap, and transform [Azor's Gateway // Sanctum of the Sun].

At end of turn the Karn's Touch effect ends, and the permanent goes back to being just a Legendary Land named Sanctum of the Sun with no power or toughness.

None of this depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Sanctum of the Sun is a 2/2 Legendary artifact creature land with the ability "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total". The requirement that Azor's Gateway be an artifact is part of the targeting restriction of the spell, after the spell resolves, it creates a continuous effect on the permanent that was targeted (in this case Azor's Gateway) that lasts until end of turn. When a double-faced card transforms it doesn't become a new object, and any effects that applied to it before the transformation will continue to apply afterwards.

entries.question: Aryana controls [Ascended Lawmage] and [Cemetery Gate]. Nicholas controls [Onakke Ogre] enchanted by their [Paralyze]. Aryana casts [Sudden Disappearance] targeting Nicholas. When the trigger resolves at the beginning of the next end step, what can Paralyze enchant?
entries.reason: The candidate says Paralyze can choose either Onakke Ogre (returning simultaneously) or Ascended Lawmage, whereas the reference states only Ascended Lawmage is legal, so the final rulings disagree.
entries.answer:
Nicholas chooses, and his legal choices are Onakke Ogre (which returns to the battlefield at the same time) or Aryana's Ascended Lawmage — but not Aryana's Cemetery Gate.

Why:

- Sudden Disappearance exiled every nonland permanent Nicholas controlled, which includes both Onakke Ogre and Paralyze itself (an Aura is a nonland permanent). At the beginning of the next end step the delayed trigger returns those cards to the battlefield under their owner's control, so Paralyze comes back under Nicholas's control.
- Because Paralyze is entering the battlefield by something other than resolving as an Aura spell, and Sudden Disappearance doesn't specify what it enchants, Nicholas chooses what Paralyze enchants as it enters, and the choice must be legal for its enchant creature ability and any other applicable effects [303.4f]. This is not targeting.
- Ascended Lawmage is a legal choice. Hexproof only stops it from being the target of spells or abilities its controller's opponents control [702.11b]; attaching an Aura on entry involves no targeting, so hexproof doesn't prevent Nicholas from choosing Ascended Lawmage. Paralyze's enters trigger would then tap Ascended Lawmage, and it wouldn't untap during Aryana's untap step unless Aryana pays {4} at the beginning of her upkeep.
- Cemetery Gate is not a legal choice. Paralyze is a black Aura (mana cost {B}), and a permanent with protection from black can't be enchanted by black Auras; if one somehow ended up attached, it would go to its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [702.16c]. So Nicholas can't choose Cemetery Gate under rule 303.4f's "legal object" requirement.
- Onakke Ogre returns to the battlefield simultaneously with Paralyze, and it's an ordinary creature with no protection or other restriction, so it's the natural (and typical) choice. Note the provided rules don't include a specific rule text about attaching to permanents entering simultaneously; if your group rules that only creatures already on the battlefield count, Nicholas's only remaining option in the two-player setup described would be Ascended Lawmage.
- Any other creature on the battlefield is also a legal choice if it has no protection/other restriction. If Paralyze has no legal object to enchant at all, it can't enter attached to anything.

Multiplayer: the analysis is unchanged in substance. Sudden Disappearance targets a single player (Nicholas), so only his nonland permanents were exiled; with more than two players, Nicholas may also choose any legal creature controlled by any other player at the table, subject to the same protection restriction [702.16c] and the legality requirement of [303.4f].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Just Ascended Lawmage. Cemetery Gate has protection from black, so it can't be enchanted by anything black. Onakke Ogre isn't on the battlefield when Nicholas chooses what to enchant. Hexproof doesn't prevent an Aura from becoming attached to the Ascended Lawmage.
entries.human_note:
there's a ruling on Brago King Eternal that actually explains this better. Here's a stack exchange about it:

---
Auras can't enchant a permanent that enters the battlefield at the same time.

There is an explicit ruling on Brago's gatherer page:

If you exile an Aura with Brago's last ability, the Aura's owner chooses what it will enchant as it comes back onto the battlefield. An aura put onto the battlefield this way doesn't target anything (so it could be attached to an opponent's permanent with hexproof, for example), but the Aura's enchant ability restricts what it can be attached to. The Aura can't enter the battlefield enchanting a permanent that enters the battlefield at the same time. If the Aura can't legally be attached to anything, it remains exiled. (202-11-10)

That's the most direct answer, but we can also derive this from the comprehensive rules.

First we have to understand what exactly happens when an aura enters the battlefield, but wasn't cast:

CR 303.4f If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player's control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn't specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura's enchant ability and any other applicable effects.

The clue here is the word "as", which means your choice (of what object to enchant) is a "replacement effect":

CR 614.1c: Effects that read "[This permanent] enters with...," "As [this permanent] enters...," or "[This permanent] enters as..." are replacement effects.

And any choices required by replacement effects must be made before the event occurs:

614.12a: If a replacement effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield requires a choice, that choice is made before the permanent enters the battlefield.

So you have to choose a permanent to enchant while all cards Brago exiled are still in exile. In your specific case, then, Brago himself isn't in play and is therefore not a valid choice for the aura to enchant.
---

so while the ruling is for a different card, this lays out the rules that lead to it. seems like we are missing some gold.

entries.question: Amaris controls [Eruth, Tormented Prophet] and, during their draw step, they attempt to dredge [Golgari Grave-Troll]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Amaris, as the affected player, chooses one replacement effect and if they choose dredge they mill six and return Golgari Grave-Troll while Eruth's replacement does nothing.
entries.answer:
Amaris gets to pick exactly one of the two replacement effects, and if they pick dredge, dredge is what happens: Amaris mills six cards and returns Golgari Grave-Troll from the graveyard to hand, and Eruth, Tormented Prophet's effect does nothing at all — no cards are exiled.

Why: both Eruth, Tormented Prophet ("If you would draw a card, exile the top two cards of your library instead") and Golgari Grave-Troll's dredge 6 ("if you would draw a card, you may instead mill six cards and return this card from your graveyard to your hand" — dredge functions only from the graveyard, per [702.52a]) are replacement effects trying to modify the same draw event. When two or more replacement effects would modify the same event, the affected player chooses which one to apply [616.1], and any of the applicable effects may be chosen [616.1e]. Amaris is the affected player, so Amaris chooses. Choosing dredge here is legal only if Amaris has at least six cards in their library; you can't announce dredge with fewer [702.52a] (Golgari Grave-Troll ruling: "You can't attempt to use a dredge ability if you don't have enough cards in your library").

Once dredge is applied, the draw event is replaced and never happens [614.6]. Eruth, Tormented Prophet's replacement effect was waiting to replace a draw that no longer occurs, so it simply doesn't do anything [614.7] — it does not get to also exile two cards, and it is not applied to the mill. Also, once Amaris announces they're applying dredge, no player can take actions until Golgari Grave-Troll is in hand and the six cards are milled (Golgari Grave-Troll ruling).

The other choice: if Amaris instead applies Eruth, Tormented Prophet, they exile the top two cards of their library and may play those cards this turn, the draw never happens, and dredge does nothing [614.6], [614.7]. Amaris may apply Eruth, Tormented Prophet even with fewer than two cards in library, exiling whatever is there and not losing the game for the attempted draw (Eruth, Tormented Prophet ruling).

Multiplayer note: only Amaris is the affected player here, so only Amaris chooses and the answer is identical at any table size. APNAP order [616.1] would matter only if multiple players had to make such choices simultaneously.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Amaris can dredge Golgari Grave-Troll instead of drawing. There are two replacement effects attempting to replace Amaris's draw. Since they are the affected player, they choose whether to exile the card with Eruth, Tormented Prophet or dredge with Golgari Grave-Troll. Once one of the replacement effects has been applied, the "draw" event no longer exists, and the other replacement effect does not apply.

entries.question: Nicole controls [Oraxid]. Can Austin cast [First Volley] targeting Oraxid with [Evermind] spliced onto it?
entries.reason: Both conclude the answer is No — splicing Evermind onto First Volley does not allow it to target Oraxid — so the candidate reaches the same final ruling.
entries.answer:
No. First Volley can't legally target Oraxid, whether or not Evermind is spliced onto it, because Oraxid has protection from red and First Volley is a red spell (mana cost {1}{R}). Splicing Evermind onto First Volley does not fix this.

Why splicing doesn't help:

- Splice is a static ability that works from your hand: "You may reveal this card from your hand as you cast a [quality] spell. If you do, that spell gains the text of this card's rules text and you pay [cost] as an additional cost" [702.47a]. Evermind's splice cost is Splice onto Arcane {1}{U}, and First Volley is an instant — Arcane, so it's a legal spell to splice onto.
- Splicing only adds rules text: it "changes a spell's text by adding the rules text of the card with splice to the spell, following that spell's own rules text. It doesn't modify or replace any of that spell's own text" [612.10]. So the spell on the stack is still First Volley — still a red spell with First Volley's own damage text — that additionally says "Draw a card." Evermind's blue color (given by its color indicator, and Evermind is blue in all zones) [204.1] [204.2] [Evermind ruling #2] stays with the Evermind card in Austin's hand; it does not recolor First Volley.
- Targets are chosen after revealing the spliced card, and every instance of "target" on the resulting spell must be chosen legally [Evermind ruling #6]. Oraxid is not a legal choice for First Volley's target because of protection from red.

Cost note, if Austin instead splices Evermind onto a First Volley aimed at a legal target: he pays First Volley's {1}{R} plus Evermind's splice cost of {1}{U} as an additional cost — a total of {2} generic, {R}, and {U}. Evermind stays in Austin's hand [702.47a].

Two caveats on grounding: the full definition of the protection keyword (including "can't be targeted by red spells") isn't among the rules provided here; I'm relying on Oraxid's printed "Protection from red" text itself. And the number of players at the table doesn't change any of this — the provided context contains no multiplayer-specific rule that would alter it; if the spell did resolve against a legal target, the 1 damage to "that creature's controller" would go to that creature's controller regardless of how many opponents are present.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Evermind has a color indicator making it blue, which is not granted by splice since it's not part of the card's text.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Gisa and Geralf] and has cast a spell with it this turn. They casts [Acrobatic Maneuver], targeting the Gisa and Geralf. After it resolves, can they cast another card from their graveyard?
entries.reason: Both conclude Yes — because Acrobatic Maneuver makes Gisa and Geralf a new object that grants a fresh once-per-turn permission to cast a Zombie creature from the graveyard, allowing Aubrey to cast another such spell (subject to timing and ownership).
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Aubrey owns Gisa and Geralf and it's still Aubrey's main phase with an empty stack, Aubrey may cast one more Zombie creature spell from their graveyard this turn.

Why: Acrobatic Maneuver exiles Gisa and Geralf and returns that card to the battlefield. An object that changes zones becomes a new object with no memory of or relation to its previous existence [400.7], and Acrobatic Maneuver's own ruling confirms the returned permanent is a new object with no connection to the one that was exiled [Acrobatic Maneuver ruling #1]. That new Gisa and Geralf therefore has its own unused "once during each of your turns" permission — exactly the situation covered by [Gisa and Geralf ruling #2]: if you cast one Zombie creature spell from your graveyard and then have a new Gisa and Geralf come under your control that same turn, you may cast another Zombie creature spell from your graveyard that turn.

Two limits to keep in mind:
- The permission only lets Aubrey cast a Zombie creature spell from the graveyard, not any card, and Aubrey must pay its costs [Gisa and Geralf ruling #6].
- Normal timing rules still apply [Gisa and Geralf ruling #3]. A creature spell needs Aubrey's main phase with an empty stack (unless it has flash). Timing assumption: I'm reading this as Aubrey casting Acrobatic Maneuver during their own main phase, so once it resolves and the stack is empty the second Zombie creature spell can be cast right away. If instead Acrobatic Maneuver was cast during an opponent's turn or during combat, Aubrey simply can't cast the Zombie creature spell until their own main phase — and the fresh permission on the new Gisa and Geralf would be available on Aubrey's next turn regardless.

One other caveat: Acrobatic Maneuver returns the card under its owner's control, so if Aubrey isn't the owner of Gisa and Geralf, it comes back under the owner's control and Aubrey gets nothing from it. This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Gisa and Geralf's effect allows Aubrey to cast one spell with that effect. If the Gisa and Geralf leaves the battlefield and then returns, it is a completely new object, generating a new effect. That effect counts no cards cast with it yet this turn.

entries.question: In a game of commander, Natasha has shuffled their commander into their library. Adan casts [Praetor's Grasp] targeting Natasha and finds Natasha's commander. Can Natasha choose to put it into the command zone?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Natasha, as the commander’s owner, may choose to move the exiled (even face-down) commander to the command zone via the commander state-based action.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Praetor's Grasp resolves and Natasha's commander is in the exile zone, the Commander state-based action applies: if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and it was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone (704.6d, 903.9a). Natasha is the owner, so Natasha gets that choice.

Details that matter here:

- Being face down doesn't matter. A commander that's been turned face down is still a commander, and the commander designation is an attribute of the card itself that it keeps in every zone (903.3). So the exiled face-down card is still Natasha's commander and still eligible for the command-zone state-based action.
- The choice is Natasha's alone, and it's a one-shot window. The state-based action only applies while the object was put into exile "since the last time state-based actions were checked" (704.6d, 903.9a). If Natasha declines at that check, the commander stays in exile.
- If Natasha declines, Adan keeps the benefit of Praetor's Grasp: "You may play that card for as long as it remains exiled," paying its costs and obeying normal timing rules (Praetor's Grasp ruling #1). If Natasha takes the command-zone option, the card leaves exile and Adan can no longer play it.
- One practical wrinkle the provided material doesn't resolve: a Praetor's Grasp ruling says other players, including the card's owner, can't look at the card while it remains exiled (Praetor's Grasp ruling #2). Nothing in the rules given here explains how Natasha is meant to be informed that the exiled card is the commander; the state-based action itself is unambiguous, but the information-handling procedure isn't covered by the context provided.

Player count: Commander games are commonly multiplayer, and nothing in the rules cited changes with the number of players — the commander's owner (Natasha) makes the choice whether the table is two players or more. Praetor's Grasp targets one opponent regardless.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Despite being face-down, it's still Natasha's commander, and they can choose to have it move to the command zone as a state-based action.

entries.question: Nico controls [Lion's Eye Diamond]. Addison casts [Wipe Away] targeting the Lion's Eye Diamond. Can Nico activate it in response?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Lion's Eye Diamond's ability is a mana ability and split second does not prevent activating mana abilities, so Nico can activate it in response.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can activate Lion's Eye Diamond while Wipe Away is on the stack.

Why: Split second on Wipe Away means "As long as this spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities" [702.61a]. Mana abilities are the explicit exception — players may still activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack [702.61b], and players still receive priority; their options are just limited (Wipe Away ruling #1).

Lion's Eye Diamond's ability qualifies as a mana ability: it doesn't require a target, it could add mana when it resolves, and it isn't a loyalty ability [605.1a]. Its own ruling confirms this: "The ability is a mana ability, so it is activated and resolves as a mana ability, but it can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant" (Lion's Eye Diamond ruling #1). Note that the timing restriction "Activate only as an instant" doesn't matter here — such wording only means the player must have priority, and effects that stop a player from casting instants don't stop the action itself unless the action is actually casting an instant spell [304.5]. Split second is exactly such an effect, so it doesn't shut off Lion's Eye Diamond.

So Nico, on receiving priority after Wipe Away is cast, discards their hand, sacrifices Lion's Eye Diamond, and adds three mana of any one color. Nico does not need to hold an instant card to do this [304.5].

Two caveats: (1) What happens to Wipe Away once its only target, Lion's Eye Diamond, is gone from the battlefield is governed by the target-legality rules on resolution, which weren't included in the context here, so I won't assert that outcome from the provided material. (2) The mana Nico adds sits in Nico's mana pool, and with Wipe Away's split second still active Nico generally can't cast a spell with it while Wipe Away remains on the stack — after Wipe Away resolves or otherwise leaves the stack, players may again cast spells and activate abilities before the next object on the stack resolves (Wipe Away ruling #6).

Multiplayer: nothing changes. Split second restricts every player equally [702.61a], and the mana-ability exception [702.61b] applies to Nico the same whether the game has two players or more; any other player could likewise activate their own mana abilities in response.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Lion's Eye Diamond's ability is a mana ability. Split second does not prevent mana abilities from being activated. "Activate only as an instant" simply means that Nico must have priority, not that Nico could actually cast an instant at that time.

entries.question: Avah controls [Dakmor Scorpion] and [Winding Constrictor]. Nelson casts [Cannibalize] targeting them both. When it resolves, they choose to exile Winding Constrictor and to put +1/+1 counters on Dakmor Scorpion. How many +1/+1 counters are placed on Dakmor Scorpion?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude Cannibalize exhales Winding Constrictor before placing counters, so Constrictor's replacement ability isn't present and only two +1/+1 counters are placed.
entries.answer:
Two +1/+1 counters are placed on Dakmor Scorpion — Winding Constrictor's replacement effect does not apply.

Why: Cannibalize reads "Choose two target creatures controlled by the same player. Exile one of those creatures and put two +1/+1 counters on the other." Its controller (Nelson) follows the instructions in the order written during resolution [608.2c]. So the exile happens first: Winding Constrictor leaves the battlefield for the exile zone. Only after that does the second instruction — putting two +1/+1 counters on Dakmor Scorpion — occur.

Winding Constrictor's ability is a replacement effect that reads "If one or more counters would be put on an artifact or creature you control, that many plus one of each of those kinds of counters are put on that permanent instead." It's a static ability of a permanent, so it can only modify a counter-placement event while Winding Constrictor is on the battlefield. By the time the counters would be put on Dakmor Scorpion, Winding Constrictor is in exile, so nothing bumps the count from two to three.

The mirrored case is worth noting: if Nelson had instead chosen to exile Dakmor Scorpion and put the counters on Winding Constrictor, Winding Constrictor would still be on the battlefield when the counters are placed and would replace two counters with three on itself.

A note on the target requirement rather than timing: Cannibalize's targets must be two creatures controlled by the same player, and per its ruling the targets are locked in on announcement while the choice of which is exiled and which gets counters is made on resolution. That ruling is what makes the order above unambiguous here — there's no reading in which the counters are placed before the exile. Player count doesn't matter: this works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since both targets must belong to one player (here, Avah) regardless of how many opponents Nelson has.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 2. Spells resolve in the order printed on the card. Winding Constrictor is exiled before placing the counters on Dakmor Scorpion.

entries.question: Alex controls [Rhythm of the Wild], [Grumgully, the Generous], [Renata, Called to the Hunt], and [Hardened Scales]. Alex then casts [Grizzled Outrider]. If they chooses to put a counter on Grizzled Outrider for Rhythm of the Wild, how many +1/+1 counters will it enter with in total?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude it enters with four +1/+1 counters—one from choosing Riot's counter mode, one from Grumgully, one from Renata, and one additional counter from Hardened Scales (which only applies once).
entries.answer:
Grizzled Outrider enters the battlefield with 4 +1/+1 counters.

How that adds up:

- Riot from Rhythm of the Wild: Grizzled Outrider is a nontoken creature Alex controls, so it has riot; Alex chooses the +1/+1 counter mode → 1 counter. (Riot is a replacement effect, so no one can respond to the choice.)
- Grumgully, the Generous: Grizzled Outrider is an Elf Warrior, i.e., another non-Human creature Alex controls, so it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter → 2.
- Renata, Called to the Hunt: Grizzled Outrider is another creature Alex controls, so it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter → 3.
- Hardened Scales: one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on Grizzled Outrider, so that many plus one are put on instead → 4.

All four of these are replacement effects modifying how Grizzled Outrider enters ([614.1c]), so Alex, as the controller of the affected object, picks the order to apply them, one at a time, repeating until none are left ([616.1], [616.1e], [616.1f], and the Hardened Scales ruling that you choose the order when multiple effects modify counter counts). The order doesn't change the result here: Hardened Scales gets only one opportunity to apply and adds exactly one counter, not a doubling ([614.5]). So whether Hardened Scales is applied right after riot (1 → 2, then +1 from Grumgully, the Generous and +1 from Renata, Called to the Hunt) or last (3 → 4), the total is 4.

One timing note: if Alex had instead chosen haste for riot, Grizzled Outrider would still get the Grumgully, the Generous and Renata, Called to the Hunt counters plus one from Hardened Scales, for 3 counters and haste. Also, per the Grumgully, the Generous and Renata, Called to the Hunt rulings, those bonuses only fail to apply to creatures entering simultaneously with them, which isn't the case here since both are already on the battlefield.

Player count doesn't matter: the choice of how to order the replacement effects belongs to Alex as controller of Grizzled Outrider, and APNAP ordering ([616.1]) only comes up if two or more players must make such choices at the same time. The answer is 4 counters in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Four. Every card on the battlefield has a replacement effect that modifies how Grizzled Outrider will enter the battlefield. When applying replacement effects, each effect has a chance to apply once and only once, so even though Alex can choose which order to apply the effects in, Hardened Scales will only get one chance to modify how many counters Grizzled Outrider enters the battlefield with, and will only ever add one additional counter.

entries.question: Ann has a [Sphere of Resistance], a Plains and a Swamp. Can Ann cast [Prismatic Ending] targeting [Drake Familiar]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling: Ann can cast Prismatic Ending with X=0 (paying the Sphere tax) and by paying {W} and {B} she spent two colors of mana, so Drake Familiar is exiled.
entries.answer:
Yes — and it will actually exile Drake Familiar.

Costs: Prismatic Ending's mana cost is {X}{W}. Sphere of Resistance says "Spells cost {1} more to cast," and that increase applies to Ann too (Sphere of Resistance ruling). Cost increases are added when the total cost is determined [601.2f]. Ann announces X as part of casting [601.2b]; with only two lands she must choose X=0, giving a total cost of {1}{W} (one generic plus one white).

Paying it: Ann taps Plains for {W} to pay the {W} symbol, and taps Swamp for {B} to pay the {1} generic (generic mana can be paid with mana of any color). She has therefore spent two colors of mana — white and black — to cast Prismatic Ending. Note this isn't the forbidden "paying extra mana just to add colors" case (Prismatic Ending ruling #3): the {1} from Sphere of Resistance is mandatory, and she's simply choosing which color pays it.

Targeting and resolution: targets are chosen when the spell is cast [115.1a], and Drake Familiar is a nonland permanent, so it's a legal target. The mana value comparison is not a targeting condition — it's checked only on resolution (Prismatic Ending ruling #1). Drake Familiar's mana value is 2 ({1}{U}), and 2 colors of mana were spent, so 2 ≤ 2 and Drake Familiar is exiled. (Compare Prismatic Ending ruling #2's example structure: more colors spent means a higher mana value can be exiled.)

Caveat on payment choice: if Ann instead paid the generic {1} with a second white source (she can't here — she has only one Plains), only one color would have been spent, Drake Familiar's mana value 2 would exceed it, and the spell would resolve doing nothing.

Player count: this doesn't change with the number of players. Sphere of Resistance's increase applies to every player's spells, and nothing here depends on who the opponents are, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes Ann can cast Prismatic Ending targeting Drake Familiar. Ann can target Drake Familiar regardless of whether the final spell will exile it or not, as any card is targetable with Prismatic Ending, and it's only exiled if the conditions are met. Then Ann chooses the value of X, in this case they can select 0, then add Sphere of Resistance's tax resulting in a required mana payment of two. If Ann chooses to use two different colors of mana, when the spell resolves it will see that two colors were spent and exile the target if it's mana value is two or less.

entries.question: Abram attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Skewer the Critics] from Nico's library. Can Abram pay Skewer the Critics's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Abram can use Robber of the Rich's "spend mana as though it were any color" effect to pay Skewer the Critics's spectacle cost with a single colorless mana, so the candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Yes — Abram can pay Skewer the Critics's spectacle cost of {R} using a single colorless mana ({C}), provided the spectacle condition is met and he casts it at a legal time.

Why it works:

- Spectacle is a static ability functioning on the stack that gives an alternative cost: "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn" [702.137a]. Skewer the Critics's spectacle cost is {R} — one red mana specifically, not one generic mana. Only one alternative cost may be applied to a spell as it's cast [118.9a].
- Robber of the Rich's granted permission says "you may cast that card and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." That applies to casting Skewer the Critics no matter which cost Abram is paying — mana cost or the spectacle alternative cost. Card text like this governs here.
- "Spend mana as though it were mana of any color" affects only how the cost may be paid; it doesn't change the cost itself and doesn't change what mana was actually spent [609.4b]. So the cost is still {R}; Abram simply spends his {C} as though it were {R}. (This is the standard way colorless mana can pay a colored requirement — absent such an effect, {C} never satisfies {R}.)

Conditions Abram still must satisfy:

1. An opponent must have lost life this turn [702.137a]. Robber of the Rich's exile trigger doesn't cause life loss, so Abram needs something like Robber of the Rich's combat damage to a player. I'm assuming Abram is casting Skewer the Critics in his postcombat main phase after Robber of the Rich (or another source) dealt damage to an opponent; damage dealt to a player causes that player to lose that much life. If no opponent has lost life yet at the time he casts it, the spectacle cost isn't available and he'd have to pay {2}{R} instead — and then Robber of the Rich still lets him spend three colorless mana as though it were any color.
2. Timing: Skewer the Critics is a sorcery, and neither Robber of the Rich nor spectacle changes when a spell can be cast. He can cast it only during his own main phase with an empty stack, on a turn he attacked with a Rogue (Robber of the Rich is a Rogue, so the attacking turn qualifies; later turns work too if he attacks with a Rogue then, even if Robber of the Rich has left the battlefield).

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any table size. Spectacle cares only that some opponent lost life this turn — it doesn't have to be Nico, the defending player whose library was raided; and if an opponent loses life and then leaves the game, spectacle is still enabled. Robber of the Rich's ability itself keys on the defending player (the controller of the attacked planeswalker or battle, if applicable) having more cards in hand than Abram.

Note also that Skewer the Critics's mana value stays 3 regardless of paying {R} via spectacle.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Abram to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Haakon, Stromgald Scourge] and has [Foulmire Knight] in their graveyard. Can Aspen cast the Adventure portion of Foulmire Knight from their graveyard?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aspen cannot cast the Adventure from the graveyard because Haakon only allows casting Knight creature spells and the Adventure side is an instant with no creature type.
entries.answer:
No. Aspen cannot cast Profane Insight (the Adventure half of Foulmire Knight) from the graveyard, but Aspen can cast Foulmire Knight itself as a creature spell from the graveyard for {B}.

Why: Haakon, Stromgald Scourge grants "As long as Haakon is on the battlefield, you may cast Knight spells from your graveyard." That permission is limited to Knight spells. When you cast an adventurer card as an Adventure, only the alternative characteristics are evaluated to see whether casting it is legal [715.3a], and those alternative characteristics replace the card's normal characteristics for that determination [601.3e]. Profane Insight's alternative characteristics are "Instant — Adventure" with cost {2}{B} — no creature type, so it is not a Knight spell, and Haakon's permission doesn't cover it. This is exactly the Garruk's Horde / Giant Killer example in [601.3e]: a permission for creature spells lets you cast Giant Killer but not Chop Down, while Melek, Izzet Paragon's instant/sorcery permission does the reverse.

The creature half works fine. While Foulmire Knight is in the graveyard it is a permanent card using its normal characteristics — a black Zombie Knight creature card with mana value 1 [Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight ruling #8]. So with Haakon, Stromgald Scourge on the battlefield, Aspen may cast Foulmire Knight from the graveyard, paying its mana cost of {B} plus any additional costs, following normal creature-spell timing (main phase, empty stack) — the only difference is the zone it's cast from [Haakon, Stromgald Scourge ruling #1].

This answer doesn't depend on player count: Haakon, Stromgald Scourge's permission is about Aspen's own graveyard, so it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.
