entries.answer_gold: No. When determining if it's legal to begin casting a spell by moving it to the stack with Haakon, Stromgald Scourge, the game takes into account any alternative characteristics it would have on the stack. Haakon, Stromgald Scourge does not permit Aspen to move an Adventure to the stack, since it's not a Knight.

entries.question: Ayaan controls [Essence of the Wild] and casts [Evil Twin]. Can they have the Evil Twin enter the battlefield as a copy of Nico's [Quakestrider Ceratops]?
entries.reason: Both conclude that neither replacement order lets Evil Twin enter as Quakestrider Ceratops — Essence of the Wild's copy effect will overwrite or preclude Evil Twin's copy effect, so it enters as Essence of the Wild.
entries.answer:
No — well, Ayaan may *choose* Nico's Quakestrider Ceratops, but the Evil Twin will still end up entering the battlefield as a copy of Essence of the Wild, not as a Quakestrider Ceratops.

Why: two copy replacement effects are trying to modify how Evil Twin enters — Evil Twin's own "You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield" ability, and Essence of the Wild's "Creatures you control enter as a copy of this creature." When two or more replacement effects would make an object a copy as it enters, the affected object's controller (Ayaan) picks one to apply, then repeats the process with whatever is still applicable [616.1], [616.1c], [616.1f]. Essence of the Wild's rulings state directly that with two copy effects like this, no matter what order they're applied, the creature enters as a copy of Essence of the Wild [Essence of the Wild ruling #4], and that copy effects are applied after control-changing effects but before all other "enters" replacement effects [Essence of the Wild ruling #6].

Both orders reach the same place:
- Evil Twin's copy effect first: Evil Twin's copiable values briefly become Quakestrider Ceratops' (a 12/8 Dinosaur) plus the granted "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature" ability. Then Essence of the Wild's copy effect is applied, overwriting those copiable values with Essence of the Wild's printed values [707.2], [707.3].
- Essence of the Wild's copy effect first: Evil Twin immediately becomes a copy of Essence of the Wild and therefore no longer has its own "enter as a copy" ability, so that effect does nothing — the same way Rusted Sentinel loses its enters-tapped ability in the example under [616.1f] and [Essence of the Wild ruling #5].

Result: a 6/6 green Avatar named Essence of the Wild with "Creatures you control enter as a copy of this creature." It does not have Evil Twin's {U}{B}, {T} destroy ability, because that clause is part of Evil Twin's own copy effect, and the copiable values that stick are Essence of the Wild's [707.3]. It also doesn't copy anything non-copiable about Ayaan's Essence of the Wild, such as tapped status, counters, or Auras/Equipment [707.2], [Essence of the Wild ruling #8].

One note on Nico: Evil Twin can copy any creature on the battlefield, including an opponent's, so Quakestrider Ceratops is a legal choice — it just gets overwritten. Player count doesn't change anything here: all the choices belong to Ayaan as the controller of the entering Evil Twin, so the APNAP tiebreaker in [616.1] never comes up, and the answer is the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer one.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Essence of the Wild and Evil Twin both have replacement effects that want to modify how Evil Twin enters the battlefield. Ayaan, as the affected player, may apply them in whatever order they wishes. Unfortunately neither order will result in Evil Twin entering as a copy of Quakestrider Ceratops. If they applies Evil Twin first, that ability will set Evil Twin's copiable values to those of Quakestrider Ceratops. Then Essence of the Wild will set them to its own copiable values. If they applies Essence of the Wild first, that will set Evil Twin's copiable values to Essence of the Wild. This will overwrite Evil Twin's ability, so it will no longer apply.

entries.question: Alex controls [Obosh, the Preypiercer] and casts their last card, [Flame Spill], targeting a 1/1 creature that Nevaeh controls. How much damage will Nevaeh take?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Nevaeh takes 6 damage (with the 1/1 taking 2), correctly explaining that excess is assigned as 1/3 and then Obosh doubles the amounts.
entries.answer:
Nevaeh takes 6 damage (and her 1/1 creature is dealt 2 damage).

How it works, in order:

1. Excess damage is calculated first, using the unmodified damage. Rule [120.4a] says that before damage is actually dealt, if the effect causing the damage redirects excess damage (as Flame Spill does), the damage event is modified accordingly, with excess measured against what would be lethal damage to the creature. The Flame Spill ruling confirms you determine "lethal" as toughness minus damage already marked, ignoring any replacement or prevention effects that will modify the damage [Flame Spill ruling #1]. Against a 1/1 with no damage marked, lethal is 1, so Flame Spill's 4 damage splits into 1 damage to the 1/1 creature Nevaeh controls and 3 excess damage to Nevaeh.

2. Then the damage is actually dealt, as modified by replacement effects [120.4b]. Obosh, the Preypiercer's ability is a replacement effect (it uses "instead") [614.1a]: "If a source you control with an odd mana value would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage." Flame Spill has mana value 3 (its cost is {2}{R}), which is odd, and Alex controls it as it resolves, so both parts of the damage are doubled. Flame Spill deals the damage simultaneously to the creature and its controller [Flame Spill ruling #2].

So: 1 → 2 damage to the 1/1 creature, and 3 → 6 damage to Nevaeh. The doubling does not increase the amount treated as "excess" — that division was locked in before doubling, exactly as with Obosh, the Preypiercer and trample assignment or divided-damage spells, where you assign/divide the unmodified damage and then double [Obosh, the Preypiercer ruling #5][Obosh, the Preypiercer ruling #8].

Assumptions: the 1/1 creature Nevaeh controls has no damage already marked on it, no toughness modifications, and no other replacement or prevention effects apply. If it already had damage marked, lethal would be smaller and even more of Flame Spill's 4 damage would be excess (e.g., with 0 toughness remaining it can't happen here, but any marked damage on a 1/1 would already have destroyed it). Also, the damage Nevaeh takes is dealt by Flame Spill, not by Obosh, the Preypiercer [Obosh, the Preypiercer ruling #19].

This result is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — Flame Spill targets a single creature and the excess goes to that creature's controller, Nevaeh, regardless of how many players are at the table. The fact that Flame Spill was Alex's last card in hand has no effect on the damage.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Six. First Alex will allocate one damage to the token and three to Nevaeh. Obosh, the Preypiercer's replacement effect will then double the three damage being dealt to Nevaeh to six.

entries.question: Alessandro activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Noor with it. Noor doesn't block it and then casts [Through the Breach], putting [Melira, Sylvok Outcast] onto the battlefield. What happens during the combat damage step?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling: Melira removes infect (via timestamp), so Inkmoth deals 1 normal combat damage and Noor loses 1 life rather than receiving a poison counter.
entries.answer:
Noor takes 1 point of normal combat damage from Inkmoth Nexus and loses 1 life — no poison counter, and no -1/-1 counters anywhere. Melira, Sylvok Outcast strips infect from Inkmoth Nexus before damage is dealt.

Why: Inkmoth Nexus's activated ability makes it a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn (infect means it damages players as poison counters and creatures as -1/-1 counters). Melira, Sylvok Outcast says "Creatures your opponents control lose infect." Both the ability-granting effect from Inkmoth Nexus and the ability-removing effect from Melira, Sylvok Outcast apply in the same layer (the layer for adding/removing abilities), so they're ordered by timestamp, later effect winning [613.3, 613.7, 613.7b]. Neither effect changes the text, existence, or application of the other, so there's no dependency to override timestamps [613.8a]. Since Melira, Sylvok Outcast entered the battlefield after Inkmoth Nexus was animated, its effect has the later timestamp and wins: Inkmoth Nexus has no infect during the combat damage step [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #2]. It's still a 1/1 with flying, so Noor is dealt 1 damage and simply loses 1 life.

Assumed timing: Noor cast Through the Breach after declining to block (during the declare blockers step), so Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield before the combat damage step but was not declared as a blocker — it neither deals nor receives combat damage. Through the Breach gives it haste and Noor must sacrifice it at the beginning of the next end step [Through the Breach]. If instead Melira, Sylvok Outcast had already been on the battlefield before Alessandro activated Inkmoth Nexus, the infect-granting effect would have the later timestamp and would win, so Inkmoth Nexus would have infect — but Melira, Sylvok Outcast's other line, "You can't get poison counters," still applies, so Noor would get no poison counters and would not lose life either [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #2].

Multiplayer note: nothing changes. Melira, Sylvok Outcast affects creatures controlled by its controller's opponents, and Alessandro is Noor's opponent regardless of how many players are at the table; the only player being dealt combat damage here is the defending player, Noor.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Inkmoth Nexus's ability gives it infect, and Melira, Sylvok Outcast's effect makes it lose infect. The effects are applied in timestamp order, so Inkmoth Nexus does not have infect. Noor will lose 1 life when damage is dealt.

(There is no dependency here because neither effect changes the text or the existence of the other, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to.)

entries.question: Alex controls [Extus, Oriq Overlord] and uses [Illithid Harvester] to try to turn it face down. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states that double-faced permanents can't be turned face down, so Illithid Harvester's ability does nothing to Extus and matches the reference.
entries.answer:
Nothing happens to Extus, Oriq Overlord — it stays face up as a 2/4 legendary Human Warlock with double strike, and it does not become a 2/2 Horror.

Why: Extus, Oriq Overlord // Awaken the Blood Avatar is a modal double-faced card (a card with a second face, Awaken the Blood Avatar, instead of a normal card back). Double-faced permanents simply can't be turned face down. If a spell or ability tries to turn one face down, nothing happens and that effect doesn't change any of its characteristics or their copiable values [712.16]. Illithid Harvester's Ceremorphosis ability is confirmed to work this way: it can't turn double-faced cards face down [Illithid Harvester ruling #11].

A few practical points:
- Illithid Harvester's ability targets "any number of target tapped nontoken creatures," so Alex can only choose Extus, Oriq Overlord at all if Extus is tapped. Choosing it as a target is legal; the ability just fails to do anything to it on resolution.
- The "They're 2/2 Horror creatures" part of Ceremorphosis is tied to the permanents being turned face down. Since Extus, Oriq Overlord is never turned face down, that characteristic-setting effect doesn't apply to it [712.16].
- Any other legal targets of the same Ceremorphosis trigger (ordinary tapped nontoken creatures) are still turned face down and become 2/2 Horrors normally.

This is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the rule about double-faced permanents doesn't depend on the number of players, and Ceremorphosis can target tapped nontoken creatures regardless of who controls them.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nothing happens. Double-faced permanents can't be turned face down.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Jibbirik Omnivore], a token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore produced by [Stolen Identity], a 1/1 Saproling token created by [Morbid Bloom], [Moonscarred Werewolf], and a token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf produced by [Twinflame]. Nash casts [Ratchet Bomb] and activates its second ability. As Ratchet Bomb's ability resolves, what is destroyed?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling—only the Morbid Bloom Saproling token and the Twinflame token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf are destroyed—and correctly explains the relevant mana-value and copy/DFC rules.
entries.answer:
Two things Autumn controls are destroyed: the 1/1 Saproling token from Morbid Bloom and the token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf made by Twinflame. The real Jibbirik Omnivore, the Stolen Identity token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore, and the actual Moonscarred Werewolf (the back face of Scorned Villager // Moonscarred Werewolf) all survive.

Assumption on timing: Ratchet Bomb was cast this turn and Nash immediately activated the second ability, so Ratchet Bomb has zero charge counters (the first ability also requires {T}, and Ratchet Bomb tapped to sacrifice itself). The ability therefore destroys each nonland permanent with mana value 0. Ratchet Bomb itself is already in the graveyard, having been sacrificed as a cost, so it isn't around to be destroyed (its own mana value is 2 anyway).

Why each permanent lives or dies:

- Jibbirik Omnivore: mana cost {1}{G}, mana value 2 [202.3a]. Survives.
- Stolen Identity's token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore: a copy takes the copiable values printed on the original, including its mana cost [707.2]. It has mana cost {1}{G} and mana value 2 [202.3a]. Survives.
- Morbid Bloom's 1/1 green Saproling token: a token has only the characteristics the creating effect gave it, and Morbid Bloom gives it no mana cost [111.3]. An object with no mana cost has mana value 0 [202.3a], which Ratchet Bomb's own ruling confirms for non-copy tokens [Ratchet Bomb ruling #2]. Destroyed.
- Moonscarred Werewolf (the transformed Scorned Villager card): while a nonmodal double-faced permanent has its back face up, its mana value is still calculated from the front face's mana cost, {1}{G}, so its mana value is 2 [202.3b] [712.8e]. Survives.
- Twinflame's token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf: this is a permanent copying the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent, and the rules explicitly set such a copy's mana value to 0 [202.3b] [712.8e]. Destroyed. (Twinflame's haste rider doesn't change this.)

Player count: Ratchet Bomb's ability says "each nonland permanent," so it isn't limited to one opponent. In a two-player game it hits both Autumn's and Nash's qualifying permanents; at a multiplayer table it also destroys every other player's nonland permanents with mana value 0 (any other non-copy tokens, 0-cost artifacts, etc.).

If instead Ratchet Bomb had been on the battlefield earlier and had charge counters when the ability resolved, the destroyed set changes: with one counter nothing listed here dies, and with two counters Jibbirik Omnivore, the Stolen Identity token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore, and Moonscarred Werewolf would be destroyed while the Saproling token and the Twinflame token would survive.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The Saproling token and the token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf. Copy effects copy mana cost, so the token Jibbirik Omnivore doesn't have a mana value of 0. Tokens that are created by an effect that sets their characteristics only have those characteristics. The Saproling token has no mana cost, so its mana value is 0. The mana value of transformed transforming double-faced cards is determined by their front face, so the Moonscarred Werewolf isn't destroyed. Copies of double-faced cards have a mana value of 0.

entries.question: Ayla controls [Living Plane] and plays [Minas Tirith]. Does it enter tapped or untapped?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—per the reference Minas Tirith enters tapped, but the candidate incorrectly applies Living Plane/self-referential checks and says it enters untapped.
entries.answer:
Minas Tirith enters untapped.

Why: Living Plane says "All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands," a continuous effect that already exists and applies to every land, including Minas Tirith. Minas Tirith's own "enters tapped unless you control a legendary creature" is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield, so you check the characteristics of Minas Tirith as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it [614.12]. On the battlefield under Living Plane, Minas Tirith would be a legendary 1/1 creature land that Ayla controls, and the card says "a legendary creature," not "another legendary creature" — so it satisfies its own condition and enters untapped.

Two caveats worth flagging:

1. The Minas Tirith ruling that "the legendary creature must already be on the battlefield as the land enters; if it enters the battlefield at the same time, the land will enter tapped" is about a *separate* legendary creature entering simultaneously with Minas Tirith [Minas Tirith ruling #1]. It doesn't stop Living Plane's pre-existing effect from being applied to Minas Tirith itself under [614.12]. If Ayla instead had some other legendary creature entering at the same moment as Minas Tirith, that one would not count.

2. Being untapped doesn't mean Minas Tirith is immediately usable as a mana source in every sense: because Living Plane makes it a creature, it's subject to summoning sickness, so its {T} abilities ("{T}: Add {W}" and "{1}{W}, {T}: Draw a card") can't be activated and it can't attack unless Ayla has controlled it continuously since the beginning of her most recent turn [Living Plane ruling #2]. So the turn Ayla plays it, it sits untapped but can't tap for {W}.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Tapped. When applying an enters-the-battlefield replacement effect, the game considers the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, so it sees that it would be a creature, but it doesn't consider the permanent to actually be on the battlefield yet. Effectively, a legendary creature is entering the battlefield.
entries.human_note: IMPORTANT!!!!!!! they say the same thing. This isn't a disagreement.

entries.question: Andy controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Andy then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
entries.reason: Both conclude Badlands can only tap for red ({R}) — the candidate reaches the same final ruling that Conversion then Magus of the Moon (by timestamp) leave it a Mountain that taps for {R}.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: applying the rules provided here, Badlands taps for red mana only ({R}) — it can no longer make {B} or {W}.

Why, step by step (all three of these are type‑changing continuous effects, so they're all applied in layer 4, in timestamp order) [613.1d] [613.7]:

1. Starting point: Badlands is printed as a nonbasic Land — Swamp Mountain with "{T}: Add {B} or {R}" [Badlands ruling #4]. It has basic land types but is not a basic land, so Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" does apply to it [Badlands ruling #3].
2. Conversion has the earlier timestamp (Andy already controlled it), so Conversion's static effect "All Mountains are Plains" applies first [613.7a]. Badlands is a Mountain, so it becomes a Plains; setting a land's subtype to a basic land type removes its old land types (Swamp and Mountain) and the mana abilities that came from them, and it gains "{T}: Add {W}" [305.7] [Badlands ruling #2] [Conversion ruling #1].
3. Magus of the Moon's static ability has the later timestamp, so it applies next [613.7a]. Badlands is still a nonbasic land, so "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" makes it a Mountain: it loses the Plains type and the white mana ability and gains "{T}: Add {R}" [305.7] [Magus of the Moon ruling #5].

End result: Badlands is a nonbasic Land — Mountain that taps for {R} only. Note that Magus of the Moon doesn't touch names or supertypes, so it's still named Badlands and still isn't basic [Magus of the Moon ruling #2].

One honest caveat about what's missing: the context you gave me contains only the timestamp rules for ordering effects inside a layer [613.7] [613.7a]. The comprehensive rules also contain a separate provision for when one continuous effect "depends on" another and therefore applies out of timestamp order; that rule was not provided here. If it applied to this pair (because Magus of the Moon changes which permanents count as Mountains for Conversion), Magus of the Moon would be applied first and Conversion second, and Badlands would end up a Plains tapping for {W} instead. I can't resolve that with the rules text I was given — but either way Badlands loses black mana entirely.

Player count doesn't change anything: Conversion affects "all Mountains" and Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, so the same analysis applies to every player's lands in a two‑player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Only {R}. Both Magus of the Moon and Conversion only apply in layer 4. The effects are applied in timestamp order, resulting in Conversion applying first to make Badlands a Plains, then Magus of the Moon applies making it a Mountain.

entries.question: Amy controls a [Trigon of Corruption] enchanted by Neil's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Amy's upkeep, they cast [Aura Graft] to attach the Curse Artifact to [Sungrass Egg]. Which artifact does Amy have the choice to sacrifice as the trigger resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the trigger refers to the artifact enchanted when it triggered (Trigon of Corruption), so Amy must sacrifice Trigon of Corruption or take the damage — moving the Aura afterward doesn't change that.
entries.answer:
Amy's choice is still Trigon of Corruption — the artifact the Curse Artifact was enchanting when the ability triggered — even though the Curse Artifact is now attached to Sungrass Egg. Amy either sacrifices Trigon of Corruption or takes 2 damage from the Curse Artifact; Sungrass Egg is not an option.

Why: the Curse Artifact's triggered ability reads "At the beginning of the upkeep of enchanted artifact's controller, this Aura deals 2 damage to that player unless they sacrifice that artifact." The words "that artifact" in the effect point back to the specific object identified by the trigger condition — the artifact enchanted at the moment the ability triggered, i.e. Trigon of Corruption. When an ability's effect refers to a specific untargeted object that its trigger condition previously referred to, the effect still applies to that same object even if that object (or the situation around it) has changed [608.2k]. Moving the Curse Artifact with Aura Graft does not rewrite the already-triggered ability's reference, and it doesn't retarget the ability to Sungrass Egg.

Similarly, "that player" is locked in as Amy, the controller of the enchanted artifact when the ability triggered, so Amy is the one who chooses and the one who would take the 2 damage [608.2k].

Assumed timing: Aura Graft was cast in response and resolved before the Curse Artifact's trigger resolved, exactly as described. If instead Aura Graft had resolved before Amy's upkeep began (so the Curse Artifact was already attached to Sungrass Egg when the ability triggered), the ability would have triggered off Sungrass Egg's controller's upkeep and "that artifact" would be Sungrass Egg.

Note also that Aura Graft's controller keeps control of the Curse Artifact going forward — its effect has no duration [Aura Graft ruling #3] — but that has no bearing on which artifact this already-triggered ability refers to.

Player count doesn't change any of this: the ability names one specific player (Amy) and one specific artifact (Trigon of Corruption), so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Trigon of Corruption. The "that artifact" that the trigger on the stack refers to is the one that Curse Artifact was attached to as the ability triggered.

entries.question: Nico controls [Blind Obedience]. Adonis's devotion to black is 0 and they cast [Erebos, God of the Dead]. Does it enter the battlefield tapped or untapped?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion (Erebos enters untapped) and gives the same core reasoning that Blind Obedience only taps creatures/artifacts and Erebos isn’t a creature as it enters due to devotion.
entries.answer:
Erebos, God of the Dead enters the battlefield untapped.

Why: Blind Obedience only taps "artifacts and creatures your opponents control" as they enter. Erebos, God of the Dead is a Legendary Enchantment Creature card, but its own static ability says that as long as its controller's devotion to black is less than five, Erebos, God of the Dead isn't a creature. Devotion to black counts {B} symbols in the mana costs of permanents you control.

To decide whether Blind Obedience's replacement effect applies, you look at the characteristics Erebos, God of the Dead would have on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects from its own static abilities that would apply once it's there [614.12]. Per the Erebos ruling, because replacement effects are considered before the God is on the battlefield, the {B} in Erebos, God of the Dead's own mana cost is not counted for this check [Erebos, God of the Dead ruling #10]. Adonis's devotion to black is 0, which is less than five, so Erebos, God of the Dead is not a creature as it enters — and it's not an artifact either. Blind Obedience simply doesn't apply to it, so it enters untapped.

After it's on the battlefield, Adonis's devotion to black becomes 1 (the {B} in Erebos, God of the Dead's mana cost now counts), still less than five, so it remains a noncreature legendary enchantment [Erebos, God of the Dead ruling #12]. Even if devotion later reached five and Erebos, God of the Dead became a creature, that would not retroactively tap it — the entering-tapped question was already settled as it entered.

Multiplayer note: Blind Obedience is worded "your opponents control," so this works the same whether the game is two players or more — Adonis is Nico's opponent either way, and the outcome (untapped) doesn't change.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Untapped. To determine what replacement effects apply to a permanent as it enters the battlefield, the game looks at the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield. On the battlefield Erebos, God of the Dead would not be a creature, so Blind Obedience's effect will not apply to it.

entries.question: Alex casts [Brainstorm] using the ability of [Jace, Telepath Unbound]. Nina casts [Memory Lapse] and counters Brainstorm. Where does Brainstorm go?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Memory Lapse's self-replacement applies first, putting Brainstorm on top of Alex's library and preventing Jace's replacement from exiling it.
entries.answer:
Brainstorm goes on top of Alex's library (the owner's library), not to exile and not to the graveyard.

Why: Memory Lapse says "Counter target spell. If that spell is countered this way, put it on top of its owner's library instead of into that player's graveyard." That second sentence is a self-replacement effect — a replacement effect that's part of the resolving spell's own effect, modifying what that spell itself does [614.15]. Jace, Telepath Unbound's −3 ability creates a separate, ordinary replacement effect ("If that spell would be put into your graveyard, exile it instead").

When two replacement effects would apply to the same event, the affected object's controller normally picks the order, but if any of them is a self-replacement effect, one of those must be applied first [616.1a]. Memory Lapse's ruling states exactly this: its self-replacement effect replaces the spell going to the graveyard before any other effect can replace that event [Memory Lapse ruling #1]. So the "Brainstorm is put into the graveyard" event is replaced with "put Brainstorm on top of Alex's library," and Jace, Telepath Unbound's replacement never gets a chance to apply, because Brainstorm is never put into the graveyard.

On top of that, Jace, Telepath Unbound's tracking ends here: once the card goes to a hidden zone such as the hand or library, the effect loses track of it and it won't be exiled even if it later ends up in the graveyard that turn [Jace, Vryn's Prodigy // Jace, Telepath Unbound ruling #7].

Timing note: none of Brainstorm's own effect happens — Memory Lapse counters it while it's on the stack, so Alex never draws three cards or puts two back [Brainstorm ruling #1]. (Contrast: if Alex had cast Brainstorm with flashback instead of via Jace, Telepath Unbound, flashback would change the destination from the library to exile [Memory Lapse ruling #1].)

Player count doesn't change the result. The choice-of-replacement rule uses APNAP order when multiple players choose simultaneously [616.1a], but here only Alex, as Brainstorm's controller/owner, is affected, and the self-replacement effect is mandatory to apply first, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Alex's library.

Two replacement effects are trying to replace the same event. Since Memory Lapse's effect is a self-replacement effect, it applies first. Once it's applied, Brainstorm is moving to the library and Jace, Telepath Unbound's effect no longer applies.

entries.question: Nathalia controls [Welding Jar] and [Duskworker]. Ariel casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Duskworker with both. In response, Nathalia activates Welding Jar's ability targeting Duskworker. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Welding Jar regenerates Duskworker before Prismari Command resolves, Command deals damage then tries to destroy, the regeneration replaces the destruction, and Duskworker ends up tapped with no damage marked.
entries.answer:
Duskworker survives. Welding Jar is sacrificed, its ability resolves first and puts a regeneration shield on Duskworker; then Prismari Command resolves, marks 2 damage on Duskworker and then tries to destroy it, and the shield replaces that destruction — all damage marked on Duskworker is removed, Nathalia taps Duskworker, and Duskworker is removed from combat if it was attacking or blocking. Duskworker ends up on the battlefield, tapped, with no damage marked and its shield used up.

Why the order works out that way:

- A regeneration shield means: "The next time this permanent would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it; if it's an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat" [614.8, 701.19a]. Welding Jar's ability is a resolving ability, so it creates that one-shot shield on Duskworker [701.19a].
- Nathalia's Welding Jar ability was activated in response, so it's on top of the stack and resolves first [608.1]. The shield exists before Prismari Command resolves. (Setting up a shield does not by itself remove Duskworker from combat — that only happens when the shield is actually used, per the Duskworker ruling.)
- Prismari Command's modes are carried out in the order printed on the card, not the order the modes were chosen [608.2c]. "Deals 2 damage to any target" is printed above "Destroy target artifact," so Duskworker takes 2 damage first (lethal for a 2/2), and only then is the destroy instruction applied.
- Nobody gets priority and no state-based actions are checked while Prismari Command is resolving [117.2e, 117.5, 704.3], so the lethal-damage state-based action never gets a chance to destroy Duskworker between the two modes [704.5g].
- The destroy instruction is then replaced by the regeneration shield, which removes the 2 marked damage and taps Duskworker [614.8, 701.19a]. When state-based actions are next checked after Prismari Command finishes resolving, Duskworker has no damage marked, so it isn't destroyed [704.3, 704.5g].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading "in response" as the Welding Jar ability resolving before Prismari Command. If instead Nathalia waited and Prismari Command resolved first, Duskworker would already have been destroyed by the destroy mode (or by lethal damage) and Welding Jar would come too late — a regeneration shield only helps if it's created before the destruction happens. Also note Duskworker's own "whenever this creature becomes blocked, regenerate it" trigger could supply a second, independent shield if it had already triggered this combat; that shield would still be waiting and would protect Duskworker from a later destruction.

Player count doesn't change anything here: Prismari Command targets specific objects/players, and both of its chosen modes target Duskworker regardless of how many opponents are at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Duskworker will end up tapped and have no damage marked on it. Welding Jar's ability will resolve first, regenerating Duskworker. When Prismari Command resolves, the game carries out the instructions in the order written. First, Prismari Command deals 2 damage to Duskworker. The replacement effect generated by the regeneration ability will not apply yet, as even though Duskworker has been dealt lethal damage, it would only be destroyed when state-based actions are checked, and state-based actions are checked when a player would get priority. Next Prismari Command tries to destroy Duskworker and the replacement effect applies, replacing the destruction event with Duskworker being tapped and having all damaged marked on it removed. Lastly Prismari Command finishes resolving and leaves the stack and state-based actions are checked. Since Duskworker no longer has any damage marked on it, it will not be die.

entries.question: Armando controls [Mana Reflection] and taps [Pyromancer's Goggles] to add {R}{R}. They spend one mana to cast [Into the Fray]. Later in the phase they spend the other mana to cast [Galvanic Discharge]. Which one(s) are copied?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Mana Reflection causes Pyromancer's Goggles to produce two separate mana and therefore create two delayed triggers, so spending each mana to cast a red instant copies both Into the Fray and Galvanic Discharge.
entries.answer:
Both are copied — Into the Fray gets copied, and Galvanic Discharge gets copied too.

Why: Mana Reflection is a replacement effect ("produces twice as much of that mana instead" — effects using "instead" are replacement effects) that increases the amount of mana the tapped permanent produces [614.1a]. When a replacement effect increases the amount of mana produced by a mana ability, any restrictions, riders, or delayed triggered abilities attached to that mana apply to all the mana produced, and if the ability creates a delayed triggered ability that triggers when the mana is spent, a separate delayed triggered ability is created for each mana produced [106.6a]. Mana Reflection's own ruling says the same thing: if the mana ability puts restrictions or riders on its mana, that applies to all the mana produced this way [Mana Reflection ruling #3]. Armando is genuinely "tapping a permanent for mana" because he's activating a mana ability of Pyromancer's Goggles that includes {T} in its cost [Mana Reflection ruling #4].

So the {R}{R} in Armando's pool consists of two separate red mana, each carrying its own copy of Pyromancer's Goggles' delayed trigger "When that mana is spent to cast a red instant or sorcery spell, copy that spell..." Each trigger watches only its own mana [Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #8].

- Into the Fray is a red instant (Arcane), so spending the first Goggles mana on it triggers that mana's delayed ability and Into the Fray is copied. Any red instant or sorcery works, even ones with targets — you may choose new targets for the copy [Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #1, Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #5]. The copy isn't cast; it's created directly on the stack and resolves before the original [Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #3, Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #6].
- Galvanic Discharge is also a red instant, so spending the second Goggles mana on it triggers that mana's delayed ability and Galvanic Discharge is copied as well. Note the copy of Galvanic Discharge independently gives Armando {E}{E}{E} and lets him pay any amount of {E} for its damage, and he can point the copy at a different creature or planeswalker if he wants [Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #5].

Timing assumption: I'm reading "later in the phase" as still within the same step/phase, so the second mana hadn't emptied from the pool and was actually spent on Galvanic Discharge. If instead the pool had emptied between the two casts (a step or phase ended), the unspent mana would simply be lost, no trigger would occur for it, and only Into the Fray would be copied. Also note the triggers work even if Pyromancer's Goggles has left the battlefield in the meantime [Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #7].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with player count — the copies happen the same way in a two-player game or at a bigger table; the only difference is the range of legal creatures/planeswalkers Armando may pick when choosing new targets for the copies.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Both are copied. Mana Reflection has a replacement effect that changes the amount of mana produced by Pyromancer's Goggles. A separate delayed trigger is created for each mana.

entries.question: Alden controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alden would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alden has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude that only the last copy effect's "+1/+1 counter" exception applies, so Clone enters with one +1/+1 counter.
entries.answer:
Clone enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter — not four.

Why: Clone's own replacement effect lets it enter as a copy of Spark Double. Because copy effects are copiable, Clone now also has Spark Double's replacement effect: "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control, except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature... and it isn't legendary." Alden may apply that inherited effect and copy Spark Double again, and again, and again.

But the "+1/+1 counter" part of Spark Double's text is an exception that is an additional effect, not a modification of the copied characteristics. Rule 707.9e says that if another copy effect is applied to the object after the copy effect that carried such an exception, that exception's effect doesn't happen. So each new application of a Spark Double copy effect wipes out the pending counter from the previous application. After four total copy applications, only the last one's exception survives, giving Clone one +1/+1 counter.

Result: Clone enters as a copy of Spark Double (a 0/0 Illusion with Spark Double's abilities, and non-legendary — the "isn't legendary" part is a characteristic modification and is copiable, per Spark Double's rulings), with a single +1/+1 counter on it, so it's a 1/1.

Two assumptions worth stating: (1) I'm assuming the Spark Double already on the battlefield isn't itself copying some other permanent; if it were, Clone would enter as whatever that Spark Double copied (per Spark Double's and Clone's rulings), though the counter math would be the same — one counter. (2) Spark Double's inherited effect can only copy a creature or planeswalker Alden controls, so every re-application must target Alden's own Spark Double (Clone's own effect, by contrast, could have copied any creature on the battlefield). That control restriction is the only thing that changes at a multiplayer table versus a two-player game: with more opponents there are simply more creatures Clone's original effect could have chosen, but the inherited Spark Double effect is still limited to permanents Alden controls, and the counter count is still one.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One. Spark Double has a copy effect that includes an exception (entering with a +1/+1 counter). If another copy effect is applied afterwards, the exception from the first effect will not happen.

entries.question: Ahmed casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Nico. At their first opportunity, Ahmed sacrifices their [Abandoned Outpost]. How many cards will Ahmed be able to exile from Nico's library?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states that sacrificing Abandoned Outpost before the gravestorm trigger resolves yields one copy, so the original plus one copy exile two cards.
entries.answer:
Two cards — one from the original Bitter Ordeal and one from a single gravestorm copy.

How it works:

1. Ahmed casts Bitter Ordeal targeting Nico. Gravestorm triggers on cast: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each permanent that was put into a graveyard from the battlefield this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies" [702.69a].
2. Ahmed's first opportunity to sacrifice Abandoned Outpost is either while paying Bitter Ordeal's cost of {2}{B} (its "{T}, Sacrifice this land: Add one mana of any color" is a mana ability that can be activated during casting) or with priority after Bitter Ordeal is cast, while the gravestorm trigger is still on the stack. Either way, Abandoned Outpost is put into the graveyard from the battlefield before the gravestorm trigger resolves.
3. The number of copies is locked in only when the gravestorm ability actually resolves, not when it triggered [608.2h]. At that moment exactly one permanent (Abandoned Outpost) has gone to a graveyard from the battlefield this turn, so Ahmed gets one copy.
4. The copy and the original Bitter Ordeal each say "Search target player's library for a card and exile it. Then that player shuffles." Both targeting Nico (Ahmed may choose a new target for the copy) exiles two cards total from Nico's library, assuming Nico has at least two cards to find.

Timing caveat: this assumes Abandoned Outpost hits the graveyard before the gravestorm trigger resolves, which "first opportunity" guarantees. If instead Ahmed waited until after the gravestorm trigger had already resolved, the count would be zero copies and only one card would be exiled.

Note on the reminder text: Bitter Ordeal's reminder says "each permanent put into a graveyard this turn," but the actual gravestorm ability counts only permanents put into a graveyard from the battlefield [702.69a]. Abandoned Outpost qualifies either way.

Multiplayer: with only Ahmed and Nico, it's two exiled cards from Nico. At a table of three or more, the count is still "each permanent put into a graveyard from the battlefield this turn" by any player, so other players' permanents dying earlier in the turn would add copies, and Ahmed could redirect the copy to search a different opponent's library instead of Nico's [702.69a].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 2. Gravestorm cares about the number of permanents put into the graveyard before the trigger resolves.

entries.question: Autumn restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]'s last ability. They put a [Quilled Slagwurm] onto the battlefield as it resolves. Can it attack on their first turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling and justification as the reference — Karn's restart places the creature under the player's control before the first turn begins, satisfying the continuous-control requirement so it can attack.
entries.answer:
Yes. Quilled Slagwurm can attack on Autumn's first turn of the new game.

Why: Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game, and the cards left in exile are put onto the battlefield as the ability finishes resolving — after the pregame procedure but before the new game's first turn [727.1] [Karn Liberated ruling #5]. A specific ruling covers exactly this: permanents put onto the battlefield due to Karn Liberated's ability are treated as having been under the starting controller's control continuously since the beginning of that player's first turn, so creatures among them can attack and their activated abilities with {T} in the cost can be activated [Karn Liberated ruling #3].

That satisfies the normal restrictions. The "summoning sickness" rule says a creature can't attack unless it has been under its controller's control continuously since their most recent turn began [302.6], and the declare-attackers step requires each chosen attacker to be untapped and to either have haste or have been controlled by the active player continuously since the turn began [508.1a]. Quilled Slagwurm has no haste, but it meets the continuous-control requirement thanks to Karn Liberated's ruling, so it's a legal attacker. It also needs to be untapped when attackers are declared; if it somehow entered tapped it would untap during Autumn's first untap step [Karn Liberated ruling #8].

One timing point: Autumn, as the player who controlled the restarting ability, is the starting player in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #10], so "their first turn" is the game's first turn. If in your format the starting player skips their first draw, that changes nothing about attacking.

Multiplayer vs. two players: the answer is the same either way. The only multiplayer wrinkle provided is that any player who had already left the game before the restart won't be in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #12]; that doesn't affect whether Quilled Slagwurm can attack, only who Autumn can attack.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Karn's ability finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, so the creature has been controlled continuously since the turn began and can attack.

entries.question: Abel plays [Exotic Orchard]. What can it tap for if Nico controls only [Throne of Makindi] without any charge counters on it?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the same bottom-line ruling that Exotic Orchard can produce any one of W/U/B/R/G based on Throne of Makindi's colored-mana ability even if its cost can't be paid (and not colorless).
entries.answer:
Abel's Exotic Orchard can be tapped for one mana of any color ", \u2014 white, blue, black, red, or green \u2014 and that mana has no restriction on how it's spent. It cannot be tapped for {C}.

Why:

1. Throne of Makindi has the ability "{T}, Remove a charge counter from this land: Add two mana of any one color." Exotic Orchard checks what a land an opponent controls "could produce," which looks only at what the ability would produce if it resolved, ignoring whether the ability's costs could be paid [106.7]. So the fact that Nico's Throne of Makindi has no charge counters (and even whether it's untapped) is irrelevant [Exotic Orchard ruling #1].

2. Because that ability adds mana of any one color, Throne of Makindi could produce {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}, so Abel chooses any one of those colors when Exotic Orchard's mana ability resolves.

3. The rider "Spend this mana only to cast kicked spells" does not carry over. Exotic Orchard ignores restrictions or riders opponents' lands put on their mana; it only cares about colors [Exotic Orchard ruling #2]. Abel's mana is unrestricted.

4. Throne of Makindi's other ability, "{T}: Add {C}," doesn't help Exotic Orchard: Exotic Orchard can only make one of the five colors and can never be tapped for colorless mana, even if an opponent's land could produce {C} [Exotic Orchard ruling #4].

Multiplayer note: Exotic Orchard says "a land an opponent controls," so at a table with more than two players, lands controlled by any opponent count, and the pool of available colors could be larger. Here only Nico's Throne of Makindi is mentioned, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game where Nico's is the only opponent's land.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Any color of mana. Exotic Orchard is limited by what an opponent's land's abilities could produce if they resolved, not if the opponent could pay the costs required.

entries.question: Abraham controls [Drought] and [Derelor]. How many Swamps would they have to sacrifice in order to cast a [Virulent Wound]?
entries.reason: Both conclude that only the printed mana cost matters for Drought, so Derelor’s added {B} doesn’t add a black symbol and Abraham need sacrifice only one Swamp.
entries.answer:
Abraham sacrifices exactly one Swamp.

Why: Drought says "Spells cost an additional 'Sacrifice a Swamp' to cast for each black mana symbol in their mana costs." Virulent Wound's mana cost, as printed near the top of the card, is {B} — one black mana symbol (rules 202.1 and 202.1a). So Drought applies exactly one "Sacrifice a Swamp" additional cost.

Derelor's effect ("Black spells you cast cost {B} more to cast") does not add a black symbol to Virulent Wound's mana cost. A cost increase applied by another effect is factored into the total cost when Abraham determines it during casting, but it does not change the spell's mana cost; the mana cost stays {B} and anything that looks at that mana cost still sees the original value (rules 118.8d and 601.2f). Since Drought counts symbols in the mana cost, not in the total cost, Derelor's extra {B} adds no additional Swamp sacrifice.

So Abraham's total cost to cast Virulent Wound is: {B} (its mana cost) + {B} (Derelor's increase) = {B}{B} in mana, plus the additional cost of sacrificing one Swamp from Drought. Note this is real mana payment — sacrificing the Swamp doesn't produce the mana, so Abraham needs {B}{B} available from other sources (or must tap the Swamp for {B} before sacrificing it, if the Swamp is untapped and he's able to).

Player count doesn't matter here: both Drought and Derelor affect only their own controller's spells, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 1. The mana cost of a spell doesn't change, regardless of what was paid for it.

entries.question: Abram controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Tropical Island], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Tropical Island a creature?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Tropical Island is not a creature because Blood Moon's earlier timestamp makes it a Mountain (removing Forest), so Life and Limb cannot animate it, matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
No — Abram's Tropical Island is not a creature. It's just a land: a Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}."

Why:

1. Both Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") create continuous type-changing effects, which are applied in layer 4 [613.1d]. Tropical Island's own entry time doesn't matter; what matters is the timestamps of Blood Moon and Life and Limb, and Blood Moon's is earlier.

2. Layer 4 normally uses timestamps, but dependency overrides timestamps when it exists [613.8a]. Here each effect depends on the other: applying Blood Moon changes Tropical Island's land subtypes from Forest Island to Mountain, which changes what Life and Limb applies to; and applying Life and Limb turns Saprolings into (nonbasic) Forest lands, which changes what Blood Moon applies to. That's a dependency loop, so rule [613.8b] says the dependency rule is ignored and the effects are applied in timestamp order.

3. Timestamp order: Blood Moon first. Setting a land's subtype replaces its existing land types [205.1a], so Tropical Island loses Forest and Island and becomes a Mountain, losing its old abilities and gaining "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #3]. Note that Tropical Island is still a nonbasic land even though it printed with basic land types, so Blood Moon does apply to it [Tropical Island ruling #2].

4. Then Life and Limb applies. At that point Tropical Island is neither a Forest nor a Saproling, so Life and Limb simply doesn't apply to it. It never becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature. (Life and Limb would still animate any actual Forests or Saprolings that Blood Moon doesn't strip — e.g., basic Forests, which Blood Moon leaves alone, and Saproling creatures, which become Forest lands [Life and Limb ruling #4].)

If the two enchantments' order were reversed (Life and Limb with the earlier timestamp), you'd still resolve the loop by timestamp: Life and Limb would first make Tropical Island a Saproling creature and Forest land, and then Blood Moon would set its land subtype to Mountain — it would remain a creature, since Blood Moon changes land types, not the creature card type or the Saproling creature type.

This analysis is player-count independent: nothing here depends on the number of players, so it's the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Applying Blood Moon's effect first would prevent Life and Limb's effect from applying to Tropical Island and applying Life and Limb's effect first would not affect how Blood Moon's effect is applied or what it does, so Life and Limb's effect is dependent on Blood Moon's effect and waits to apply until afterwards. Since Blood Moon's effect makes Tropical Island no longer a Forest, Life and Limb doesn't apply to it at all.

entries.question: Nixon has a [Southern Elephant] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Addison casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nixon. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nixon know which manifested card is which?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the +1/+1 counters remain on Skullbriar when it is manifested (making it a 5/5), whereas the reference says the counters cease to exist once it’s face down on the battlefield, so the rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Short answer: the three +1/+1 counters stay on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave the whole way, so it arrives as a face-down manifested permanent that is a 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters on it — a 5/5. Because Southern Elephant will manifest as a plain 2/2, everyone at the table (including Nixon) can tell which face-down permanent is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, even though the pile was shuffled.

Why the counters survive:
- Normally counters on an object cease to exist when it changes zones ([122.2]), but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Card text beats the general rule here.
- Ghastly Conscription moves the cards graveyard → exile → battlefield. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has its abilities in the graveyard, so the counters remain when it's exiled, and it still has its abilities as a card in the face-down exile pile (being exiled face down only limits who may examine it — [406.3]), so the counters remain again when it's manifested onto the battlefield. That the ability must be present in the zone the card is leaving is exactly what [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2] describes.
- Those counters aren't "placed" on it, so counter-doubling or counter-hosing effects don't interact with them ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]), and it retains counters of every kind, not just +1/+1 ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #6]).

What the manifested permanent is: manifesting turns the card face down and puts it onto the battlefield as a 2/2 face-down creature with no name, no text, no subtypes, and no mana cost ([701.40a], [708.2], [708.2a], [Ghastly Conscription ruling #9]). Face down, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has no abilities and is not legendary — but the three counters are on the permanent independently of its characteristics, making it 5/5. Southern Elephant manifests as an ordinary 2/2.

So, does Nixon know which is which? Yes, in practice. The shuffle is meant to hide which manifested card is which ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #4]), and Nixon may not look at face-down permanents they don't control ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #14]) — Addison cast Ghastly Conscription, so Addison manifests and controls both permanents and may look at them. But the visible +1/+1 counters give it away: the 5/5 is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and the 2/2 is Southern Elephant. Note also that Addison is the one who could turn either face up by paying its mana cost as a special action — {B}{G} for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave or {3}{G} for Southern Elephant ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #3]).

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table; Ghastly Conscription targets one player's graveyard either way. One multiplayer wrinkle from the card's own rulings: if Addison manifests a card owned by Nixon and Addison later leaves the game, that card is exiled ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #7]).

Timing note: I'm assuming the counters were already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave in the graveyard before Ghastly Conscription resolved. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave somehow had no counters at the moment Ghastly Conscription resolved, both manifested permanents would be indistinguishable 2/2s and Nixon would not know which is which.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nixon will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Southern Elephant.
entries.human_note: it changes zones while face down so it has no abilities when it changes from exile (where it does have the counters) to the battlefield (the change in which it loses the counters is exile to battlefield)

entries.question: Asa casts [Chatterstorm]. In response, Nico casts [Gather Specimens]. After everything resolves, Asa activates the second ability of [Homeward Path]. Who gains control of the token?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Asa — as the token's creator and owner — regains control because Gather Specimens only changed who the tokens entered under, and Homeward Path returns creatures to their owners.
entries.answer:
Asa gains control of the Squirrel token (and of every Squirrel token made by the Chatterstorm storm copies).

Why:

1. Chatterstorm resolves and creates a 1/1 green Squirrel creature token for Asa. Because Nico cast Gather Specimens in response, Gather Specimens resolved first, so its replacement effect is already active: "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." Gather Specimens explicitly affects token creatures as well as nontoken creatures [Gather Specimens ruling #8], so each Squirrel token enters the battlefield under Nico's control instead of Asa's.

2. Ownership, however, does not change. Rule [111.2] says the player who creates a token is its owner; Asa cast Chatterstorm and its storm copies, so Asa creates the tokens and is their owner. Gather Specimens only alters who the tokens enter under the control of, not who made them.

3. Homeward Path's second ability, "{T}: Each player gains control of all creatures they own," then hands each Squirrel token back to its owner, Asa. Note this ability doesn't care who activated it — Asa would get the Squirrels back even if Nico had tapped Homeward Path.

Note on the Homeward Path ruling in your context: it says "The owner of a token is the player under whose control the token was put onto the battlefield," which would point at Nico. That ruling predates the current wording of rule [111.2], which is the operative rule and defines token ownership by who creates the token. I'm following [111.2], so Asa is the owner.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Gather Specimens was cast in response and therefore resolved before Chatterstorm, which is what the question describes. If instead Chatterstorm had already resolved and the tokens were already on the battlefield when Gather Specimens resolved, Gather Specimens would do nothing to them at all [Gather Specimens ruling #1] — the Squirrels would already be Asa's, and Homeward Path would simply be redundant.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any table size. Gather Specimens affects creatures that would enter under any opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #5], and Homeward Path's ability returns creatures to every player who owns them, so at a table of three or more, other players also reclaim any creatures they own that someone else controls.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Asa does. Tokens are owned by the player that created them. Asa still created the token, regardless of under whose control it entered the battlefield.

entries.question: Aaliyah controls a [Squandered Resources] and a [Glacial Floodplain]. Nicolas controls [Blood Moon]. If Aaliyah sacrifices Glacial Floodplain to Squandered Resources, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same correct conclusion—Squandered Resources can only produce {R} because Blood Moon turns Glacial Floodplain into a Mountain, leaving it able to produce only red mana.
entries.answer:
Only {R}. Aaliyah's Squandered Resources will let her add one red mana, not {W} or {U}.

Why: Blood Moon reads "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Glacial Floodplain is a nonbasic land (snow supertype and being a Snow Land doesn't make it basic), so Blood Moon sets its subtype to Mountain. When an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land loses its old land types, loses all abilities generated from its rules text and its old types, and gains the mana ability for the new type [305.7]. Blood Moon's rulings confirm this: Glacial Floodplain loses the Plains and Island types, loses "This land enters tapped" and its {W}/{U} abilities, and gains just "{T}: Add {R}." (Blood Moon's own text overrides the general behavior of the land's printed abilities here.) It keeps its name and the snow supertype, but those don't add mana abilities.

Squandered Resources produces "one mana of any type the sacrificed land could produce." The type of mana a permanent "could produce" is any type an ability of that permanent would produce if that ability resolved at that time, ignoring whether costs could be paid [106.7]. Using Glacial Floodplain as it last existed on the battlefield under Blood Moon, its only mana ability would produce {R}, so {R} is the only option. Note {R} is red mana specifically — not generic and not any colorless mana.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Blood Moon is on the battlefield at the moment Aaliyah sacrifices Glacial Floodplain. If Blood Moon were removed (or hadn't yet resolved) before the sacrifice, Glacial Floodplain would have its printed abilities and Squandered Resources could produce {W} or {U} (Aaliyah's choice).

Also worth noting: the mana is produced by Squandered Resources, not by Glacial Floodplain, so it isn't snow mana even though Glacial Floodplain has the snow supertype (see the Glacial Floodplain rulings — snow is a supertype and mana for {S} must come from a snow source).

Player count doesn't matter here: Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands on the battlefield regardless of who controls them, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Just {R}. Squandered Resources cares about what colors of mana it could produce on the battlefield.

entries.question: Neil controls [Willow Elf] enchanted with [Felidar Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Anger of the Gods]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Felidar Umbra is destroyed and sent to the graveyard while Willow Elf remains on the battlefield (not exiled) and would only be exiled if it dies later that turn.
entries.answer:
Willow Elf survives, and Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead and goes to Neil's graveyard. Willow Elf is not exiled.

Why:

1. Anger of the Gods resolves and deals 3 damage to each creature, including Willow Elf (a 1/1).
2. The next time state-based actions are checked, Willow Elf has damage marked on it that is greater than or equal to its toughness, so it has been dealt lethal damage and would be destroyed [704.5g]. "Destroy" means to move the permanent from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard [701.8a].
3. Umbra armor — the static ability on Felidar Umbra reading "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a] — replaces that destruction. It applies no matter why the creature would be destroyed, including lethal damage, and it is mandatory [Felidar Umbra ruling #6], [Felidar Umbra ruling #4]. So all 3 damage is removed from Willow Elf and Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead. Note that with lethal damage it's the game rules for lethal damage, not Anger of the Gods, that cause Felidar Umbra to be destroyed [Felidar Umbra ruling #8].
4. Anger of the Gods' second sentence is a separate replacement effect that applies to Willow Elf dying — "dies" means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield [700.4]. Because Willow Elf is never destroyed, it is never put into a graveyard, so there is no dying event to replace and nothing to exile. Under rule 616.1g, when one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer effect must be applied first; being put into the graveyard is contained within the destruction, so umbra armor is applied first and removes the inner event entirely [616.1g].
5. Felidar Umbra itself was not dealt damage by Anger of the Gods, so its destruction is a normal trip to the graveyard — Anger of the Gods' exile clause doesn't touch it.

One thing to watch for the rest of the turn: Willow Elf was dealt damage by Anger of the Gods, so if it would die later this turn for any reason at all, it gets exiled instead [Anger of the Gods ruling #1] — and Felidar Umbra is no longer around to save it.

Other creatures: Anger of the Gods hits every creature on the battlefield, and any of them that would die from that damage are exiled instead. That's true whether this is a two-player game or a multiplayer game; the outcome for Willow Elf and Felidar Umbra is identical either way, since only Neil (the controller of the affected permanent) makes any replacement-effect choice here. Rule 616.1g's APNAP-order clause would only matter if multiple players had to choose among competing replacement effects simultaneously [616.1g].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Felidar Umbra is destroyed and moves to the graveyard. Willow Elf remains on the battlefield. If it would die later in the turn, it'll be exiled instead. Felidar Umbra's effect replaces the "destroy" event while Anger of the Gods's effect replaces the "die" event, so Felidar Umbra has to be applied first.

entries.question: Asa controls [Library of Leng] and is discarding a card due to [Azra Oddsmaker]'s ability. Can they put the discarded card on top of their library? If so, what happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—the reference says Library of Leng can apply to the discard (so Asa may put it on top), while the candidate says it cannot—so the rulings disagree.
entries.answer:
No — Asa must put the discarded card into their graveyard. Library of Leng doesn't apply to Azra Oddsmaker's discard, because that discard is a cost, not an effect.

Why: Azra Oddsmaker's triggered ability reads "you may discard a card. If you do, choose a creature..." That's exactly the template covered by rule 118.12 — "[A player] may [do something]. If [that player] [does]..." — and that rule states the "[do something]" action is a cost, paid as the triggered ability resolves. Library of Leng's replacement only works "If an effect causes you to discard a card," and its ruling is explicit that you can't use it when you discard as a cost, because costs aren't effects (rule 609.1 confirms an effect is something produced by a resolving spell/ability or a static ability, and text itself is never an effect) [Library of Leng ruling #5].

What does happen: if Asa chooses to discard, the card goes from hand to graveyard, Asa has paid the cost, and Azra Oddsmaker's ability continues — Asa chooses a creature, and whenever that creature deals combat damage to a player this turn, Asa draws two cards. Note that under rule 118.12 the "If you do" clause checks whether the player started to pay the cost, so even if some other effect altered what actually happened during the discard, the cost would still count as paid (compare rule 118.11). Library of Leng's other ability — Asa has no maximum hand size — is unaffected and still applies.

If instead the discard came from an effect that just tells you to discard (e.g., a resolving spell's instruction, not an "If you do" cost), Library of Leng would let Asa put that card on top of their library instead, and it would still count as a discard for anything that triggers on discarding [Library of Leng ruling #4].

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so it works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Discarding a cost to the ability is a cost [118.12], but that doesn't stop it from being an effect as well. Library of Leng only changes where the card moves to, not that it was discarded, so the cost was paid and the remainder of Azra Oddsmaker's ability will resolve as normal.
