RG is right on this one, but its super confusing as to why. because the cost is part of an ability resolving, its part of an effect, so while it IS a cost being paid, paying that cost is PART OF AN EFFECT. I'm not sure we'll ever be able to answer this one right.

entries.question: Noah controls [Compost]. Ainsley controls [Dune Beetle] and a token that was created as a copy of [Bogstomper]. Ainsley casts [Soulscour]. How many times does Compost trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Compost triggers zero times because the Bogstomper token isn’t a card and Compost is destroyed simultaneously (and its "from anywhere" trigger gets no leaves-the-battlefield look-back).
entries.answer:
**Zero times.** Compost is itself a nonartifact permanent, so Soulscour ("Destroy all nonartifact permanents") destroys Compost at the same moment it destroys Dune Beetle and the Bogstomper token, and Compost's ability isn't one that "looks back in time."

Why:

1. **The token never counts.** Compost reads "Whenever a black card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere." A token created as a copy of Bogstomper is a token, not a card, so its going to the graveyard is not a black *card* being put into a graveyard. That event can never trigger Compost regardless of anything else.

2. **Dune Beetle is a black card, but Compost is gone at the same instant.** Trigger conditions are normally checked using the objects that exist *immediately after* the event, and an enchantment's abilities function only while it's on the battlefield [113.6], [603.10]. Since Soulscour destroys Compost simultaneously with Dune Beetle, Compost is already in Noah's graveyard when the game checks the event.

3. **The "look back in time" exception doesn't rescue it.** The game does look back for leaves-the-battlefield abilities — that's why a "whenever a creature dies" artifact still triggers when it's wiped alongside the creatures [603.10a]. But rule [603.6c] says an ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone "from anywhere" is *never* treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even when the object came from the battlefield. Compost's ability is a "from anywhere" ability, so it gets no look-back and simply doesn't trigger on a simultaneous mass destruction that includes Compost.

Contrast: if Compost survived (say Soulscour were replaced by targeted removal on just Ainsley's board, or Compost were somehow indestructible/not destroyed), Compost would trigger **once** — for Dune Beetle only, still nothing for the Bogstomper token. Compost's own ruling confirms it triggers on black cards discarded, milled, countered, or dying from the battlefield, but all of those require a *card*.

Multiplayer note: the same analysis holds at any table size. With more players, Soulscour would also destroy other opponents' permanents, and each black *card* put into an opponent's graveyard would be a separate trigger event — but because Compost leaves the battlefield simultaneously and gets no look-back, none of those trigger either. Cards owned/put into Noah's own graveyard never trigger Compost, since it only cares about an opponent's graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
0. Soulscour destroys all permanents simultaneously. Compost's trigger checks immediately after the event in question to see if it should trigger. However by that time Compost is in the graveyard, and its ability doesn't function there.

(Compost doesn't fit the "leaves-the-battlefield" trigger exception because it's a "from anywhere" trigger.)

entries.question: Noor controls [Rhystic Study]. Alex casts [Mishra's Domination]. As Rhystic Study's trigger resolves, who makes their choice first? Does Noor choose whether or not to draw a card, and if yes, Alex may pay the mana to prevent it? Or does Alex choose to pay the mana first, and if they don't, Noor has the choice to draw a card?
entries.reason: The candidate states Alex chooses whether to pay {1} first and Noor may draw only if Alex doesn't or can't pay, which matches the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
Alex chooses first. When Rhystic Study's triggered ability resolves, Alex decides whether to pay {1} (one generic mana, payable with mana of any color or with colorless mana); only if Alex declines or can't pay does Noor then choose whether to draw a card.

Why: Rhystic Study reads "Whenever an opponent casts a spell, you may draw a card unless that player pays {1}." A "[Do something] unless [a player does something else]" template means the same thing as "[That player] may [do something else]. If [that player doesn't], [do something]" [118.12a]. So the ability is functionally "Alex may pay {1}. If Alex doesn't, Noor may draw a card." The payment is a cost paid on resolution of the triggered ability, and the "if that player doesn't" clause checks whether Alex chose to pay [118.12a].

Rhystic Study's own ruling confirms the order explicitly: "You don't have to decide whether or not to draw a card until after the player decides whether or not to pay" [Rhystic Study ruling #1]. Note also that drawing is still optional for Noor — even if Alex declines to pay, Noor may choose not to draw.

Timing detail: Rhystic Study's triggered ability goes on the stack above Mishra's Domination and resolves first, so Alex makes the pay-or-not decision while Mishra's Domination is still on the stack, before it resolves and attaches to a creature. The trigger (and thus the payment choice) happens even if Mishra's Domination is countered [Rhystic Study ruling #2].

Player count doesn't change this: only "that player" — Alex, the caster of Mishra's Domination — gets the option to pay {1}, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Alex chooses first.

entries.question: Allison controls [Leyline of Anticipation]. In their draw step, they casts [Relentless Assault]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Relentless Assault cast in the draw step untaps nothing and creates no extra combat/main phase.
entries.answer:
Relentless Assault resolves and does essentially nothing: no creatures untap and no extra phases are created.

Why:

1. **Casting it is legal.** Leyline of Anticipation says "You may cast spells as though they had flash," so Allison can cast the sorcery Relentless Assault during their own draw step, when they'd otherwise be unable to cast a sorcery. Card text like this overrides the general sorcery-timing restriction.

2. **The untap clause does nothing.** Relentless Assault untaps all creatures that attacked this turn. In the draw step, the combat phase of this turn hasn't happened yet, so no creature has attacked this turn. An effect that attempts to do something impossible (or that has no legal objects to affect) simply does as much as it can — here, nothing [609.3].

3. **No extra combat or main phase.** Relentless Assault says "After this main phase, there is an additional combat phase followed by an additional main phase," and its ruling is explicit: it creates an additional combat and main phase only if it resolves during a main phase [Relentless Assault ruling #1]. Since Allison cast it in the draw step, it resolves in the draw step, and there is no "this main phase" to attach the new phases to. Effects that add phases insert them directly after a specified phase [500.8]; with no specified phase, nothing is added. The turn proceeds normally into Allison's precombat main phase, and the {2}{R}{R} is wasted.

Timing assumption: since a step can't end with a spell on the stack, Relentless Assault both is cast and resolves during the draw step. If instead Allison waited and cast it during either main phase (which Leyline of Anticipation doesn't even require, since sorceries are already castable then), it would resolve in a main phase and would grant the extra combat phase plus extra main phase, and would untap any creatures that had already attacked that turn.

Player count doesn't change any of this — the answer is the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer, since everything here happens on Allison's own turn and affects only Allison's phases.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: There is no "this main phase" to add the combat step after, so no additional phase is created. The turn proceeds as normal.

entries.question: Albert, Brielle, and Campbell are playing a multiplayer game. Brielle controls [Stalking Leonin]. Albert casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Brielle's next turn. After Brielle begins their turn, can Albert see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
entries.reason: The candidate asserts Albert can see Brielle's secret choice under rule 723.4 while the reference correctly states the choice was a past hidden event and is not visible to Albert unless the ability is activated, so the conclusions conflict.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Brielle's turn begins and Albert is controlling Brielle, Albert can see which opponent was secretly chosen for Brielle's Stalking Leonin.

Why: Stalking Leonin's enters-the-battlefield trigger has Brielle "secretly choose an opponent," and that choice is recorded somehow (for example, by writing the player's name on a slip of paper kept with Stalking Leonin) — it is hidden information about Stalking Leonin, an object in the game, that Brielle knows. Rule 723.4 says that if information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it's visible to both that player and the controller of that player. So Albert, as the controller of Brielle, sees it. Worst Fears' own reminder text says the same thing in short form — "You see all cards that player could see and make all decisions for them" — and its rulings confirm that while controlling another player you can see all cards in the game that player can see, including cards in hand and face-down cards that player controls.

Two limits worth noting. First, this only extends to in-game information: rule 723.4 specifies that information about cards outside the game (such as a sideboard) that would be visible to Brielle is visible only to Brielle, not to Albert. The Stalking Leonin choice is in-game information, so it isn't covered by that exception. Second, Albert controls Brielle, not Brielle's permanents — per Worst Fears' rulings, Albert only controls the player and doesn't control any of Brielle's permanents, spells, or abilities. Albert still makes Brielle's decisions, so Albert could decide to activate Stalking Leonin's last ability, paying its cost by revealing the chosen player — but that ability needs a legal target, a creature attacking Brielle controlled by the chosen player, and during Brielle's own turn Brielle is the active player, so there generally won't be creatures attacking Brielle to target.

This answer is for the three-player game as described (Albert, Brielle, Campbell); rule 723.4 works the same regardless of the number of players, and Campbell's presence doesn't change it. Campbell does not gain any right to see the secret choice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Brielle. Albert can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

The info isn't visible, but it IS known to the player, so I guess its the same as putting a card on top of your library, where you know what it was but its not information visible. the ruling from RG is  correct, but we also probably need to find info that says a secret choice is not visible to the player who made it, even if realistically in game they'd be able to look at it if its written down because having to remember that when there's so many other things going on, then also trusting that the person didn't change the answer if they didn't write it down, is some nuance. the writing down is more about not being able to cheat, but that still doesn't make it visible info.

entries.question: Abdullah controls [Primal Vigor] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Primal Vigor to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: The candidate says it enters with one counter, but the correct ruling is two since both replacement effects are applied as Rescuer Sphinx enters and Primal Vigor still affects the counter.
entries.answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Why: Rescuer Sphinx's ability ("As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it") is a replacement effect that modifies how Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield [614.1c], and such an effect may cause another object to change zones as part of applying it [614.13a]. The choice is made and carried out before Rescuer Sphinx is actually on the battlefield, and no player may take actions in between [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #3].

So the sequence is: Abdullah applies Rescuer Sphinx's replacement effect, returning Primal Vigor from the battlefield to his hand, and only then is it established that Rescuer Sphinx enters with a +1/+1 counter. Primal Vigor's doubling ability is a static ability that functions only while Primal Vigor is on the battlefield; once it has been returned to hand it is no longer an existing continuous effect that could apply. When you determine which replacement effects apply to a permanent entering the battlefield, you look at the replacement effects that have already modified how it enters plus the continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it [614.12], [614.12a], [616.1]. At that moment Primal Vigor's effect no longer exists, so nothing doubles the counter.

Note also that Primal Vigor's second ability can't be applied "first": it only applies if one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature [614.16], and until Rescuer Sphinx's own replacement effect is applied (including the return), the number of counters Rescuer Sphinx would enter with is zero. The replaced event simply never happens in the un-doubled-then-doubled way — the modified event is what occurs [614.6].

If instead Abdullah returned some other nonland permanent (or returned nothing but had another way to get the counter), Primal Vigor would still be on the battlefield and would double the counter — Rescuer Sphinx would enter with two +1/+1 counters, since Primal Vigor explicitly affects permanents that enter with counters [Primal Vigor ruling #3], and it doesn't matter who controls the creature getting the counters [Primal Vigor ruling #2].

Player count doesn't change any of this: the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table. The only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that if several players must order overlapping replacement effects at the same time, those choices are made in APNAP order [616.1] — which doesn't come up here, since Abdullah controls Rescuer Sphinx and makes all the relevant choices himself.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two. Both cards have a replacement effect. Abdullah will choose whether they are returning a permanent, but won't actually complete the action until Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield. Therefore Primal Vigor will still apply to the +1/+1 counter being from Rescuer Sphinx's ability.
entries.human_note:
(cited ruling #3 is out of range — Rescuer Sphinx has 3 rulings, #0-#2)

I think this decision hinges on that the entire ability (as it enters) resolves before the permanent actually leaves the battlefield. I think there's a few questions that mirror this same type of issue (hinging on "as")

entries.question: Arturo uses [Vengeful Ancestor] to goad [Craw Wurm]. After it's been goaded, Nico uses [Brokers Confluence], causing Craw Wurm to phase out. On Nico's turn, what are Nico's legal combat choices?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Craw Wurm remains goaded after phasing in and therefore Nico must attack with it, attacking a non-goading player if able (or Arturo in a two‑player game).
entries.answer:
Craw Wurm phases back in at the start of Nico's untap step, and it is still goaded — so Nico must attack with Craw Wurm, and must send it at a player other than Arturo if that's possible.

Why:

1. Phasing means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist while phased out, but it never actually leaves the battlefield or changes control ([702.26d]). Brokers Confluence's mode says "Target creature phases out. (Treat it and anything attached to it as though they don't exist until its controller's next turn.)" Since Nico controls Craw Wurm, Craw Wurm phases in at the beginning of Nico's next turn (untap step), before Nico's combat phase.

2. Goad is a designation, not an ability and not a copiable value ([701.15b]); the designation from Vengeful Ancestor's trigger lasts "until the next turn of the controller of that spell or ability" — i.e., until Arturo's next turn ([701.15a]). That's a fixed duration, not a "for as long as" duration that tracks the creature, so it isn't the kind of effect that ends because Craw Wurm phased out ([702.26f]); phasing also doesn't count as Craw Wurm leaving or re-entering the battlefield for effects that check its history ([702.26d]). So as long as Arturo's next turn hasn't begun, Craw Wurm is still goaded when it phases in.

3. Consequences for Nico's declare-attackers step ([701.15b]): Craw Wurm attacks each combat if able, so Nico cannot simply leave it home if it's untapped and otherwise able to attack. It must attack a player other than Arturo if able.
   - Two-player game (Nico vs. Arturo only): there is no other player to attack, so that part of the requirement can't be satisfied; Craw Wurm still has to attack, and it attacks Arturo (or a planeswalker/battle Arturo controls, if attacking one satisfies the requirement to attack).
   - Multiplayer: Nico must choose some opponent other than Arturo as the defending player for Craw Wurm if any such attack is legal; only if no non-Arturo player can legally be attacked may Craw Wurm attack Arturo.
   - Nico's other creatures are unaffected — Nico may attack with them or not, as normal.

4. Don't forget the payoff: Vengeful Ancestor's second ability, "Whenever a goaded creature attacks, it deals 1 damage to its controller," triggers when Craw Wurm attacks, so Craw Wurm deals 1 damage to Nico.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nico cast Brokers Confluence during someone else's turn (e.g., Arturo's turn, after Vengeful Ancestor's goad trigger resolved), so Craw Wurm is already phased back in by Nico's combat. If instead Nico phased Craw Wurm out during Nico's own turn before combat, Craw Wurm would stay phased out until Nico's *following* turn — it would miss that combat entirely (it's treated as not existing, so the "attacks if able" requirement does nothing), and by the time it phases in the goad may already have expired if Arturo's turn has begun in the meantime.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Craw Wurm must attack, and since there aren't any other players in the game, it has to attack Arturo. Goaded creatures must attack, and must attack a player other than the one that goaded them if able. Phasing doesn't cause Craw Wurm to no longer be goaded, as the duration on the continuous effect hasn't ended when Craw Wurm phases back in.

entries.question: Arabella controls [Sylvok Explorer]. Nolan controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. If Arabella taps the Sylvok Explorer, what type(s) of mana can they produce?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Sylvok Explorer produces no mana because Nolan's Gaea's Cradle could produce no mana (Nolan controls no creatures), so there is no color for Sylvok Explorer to produce.
entries.answer:
Arabella's Sylvok Explorer produces no mana at all.

Sylvok Explorer says "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only opponent's land here is Nolan's Gaea's Cradle, which reads "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control." Nolan controls no creatures, so if Gaea's Cradle's mana ability resolved right now it would add zero mana — zero green mana is still no mana. Rule 106.7 says that when checking what mana a permanent "could produce," you look at what its ability would produce if it resolved at that time (ignoring whether its costs could be paid), and if the permanent wouldn't produce any mana under those conditions, there's no type of mana it could produce. So Gaea's Cradle currently could produce no type of mana, and Sylvok Explorer's ability has no color to choose.

Practical result: Arabella can still activate the ability (tapping Sylvok Explorer), the ability resolves, and it simply adds nothing. Note that Arabella's own lands, and the fact that Arabella controls a creature (Sylvok Explorer itself), are irrelevant — Gaea's Cradle counts only creatures Nolan controls, and Sylvok Explorer looks only at lands opponents control.

Multiplayer difference: with exactly two players, the answer above is the whole story. At a table with more than two players, Sylvok Explorer checks lands controlled by *any* opponent, so if a third player controlled, say, a Mountain, Sylvok Explorer could produce {R}. Likewise, if Nolan gained a creature (or any other opponent's land could produce mana) before Sylvok Explorer's ability is activated, the answer changes accordingly.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None. Gaea's Cradle couldn't produce any mana, so neither can Sylvok Explorer.

entries.question: Addisyn casts [Read the Runes] for X=2 and chooses to discard a card and sacrifice [All-Seeing Arbiter]. Will All-Seeing Arbiter trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the sacrifice happens before the discards under Read the Runes' ordering, so All-Seeing Arbiter is gone before the discard and cannot trigger.
entries.answer:
No. All-Seeing Arbiter will not trigger.

Why: Read the Runes says "Draw X cards. For each card drawn this way, discard a card unless you sacrifice a permanent." Per rule [118.12a], "[do something] unless [a player does something else]" means "you may sacrifice a permanent; if you don't, discard a card" — so the sacrifice is the optional alternative to each discard. With X=2, Addisyn has two such instances and chooses to satisfy one by sacrificing All-Seeing Arbiter and the other by discarding a card.

The order is fixed by the Read the Runes ruling: you draw the cards, then sacrifice any permanents you want to sacrifice, then discard the required number of cards, with no chance to act in between. So All-Seeing Arbiter is already in the graveyard at the moment the discard actually happens.

All-Seeing Arbiter's "Whenever you discard a card, target creature an opponent controls gets -X/-0..." is an ability of a permanent, and under rule [113.6] abilities of objects other than instants and sorceries function only while that object is on the battlefield. Since All-Seeing Arbiter left the battlefield (sacrificed) before the discard event occurred, its triggered ability isn't on the battlefield to see the discard and does not trigger.

Assumption about timing: I'm treating the sacrifice and the discard as happening in the order the Read the Runes ruling dictates (all sacrifices first, then all discards). If the discard could somehow be made to happen while All-Seeing Arbiter was still on the battlefield, the ability would trigger and you'd choose a target creature an opponent controls, with X equal to the number of different mana values among cards in your graveyard — but Read the Runes doesn't allow that ordering.

Player count doesn't change any of this. The only multiplayer-relevant piece would be that, had All-Seeing Arbiter's ability triggered, you'd pick a creature controlled by any one opponent; with two players that's simply your single opponent's creature.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Addisyn will first choose whether they are sacrificing permanent, if they don't then they discard a card. Because it happens in this order, All-Seeing Arbiter will not be around to when Addisyn is discarding a card.

entries.question: Addison has six cards in their graveyard and casts [Epicenter] targeting Nataly. In response, Nataly casts [Blossoming Calm]. Before it resolves, Addison casts [Dampen Thought] targeting themself. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Epicenter won't resolve because Nataly becomes an illegal target before it resolves, so no lands are sacrificed and the threshold replacement never applies.
entries.answer:
Epicenter does nothing at all — it is removed from the stack and put into Addison's graveyard without resolving, so nobody sacrifices any land, and Nataly keeps hexproof and the 2 life.

Step by step (the stack resolves last-in, first-out):

1. **Dampen Thought** (cast last) resolves first. It targets Addison, who has no hexproof, so the target is legal: Addison mills four cards. Addison's graveyard goes from 6 to 10 cards, and Dampen Thought itself is put into that graveyard as the last part of its resolution (11 cards). Addison is now well past the seven-card threshold count [Dampen Thought ruling #4].

2. **Blossoming Calm** resolves next. Nataly gains hexproof until Nataly's next turn and gains 2 life. Because of rebound, Blossoming Calm is exiled as it resolves instead of going to the graveyard, and Nataly may cast it from exile for free at the beginning of Nataly's next upkeep (that recast is optional).

3. **Epicenter** tries to resolve last. On resolution the game rechecks target legality [608.2b]. Nataly now has hexproof, meaning Nataly can't be the target of spells or abilities Nataly's opponents control, so Nataly is an illegal target for Epicenter. Epicenter's only instance of the word "target" is now illegal, so the spell doesn't resolve; it is removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard, and **none** of its effects happen [608.2b]. Addison also can't move the target to another player — targets can't be changed unless a spell or ability explicitly says so [115.1a].

Why the threshold clause doesn't save it: "Each player sacrifices all lands they control instead" is a self-replacement effect that would modify Epicenter's own effect as it resolves [614.15], and later text modifying earlier text is only applied while following the spell's instructions during resolution [608.2c]. Since Epicenter never resolves, that replacement is never applied, even though Addison now has seven or more cards in the graveyard. Milling into threshold in response was a wasted effort here.

Note on terminology: the definition of hexproof isn't among the rules quoted in this context, but it is the keyword Blossoming Calm grants — a player with hexproof can't be targeted by opponents' spells and abilities; that characteristic change is exactly the kind of "other change to the game state" that makes a target illegal under [608.2b].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the casting order stated in the question (Epicenter, then Blossoming Calm, then Dampen Thought, with nothing resolving in between). If instead Dampen Thought had resolved before Blossoming Calm was ever cast, nothing changes for Epicenter — hexproof still applies before Epicenter resolves. But if Blossoming Calm had resolved before Addison cast Epicenter, Addison simply couldn't choose Nataly as a target at all and would have to target a different (legal) player.

Multiplayer: the outcome is the same with two players or more — Epicenter never resolves, so no player sacrifices anything. The difference is only in what was lost: with more than two players, a resolving threshold Epicenter would have made *every* player, including Addison, sacrifice all their lands, and hexproof on Nataly alone doesn't protect anyone else — had Addison targeted some other, non-hexproof player, Epicenter would have resolved and the threshold clause would have wiped every player's lands.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Neither player will sacrifice any lands. The text on Epicenter is a self-replacement effect and changes what the spell is doing. However, before the replacement effect would be applied the game checks to see if all the targets for the spell are still legal. Nataly is no longer a legal target, therefore the spell won't resolve.

entries.question: Anson controls [Zirda, the Dawnwaker], [Sundial, Dawn Tyrant], and [Mobilized District]. How much does Anson have to pay to activate the second ability of Mobilized District?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling — the two reductions can be applied in either order, allowing the cost to be either {0} (best order) or {1} (other order).
entries.answer:
Anson can pay as little as {0} (all generic), because he chooses the order in which the two cost reductions apply. At worst — if he applies them in the other order — it's {1}.

Why: the ability in question is Mobilized District's second ability, "{4}: This land becomes a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance until end of turn," whose starting activation cost is {4} — four generic mana, no colored or {C} symbols involved. Two separate reductions apply:

- Mobilized District's own text: "This ability costs {1} less to activate for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control." Anson controls two such permanents — Zirda, the Dawnwaker (legendary creature) and Sundial, Dawn Tyrant (legendary artifact creature) — so that's {2} less. Mobilized District itself isn't legendary and isn't a creature right now, so it doesn't count.
- Zirda, the Dawnwaker: "Abilities you activate that aren't mana abilities cost {2} less to activate. This effect can't reduce the mana in that cost to less than one mana." Mobilized District's animation ability doesn't produce mana as it resolves, so it isn't a mana ability and Zirda, the Dawnwaker's reduction applies. (Zirda, the Dawnwaker would not reduce Mobilized District's "{T}: Add {C}" mana ability.)

An activation cost is handled like a spell's mana cost, and when multiple cost reductions apply the player may apply them in any order (602.2b, 601.2f). So:

- Best order — Zirda, the Dawnwaker first: {4} − {2} = {2} (Zirda, the Dawnwaker's floor isn't broken, since the result is still one or more mana), then Mobilized District's own reduction: {2} − {2} = {0}. Total cost {0}.
- Other order — Mobilized District's own reduction first: {4} − {2} = {2}, then Zirda, the Dawnwaker can only take it down to one mana, so {2} − {1} = {1}. Total cost {1} generic.

Zirda, the Dawnwaker's own ruling confirms its reduction is capped: "The activation cost is reduced by only {1} if doing so reduces that cost to one mana." That cap limits only Zirda, the Dawnwaker's own reduction, not Mobilized District's separate self-reduction, which is why applying Zirda, the Dawnwaker first gets Anson to {0}. Cost reductions never take a cost below {0} (601.2f). Once Anson locks in the total, later cost-changing effects don't matter (601.2f).

Player count doesn't change this: only permanents Anson controls are counted, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Anson can either pay {1} or {0}.

There are two effects that are reducing the cost of the second ability of Mobilized District. Because of this, Anson can choose the order in which they will apply. If Anson applies the reduction of effect from Mobilized District first then from Zirda, the Dawnwaker, Anson will pay {1} because Zirda, the Dawnwaker can't reduce a cost to less than one mana. Alternatively, Anson can apply the reduction from Zirda, the Dawnwaker first then from Mobilized District. This would require Anson to spend {0} because the effect from Zirda, the Dawnwaker reduces the cost to {2} then the reduction for Mobilized District reduces it to {0}.

entries.question: Anderson controls [Quirion Explorer]. Nico controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Anderson taps Quirion Explorer, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Explorer produces no mana (except a narrow ETB-trigger window), while the reference says it can produce any color because Crumbling Vestige’s triggered mana ability is considered, so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Quirion Explorer produces no mana. Anderson can still tap it — the ability can be activated and it resolves — but it adds nothing to Anderson's mana pool.

Why: Quirion Explorer's ability adds "one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only land Nico controls is Crumbling Vestige, whose mana ability is "{T}: Add {C}." {C} is colorless mana, not a color — it is not {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}, and it is not generic mana either. Since Crumbling Vestige could produce no *colored* mana, there is no legal color for Quirion Explorer's ability to add, so it produces nothing [106.7]. This is exactly the case covered by Quirion Explorer's own ruling: if the opponent only has lands that produce colorless or no mana, the ability can still be activated, it just won't produce any mana [Quirion Explorer ruling #1].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Crumbling Vestige is already on the battlefield and its "When this land enters, add one mana of any color" trigger has already resolved (or never was on the stack). If instead Crumbling Vestige has just entered and that triggered mana ability is still pending, there is a reasonable argument under 106.7 — which speaks of "any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time" — that the pending trigger makes any of the five colors available to Quirion Explorer. The rules text provided here doesn't cleanly settle whether a once-only enters-the-battlefield mana trigger counts for "could produce," so treat that narrow window as unresolved by the provided material; in every other case the answer is no mana.

Multiplayer note: Quirion Explorer says "a land an opponent controls," so at a table with more than two players you check the lands of *all* of Anderson's opponents, not just Nico's — if any other opponent controlled, say, a Forest, Quirion Explorer could add {G}. With only Anderson and Nico, Crumbling Vestige is the only land to check.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Any color. Quirion Explorer checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

entries.question: Andi controls [Karn Liberated], which has exiled an [Anvil of Bogardan]. They activate Karn Liberated's -14 ability, and restarts the game. How many cards will they draw during their first turn?
entries.reason: The candidate diverges by allowing a different outcome in multiplayer (claiming Andi draws two and discards one in 3+ player games), whereas the reference's correct ruling is that Andi draws 0 on their first turn.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: In a two-player game, Andi draws zero cards during their first turn. In a game with three or more players, Andi draws two cards (their normal draw for the turn plus Anvil of Bogardan's extra card) and then discards one.

Why:

1. Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game, and the player who controlled the restarting ability — Andi — is the starting player in the new game [727.1a]. Anvil of Bogardan, having been exiled with Karn Liberated by one of its first two abilities, stays in exile through the restart and is then put onto the battlefield under Andi's control after the pregame procedure but before the new game's first turn [Karn Liberated ruling #5, Karn Liberated ruling #7]. So Anvil of Bogardan is already on the battlefield when Andi's first turn begins, and it's treated as having been under Andi's control since the beginning of that turn [Karn Liberated ruling #3].

2. Two-player game: the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn [103.8a]. To skip a step is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist [500.11], and anything scheduled for a skipped step simply doesn't happen [614.10a]. Since Anvil of Bogardan's ability triggers "at the beginning of each player's draw step," and Andi has no first-turn draw step at all, the ability never triggers — no extra draw and no discard. Note this is different from Anvil of Bogardan ruling #1: that ruling covers the case where the draw *event* inside the resolving ability is replaced, in which case the discard still happens. Here the whole step, and therefore the trigger itself, never occurs. Total cards drawn on Andi's first turn: 0.

3. Three or more players: rule 103.8a's skipped draw step applies only "in a two-player game," so Andi does get a draw step on turn one. Andi draws their card for the turn, then Anvil of Bogardan's ability goes on the stack (it's put on the stack after the turn-based draw has already happened) [Anvil of Bogardan ruling #4], resolves, Andi draws an additional card and discards a card. Total drawn: 2, with one discard.

Not counted above: the seven-card opening hand (and any mulligans) is part of the new game's pregame procedure [727.1a], not a draw during Andi's first turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. Their entire draw step is skipped. Andi will be the starting player in the new game. Because they is the starting player they'll skip their first draw step. Anvil of Bogardan triggers at the beginning of the draw step, but it doesn't get a chance to trigger if that step is skipped.
entries.human_note: the answers are the same. more out of range errors though.

entries.question: Nico controls [Drought]. How many Swamps would Ava have to sacrifice in order to cast [Beckon Apparition]?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes that Beckon Apparition's {W/B} hybrid symbol counts as a black symbol for Drought, so casting it requires sacrificing one Swamp.
entries.answer:
Ava must sacrifice exactly one Swamp.

Beckon Apparition's mana cost is a single hybrid symbol, {W/B}. A hybrid symbol is a colored mana symbol that is *all* of its component colors, so {W/B} is both a white mana symbol and a black mana symbol [107.4e]. Drought counts black mana symbols in the spell's mana cost, and its ruling is explicit that a hybrid symbol which is partly black counts as a black mana symbol regardless of which half you actually pay [Drought ruling #2]. Beckon Apparition's cost contains one such symbol, so Drought adds one additional cost of "Sacrifice a Swamp."

Two practical notes:

- It doesn't matter that Ava pays the {W/B} with white mana; the symbol is still black for Drought's purposes [107.4e][Drought ruling #2].
- Drought's second ability says "Spells cost an additional..." without limiting it to its controller, so it applies to Ava's spells even though Nico controls Drought. If Ava controls no Swamp, she can't pay the additional cost and therefore can't cast Beckon Apparition at all.

The total cost is thus {W/B} (payable with one white or one black mana) plus sacrificing one Swamp. This is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — Drought's wording doesn't single out any particular player, so every player's black-symbol spells are taxed identically.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 1. Hybrid mana symbols are the colors of their constituent mana symbols.

entries.question: Nico controls [Solemnity]. Aimee controls [Vizier of Remedies] and a tapped [Barrenton Medic]. Can Aimee untap Barrenton Medic with its own ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion and reasoning as the reference: Solemnity prevents putting -1/-1 counters so Barrenton Medic's activation cost can't be paid and Vizier of Remedies cannot replace or allow that forbidden event.
entries.answer:
No — Aimee can't activate Barrenton Medic's untap ability while Nico's Solemnity is on the battlefield, even with Vizier of Remedies.

Why:

1. Barrenton Medic's untap ability has the cost "Put a -1/-1 counter on this creature." That's a cost, paid on activation, not on resolution [Barrenton Medic ruling #1].
2. Solemnity says "Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands." This is a "can't happen" effect. Rule [614.17b] says that if an event can't happen, a player can't choose to pay a cost that includes that event. Solemnity's own ruling states this directly: if the cost of an ability requires putting counters on a creature, that cost can't be paid [Solemnity ruling #8].
3. Vizier of Remedies doesn't rescue the activation. Vizier of Remedies is an ordinary replacement effect ("if one or more -1/-1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many minus one are put on it instead"), and rule [614.17c] says an event that can't happen may only be replaced by a self-replacement effect — other replacement effects can't modify or replace it. So Vizier of Remedies never gets to shrink the payment to "zero counters"; the cost still reads as putting a -1/-1 counter on Barrenton Medic, Solemnity forbids that event, and the ability simply can't be activated.

Note that Solemnity's controller doesn't matter — Nico controlling it still shuts off Aimee's cost, since Solemnity is worded globally. That also means the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: Solemnity applies to every player's creatures, so no player could pay a "put a counter on it" cost, and none of the rules provided treat this differently based on player count.

Aimee's other option is unaffected: Barrenton Medic's {T} damage-prevention ability doesn't involve counters, but of course it requires Barrenton Medic to be untapped, which it currently isn't.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Since Solemnity prevents counters from being put on creatures, Aimee can't activate Barrenton Medic's ability, as its cost cannot legally be paid. Vizier of Remedies's replacement effect won't apply as events that can't happen can only be replaced by self-replacement effects.

entries.question: Aislinn controls [Anointed Procession] and a [Skullmulcher]. They cast [Tempt with Reflections] targeting the Skullmulcher. Can Aislinn apply the devour replacement effect before the Anointed Procession replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Anointed Procession's replacement applies to the token-creation event first, so devour doesn't get applied once to all tokens but is applied separately to each token as it enters.
entries.answer:
No. Aislinn must apply Anointed Procession's doubling effect first, and only then may each resulting token's devour ability be applied — one token at a time.

Why: entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token. When one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within the first, the outer effect must be chosen and applied first [616.1g]. Anointed Procession modifies the token-creation event ("If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead"), while devour ("As this creature enters, you may sacrifice any number of creatures. It enters with that many +1/+1 counters on it") modifies the entering-the-battlefield event contained inside it. So the number of tokens is locked in first, then the "as enters" ability is applied individually for each token [Anointed Procession ruling #1], [Tempt with Reflections ruling #9].

Practical consequences:
- There is no single "devour once, counters on everybody" option. Each Skullmulcher token separately asks Aislinn how many creatures to sacrifice, and a creature sacrificed to one token isn't available to the next. Sacrificing exactly 1 creature total means exactly one token enters with one +1/+1 counter; the rest enter as 3/3s with no counters.
- The tokens can't feed each other: all the tokens are created and enter the battlefield simultaneously [Anointed Procession ruling #2], and devour can't devour creatures that enter at the same time as the devouring creature [Skullmulcher ruling #1].
- Each token that devoured at least one creature will also trigger "When this creature enters, draw a card for each creature it devoured"; the ones that devoured nothing draw nothing.

How many tokens: Tempt with Reflections creates one copy for Aislinn, lets each opponent create their own copy, and then creates an additional copy for Aislinn per accepting opponent. Anointed Procession only doubles tokens created under Aislinn's control, so opponents' copies aren't doubled. In a two-player game Aislinn gets 2 tokens (4 if the single opponent accepts); at a multiplayer table with, say, three opponents where two accept, Aislinn gets 2 from the initial creation plus 2 for each accepting opponent, i.e. 6 total, while each accepting opponent gets just 1. Opponents decide in turn order starting with the player to Aislinn's left, and all accepted copies happen simultaneously [Tempt with Reflections ruling #5], [Tempt with Reflections ruling #6].

Timing note: I'm assuming Anointed Procession is already on the battlefield when Tempt with Reflections resolves. If it entered only after the tokens were created, it wouldn't double anything for that resolution at all.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Skullmulcher: Skullmulcher's own effect and Anointed Procession's effect. Skullmulcher's effect applies to it entering the battlefield however, while Anointed Procession's effect applies to it being created, so Anointed Procession's effect must be applied first. After that is applied the original Skullmulcher's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Skullmulchers entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

entries.question: Bailey controls [Pandemonium]. Anderson casts [Gray Ogre] and targets Bailey's [Jibbirik Omnivore] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Chelsea casts [Incinerate] targeting Anderson causing them to lose the game. Will Bailey's creature die?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Bailey controls the Pandemonium trigger and, after Anderson leaves, Bailey chooses another player (e.g. Chelsea) to make the "may" choice, so the Omnivore only dies if that chosen player elects to have the damage dealt.
entries.answer:
Not automatically — Bailey's Jibbirik Omnivore dies only if the player who inherits Anderson's choice says "yes" to the damage, and that player will be Chelsea (or another opponent Bailey picks).

How it plays out, assuming Incinerate resolves and Anderson loses the game before the Pandemonium trigger resolves (that's the order stated in the question):

1. The Pandemonium trigger is Bailey's. Even though Gray Ogre entered under Anderson's control, the ability's source is Bailey's Pandemonium, so Bailey controls the triggered ability while Anderson makes the "may" choice and chose the target [113.8, 603.3a, Pandemonium ruling #2]. Because Bailey (not Anderson) controls the ability, it stays on the stack when Anderson leaves.

2. The target was locked in when the ability went on the stack; Jibbirik Omnivore is still on the battlefield, so the ability still has a legal target and will resolve.

3. The only remaining choice is Anderson's optional "may have it deal damage" [608.2d]. Anderson has left the game, so rule 800.4g applies: the controller of the object (Bailey) chooses another player to make that choice, and since the choice originally belonged to an opponent of Bailey, Bailey must choose another opponent if possible — here, Chelsea.

4. If Chelsea chooses to have Gray Ogre deal the damage, it deals damage equal to its power. Pandemonium doesn't check power until resolution, and if Gray Ogre is no longer on the battlefield (it left with Anderson), it uses the power it had right before it left — 2 [Pandemonium ruling #1]. Two damage to the 3/2 Jibbirik Omnivore is lethal damage, so it is destroyed unless Bailey has a regeneration or damage-prevention effect. Incinerate's "can't be regenerated" clause is irrelevant: Incinerate damaged Anderson, not Jibbirik Omnivore [Incinerate].

5. If Chelsea declines, no damage is dealt and Jibbirik Omnivore survives.

Timing caveat: if instead the Pandemonium trigger had somehow resolved before Anderson lost the game, Anderson would make the choice personally and Gray Ogre (still on the battlefield) would deal 2 to Jibbirik Omnivore if Anderson said yes — same lethal result, just no substitute chooser.

Multiplayer note: this answer depends on there being at least three players — rule 800.4g exists precisely because multiplayer games continue after a player leaves. In a two-player game, Anderson losing would simply end the game, so the trigger would never resolve. The provided rules don't spell out exactly what happens to Gray Ogre itself when Anderson leaves; I'm relying on the Pandemonium ruling that covers the case where the creature is gone at resolution.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The triggered ability of Pandemonium includes a choice to be made upon resolution. However the player that is supposed to make that choice is no longer in the game, therefore the controller of the trigger chooses another player to make that choice. In this case Bailey will choose another player to decide whether Pandemonium's trigger will deal damage to Jibbirik Omnivore. Bailey is the controller of the trigger since they control the enchantment that generated the trigger, even though Anderson is the player making choices about the trigger.

entries.question: Alice controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: the token is a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a Mountain land with "{T}: Add {R}."
entries.answer:
The Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a land — but a Mountain land, not a Forest. Its full characteristics: card types creature and land; creature type Saproling; land type Mountain; power/toughness 1/1; color green; and it has the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" (not "{T}: Add {G}").

Why:

1. Life and Limb applies first. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." So the token becomes a creature *and* a land, with the creature type Saproling and the land type Forest, keeping the correlation of subtype to card type (Forest is only a land type, Saproling only a creature type) [Life and Limb ruling #4]. As a Forest it would have "{T}: Add {G}" [Life and Limb ruling #3].

2. Blood Moon then applies, and it applies *because* Life and Limb applied. Both are type-changing effects in the same layer, so order is set by the dependency system, which overrides timestamps: an effect depends on another if applying the other would change what the first effect applies to [613.8a]. Applying Life and Limb turns the token into a land — and a token has no basic supertype, so it is a nonbasic land — which brings it within Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Blood Moon therefore depends on Life and Limb and waits to apply until after it [613.8b]. (Timestamp order gives the same sequence here anyway, since Life and Limb entered first.)

3. Blood Moon sets the land's subtype to the basic land type Mountain. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type removes its old land types and the abilities from those land types, and grants the new basic land type's mana ability; it does not add or remove card types or supertypes [305.7]. So the token loses the land type Forest and the green mana ability and gains the land type Mountain and "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #3]. It stays a creature, and it keeps the creature type Saproling, because that is a creature type, not a land type [305.7], [Life and Limb ruling #4]. Its name is still "Saproling"; Blood Moon doesn't change names or supertypes [Blood Moon ruling #2].

4. No dependency loop arises here. Because the token is still a Saproling after Blood Moon applies, Life and Limb still applies to it, so it remains a 1/1 green creature (Blood Moon does nothing to power, toughness, or color). Note the caveat: if Alice also controlled a *nonbasic* Forest (say a dual land), Blood Moon would strip its Forest type and thus change what Life and Limb applies to, making the two effects mutually dependent; in that dependency loop, dependency is ignored and the effects apply in timestamp order — Life and Limb, then Blood Moon [613.8b] — which yields the same result for this token.

Player count doesn't matter: these are continuous effects that apply to objects on the battlefield regardless of who controls them, so the answer is identical in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 1/1 green Land Creature - Mountain Saproling with "{T}: Add {R}.". Applying Life and Limb's effect would allow Blood Moon's effect to apply to the Saproling and applying Blood Moon's effect first would not affect how Life and Limb's effect is applied or what it does, so Blood Moon's effect is dependent on Life and Limb's effect and waits to apply until afterwards. Since Life and Limb's effect makes the Saproling a nonbasic land, Blood Moon then applies and turns it into a Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}." and no other abilities.

entries.question: Anson controls [Mana Reflection] and [Deathrite Shaman]. They activate Deathrite Shaman's first ability, exiling a [Watery Grave] from Nola's graveyard. How much mana is produced?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — Deathrite Shaman's targeted ability is not a mana ability, so Mana Reflection doesn't double it and it produces only one mana.
entries.answer:
One mana of any color — Mana Reflection does not double it.

Why: Mana Reflection reads "If you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead." "Tapping a permanent for mana" specifically means activating a *mana ability* of that permanent that includes {T} in its activation cost [106.12, 106.12b, Mana Reflection ruling #4]. Deathrite Shaman's first ability, "{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color," requires a target, and an ability with a target is never a mana ability even though it could add mana [605.1a, 605.5a, Deathrite Shaman ruling #2]. So activating it is not "tapping Deathrite Shaman for mana," Mana Reflection's replacement effect never applies, and Anson gets exactly one mana of the color of their choice when the ability resolves.

A couple of practical points:
- Because it isn't a mana ability, the ability uses the stack and can be responded to [605.5a, Deathrite Shaman ruling #2]. If the targeted Watery Grave leaves Nola's graveyard in response so the target is illegal on resolution, the ability doesn't resolve at all and Anson adds no mana whatsoever [Deathrite Shaman ruling #1].
- Watery Grave's own "{T}: Add {U} or {B}" is irrelevant here — it's sitting in a graveyard being exiled, not being tapped, and Anson's mana comes from Deathrite Shaman's ability, which lets Anson choose any one color, not just {U} or {B}.

The number of players at the table doesn't change any of this; nothing in the interaction depends on how many opponents Anson has (Deathrite Shaman's targeting is "target land card from a graveyard," any graveyard, and Nola's graveyard qualifies whether the game is two-player or multiplayer).

entries.question: Alfredo controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Knight Errant]s with magnet counters on them. Nico controls one [Soaring Drake] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nico's legal blocks?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Nico's Soaring Drake must block one of the attacking Knight Errants (it can choose which) and cannot legally refrain from blocking or block both.
entries.answer:
Nico must block with Soaring Drake, and he may choose which of the two Knight Errants it blocks. Blocking one Knight Errant (either one) is his only legal declaration; declaring no blocks is illegal, and Soaring Drake can't block both Knight Errants at once.

Why: Magnetic Web's second ability reads "Whenever a creature with a magnet counter on it attacks, all creatures with magnet counters on them block that creature this turn if able." Both Knight Errants attacked with magnet counters, so that ability triggered twice, creating two separate blocking requirements on Soaring Drake (which also has a magnet counter): block Knight Errant #1 if able, and block Knight Errant #2 if able.

When blockers are declared, the defending player first checks restrictions — effects saying a creature can't block or can't block unless a condition is met [509.1b]. Neither Knight Errant has an evasion ability, and Soaring Drake having flying doesn't stop it from blocking a nonflying attacker, so there are no restrictions in play here.

Next, the defending player must obey as many requirements as possible without breaking any restriction; if the number of requirements obeyed is fewer than the maximum possible, the declaration is illegal [509.1c]. Soaring Drake is a single creature with no ability letting it block more than one attacker, so the maximum number of these two requirements it can satisfy is one. Blocking either Knight Errant satisfies that maximum and is legal; blocking neither satisfies zero requirements when one was possible, so it's illegal.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the magnet counters were already on both Knight Errants and on Soaring Drake when attackers were declared, so both triggers happened and Soaring Drake was a legal blocker. If Soaring Drake only got its magnet counter after attackers were declared, the triggers would have checked "all creatures with magnet counters" on resolution — but as printed, the effect applies to Soaring Drake so long as it has a magnet counter when blockers are declared; if it had no counter at that time, Nico would be free to block or not.

Multiplayer note: rules 509.1b and 509.1c are written in terms of "the defending player" checking "each creature they control." With only Nico defending, only his Soaring Drake matters. At a table with more than two players, each defending player evaluates only the creatures they control, so a magnet-counter creature controlled by a player who isn't being attacked simply isn't part of that declaration; the provided rules don't add any other multiplayer-specific wrinkle here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nico can block either Knight Errant with their Magnetic Web. When declaring blockers, Nico must fulfill the maximum number of requirements, while not violating any restrictions.

entries.question: At the beginning of the game, Alianna announced [Zirda, the Dawnwaker] as their companion. During the game, Alianna cast [Glistening Goremonger] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alianna restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Alianna may reveal Zirda as companion after the restart because Glistening Goremonger supposedly meets Zirda's requirement, which contradicts the reference's ruling that Glistening Goremonger violates Zirda and thus cannot be a companion.
entries.answer:
Short answer: the game restarts, and Alianna's Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger card — which came in from outside the game via Wish — is shuffled into Alianna's library for the new game. During the new game's pregame procedure Alianna may reveal Zirda, the Dawnwaker as their companion again, and the condition is still met, because Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger is a permanent card that has an activated ability ({3}{B/P}: Transform this creature).

Details:

1. Restarting. Karn Liberated's −14 immediately ends the current game with no winner, loser, or drawer, and the same players begin a new game using the normal starting procedure of rule 103, with the exception in rule 727.2 [727.1] [727.2] [Karn Liberated]. Non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated stay in exile and enter the battlefield under Alianna's control after the pregame procedure finishes [Karn Liberated].

2. The Wished card. Rule 727.2 says every Magic card involved in the ended game is involved in the new game, even if it wasn't originally part of it — its example is exactly a creature card brought in from outside the game with a Wish-style effect, which becomes part of that player's library in the new game [727.2] [Wish]. So Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger is now one of Alianna's deck cards; it can't be shuffled back into the sideboard, since players can't move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated]. (Pedantic note: Glistening Goremonger is the back face; what Alianna actually cast with Wish was the front face, Pyretic Prankster.)

3. Companion in the new game. Companion is a keyword that functions from outside the game: before the game begins you may reveal one card you own from outside the game whose companion condition is satisfied by your starting deck, and once during the game you may pay {3} as a special action to put it into your hand [702.139a] [103.2b]. Because a restart runs the full starting procedure, the companion-reveal step happens again [727.1] [103.2b], and the "once during the game" {3} special action is fresh for the new game [702.139a].

4. Is Zirda, the Dawnwaker still legal? Zirda, the Dawnwaker requires that each permanent card in your starting deck have an activated ability [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger is a creature (permanent) card, and it has the activated ability "{3}{B/P}: Transform this creature. Activate only as a sorcery." — activated abilities are the ones written "[Cost]: [Effect]" [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. So adding it to the deck does not break the condition, and Alianna may reveal Zirda, the Dawnwaker again. Zirda, the Dawnwaker itself was never brought into the game (it stayed outside the game as a revealed companion), so it is available to be revealed once more.

5. Timing assumption. I'm assuming Alianna never paid the {3} to put Zirda, the Dawnwaker into their hand before the restart. If Alianna had already paid {3} and Zirda, the Dawnwaker was in hand (or graveyard, battlefield, etc.) when the game restarted, then Zirda, the Dawnwaker would be a card "involved in the game" and would be shuffled into Alianna's library for the new game [727.2], and a card sitting in your starting deck can't function as your companion — the companion ability has no effect from inside the deck [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. Alianna would then have no companion in the new game.

6. Two players vs. multiplayer. With more than two players, the controller of the restarting ability (Alianna) is the starting player in the new game, any player who had already left the game before the restart is not in the new game [Karn Liberated], and companions are revealed starting with the starting player and proceeding in turn order — once a player declines, they can't change their mind [103.2b] [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. In a two-player game that just means Alianna declares first. Nothing else about this interaction differs by player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Glistening Goremonger will be shuffled into Alianna's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Glistening Goremonger violates Zirda, the Dawnwaker's companion restriction, Alianna can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.

entries.question: Amos controls [March of the Machines] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and casts [Lust for War] targeting their [Gilded Sentinel]. What will happen when Lust for War resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate claims Lust for War enters attached and then becomes an artifact creature and falls off, while the reference says it cannot legally enchant and is put directly into its owner's graveyard, so the conclusions differ.
entries.answer:
Lust for War will resolve and enter the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel, but it will immediately fall off and go to Amos's graveyard — it never gets to do anything.

Step by step:

1. While Lust for War is still a spell on the stack, Mycosynth Lattice doesn't affect it. Mycosynth Lattice only makes permanents artifacts, and spells on the stack aren't permanents (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2).
2. Gilded Sentinel is a legal object for Lust for War's "Enchant creature" ability, so Lust for War resolves and enters the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel ([303.4d]).
3. The instant Lust for War is on the battlefield, Mycosynth Lattice makes it an artifact in addition to being an enchantment — Aura. March of the Machines then sees a noncreature artifact and turns it into an artifact creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value. Lust for War's mana value is 3 ({2}{R}), so it becomes a 3/3 artifact creature that is still an enchantment — Aura (March of the Machines ruling #2).
4. An Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything. The next time state-based actions are checked, Lust for War becomes unattached from Gilded Sentinel, and then as a second state-based action it's put into its owner's graveyard ([303.4d], Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4).

So Gilded Sentinel is never actually enchanted for any meaningful length of time: neither the "deals 3 damage when tapped" trigger nor the "attacks each combat if able" requirement will ever apply. Note that Lust for War dies because it's an Aura that's a creature, not because of a toughness problem — as a 3/3 it isn't destroyed for lethal damage or 0 toughness.

One timing note: this assumes Gilded Sentinel is still a legal target when Lust for War resolves. If Gilded Sentinel had left the battlefield or otherwise become an illegal target first, Lust for War would simply fail to resolve and be put into the graveyard as a countered spell instead — the same end zone, just for a different reason.

Player count doesn't matter here. Nothing in this interaction involves choosing an opponent or a defending player, so the result is identical in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Lust for War cannot legally enchant anything, so it will be put directly into its owners graveyard.
entries.human_note: our rulings say basically the same thing, but 303.4i is the operative rule here in that it would be put directly into its graveyard. but the way I'm reading it is that it doesn't become unable to attach until it is actually on the battlefield because those effects from the other 2 cards don't apply until its on the battlefield anyway, so it can't be invalid until it hits the battlefield, otherwise its valid in any other zone. this is such a corner case.

entries.question: Avery controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Wayward Angel is a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities because its threshold P/T effect began applying before Turn to Frog removed the static ability, so the +3/+3 still applies.
entries.answer:
Wayward Angel becomes a 4/4 blue Frog creature with no abilities.

Breakdown by layer (rule 613.1e–613.1g). Wayward Angel's Threshold ability is a static ability, so its continuous effect has Wayward Angel's own timestamp (rules 613.7a, 613.7d), which is earlier than the effect from Turn to Frog, which gets its timestamp when it resolves (rule 613.7b). Earlier timestamps apply first within a layer (rule 613.7).

- Color (layer 5, rule 613.1e): Threshold makes Wayward Angel black first (and only black — see the Wayward Angel ruling that it is black, not white and black); then Turn to Frog's later effect makes it blue. Final color: blue only ([Turn to Frog ruling #2]: it loses all other colors and creature types).
- Types: Turn to Frog makes it a Frog, so Angel and Horror are gone. It keeps any other card types or supertypes it had ([Turn to Frog ruling #2]) — Wayward Angel has none beyond "creature."
- Abilities (layer 6, rule 613.1f): The Threshold effect first grants trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature"; then Turn to Frog's later ability-removal strips everything — flying, vigilance, trample, the upkeep sacrifice trigger, and the Threshold static ability itself. Wayward Angel has no abilities.
- Power/toughness (layer 7, rule 613.1g): Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b ([Turn to Frog ruling #1]). The Threshold effect's +3/+3 part still applies in layer 7c: under rule 613.6, once an effect starts applying, its other parts keep applying in their own layers even though the ability that generated it was removed in layer 6. That matches [Turn to Frog ruling #3], that power/toughness-modifying effects apply no matter when they started. So 1/1 base +3/+3 = 4/4.

Caveat on timing/graveyard size: this assumes Avery still has seven or more cards in the graveyard at the time Turn to Frog resolves, so the Threshold effect is already applying. If the graveyard had fewer than seven cards when Turn to Frog resolved, no Threshold effect would ever start applying (and the ability is then removed), leaving a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities.

Nothing here depends on the number of players — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities. Wayward Angel's last ability begins to apply in layer 5. It's removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply, it will continue doing so in later layers. Wayward Angel has the earlier timestamp, so it gives itself trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" before Turn to Frog removes its abilities in layer 6.

entries.question: Aubrey casts [Shahrazad]. As the subgame begins, Aubrey wins the die roll. Can Aubrey choose to play second?
entries.reason: Both conclude Aubrey cannot choose to play second because rule 729.2 randomly determines the subgame's starting player.
entries.answer:
No \u2014 under rule 729.2 there's no choice to make. When the Shahrazad subgame starts, the game "randomly determine[s] which player goes first," so whoever the random determination (the die roll) picks is simply the starting player. If that random determination picked Aubrey, Aubrey goes first and cannot elect to play second. [729.2]

Why it works that way: rule 729.2 replaces the normal "winner of the die roll chooses" step of starting a game. The subgame otherwise follows rule 103, "Starting the Game" \u

One wrinkle worth flagging: an older ruling on Shahrazad states, "You randomly chose which player chooses to go first or draw first," which would let Aubrey pick. Rule 729.2 as given says the random determination sets the starting player itself, with no intervening choice, so the rule text is the safer answer at a rules-enforced table; if your group is going by the card ruling instead, Aubrey could choose to play second. [729.2] [Shahrazad ruling #3]

Other setup points for the subgame: each player moves all cards from their main-game library into a brand-new subgame library and shuffles, and no other main-game cards come along (except as specified by 729.2a\u2013c). Each player then draws an opening hand (usually seven); a player with too few cards to draw that hand loses the subgame. [729.2] [Shahrazad ruling #1]

Player count: the provided rules only say "randomly determine which player goes first," without specifying turn order among three or more players, so for a multiplayer table the context doesn't tell us how the rest of the seating order is set \u2014 only that the first player is determined randomly. Shahrazad itself then makes each player who doesn't win the subgame lose half their life, rounded up, which in multiplayer means every non-winner. [729.2] [Shahrazad]

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The starting player in a subgame is determined randomly.

entries.question: Ainsley's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Ainsley chooses the order in which cards are put into their graveyard when Morality Shift resolves.
entries.answer:
Ainsley chooses the order. When Morality Shift resolves and Ainsley's library becomes their graveyard, Ainsley (as the owner of those cards) arranges them in whatever order they like as they go in.

Why: a graveyard is an ordered zone, and when an effect puts two or more cards into the same graveyard at the same time, the owner of those cards may arrange them in any order [404.3]. Morality Shift's own ruling confirms this directly: "You can choose the order of the cards being placed into the graveyard" [Morality Shift ruling #1]. So there's no requirement to preserve the old library order — Ainsley can stack the new graveyard top-to-bottom however it benefits them.

Two other points: the cards that were in Ainsley's graveyard become their library, and Morality Shift then instructs them to shuffle that library, so the old graveyard's order is randomized and irrelevant. And Morality Shift works even if Ainsley's graveyard or library was empty [Morality Shift ruling #2] — if the library was empty, there are simply no cards to order.

This exchange only touches Ainsley's own graveyard and library, so the answer is the same whether the game has two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: In the order of Ainsley's choice.

entries.question: Autumn, Bethany, and Chaim started playing a multiplayer game. Chaim lost the game, and then Autumn restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Autumn draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that the restarted game is a two-player game (Chaim left) and Autumn, as the starting player, skips the first-turn draw step.
entries.answer:
No — Autumn will not draw a card during the draw step of the first turn of the restarted game (beyond the opening hand of seven).

Why: Karn Liberated's −14 ability restarts the game. A restarted game immediately ends the old game and all players in it begin a new game following the normal starting-the-game procedures [727.1]. The Karn Liberated ruling states that any player who left the game before it was restarted won't be involved in the new game, and that the player who controlled the restarting ability is the starting player in the new game. Since Chaim had already lost (left) the game, only Autumn and Bethany are in the new game, and Autumn plays first.

A "two-player game" is defined as a game that begins with only two players [100.1a], and a multiplayer game is one that begins with more than two players [800.1]. The restarted game begins with just Autumn and Bethany, so it is a two-player game, not a multiplayer game — even though the original game was multiplayer. In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn [103.8a]. Autumn is that player, so Autumn skips the draw step and draws no card on turn one.

Contrast: had Chaim still been in the game at the moment of the restart, the new game would begin with three players and would be a multiplayer game [800.1], so rule 103.8a's skip wouldn't apply and Autumn would draw normally on the first turn.

Autumn does still shuffle, draw an opening hand of seven, and may mulligan as normal per the Karn Liberated ruling, and Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving (putting the exiled non-Aura permanent cards onto the battlefield) after the pregame procedure but before the first turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The game began with 2 players, so it is a two-player game.. Autumn will skip their draw step.

entries.question: Addison casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Natalee's [Memnite]. In response, Natalee casts [Resounding Roar] on the Memnite. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude Resounding Roar's pump ends in the cleanup step leaving the -1/-1 counter to make Memnite 0/0 so it dies that turn and Virulent Wound's delayed trigger gives Natalee a poison counter.
entries.answer:
Memnite dies during the cleanup step of that turn, and Natalee gets a poison counter from Virulent Wound's delayed triggered ability.

How it plays out:

1. Resounding Roar was cast in response, so it resolves first: Memnite (a 1/1) gets +3/+3 until end of turn, making it 4/4.
2. Virulent Wound then resolves, putting a -1/-1 counter on Memnite (now 3/3) and creating a delayed triggered ability: "When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter" [610.2, 603.7b].
3. Memnite survives the rest of the turn as a 3/3.
4. In the cleanup step, all "until end of turn" effects end simultaneously with damage removal [514.2]. Resounding Roar's +3/+3 wears off, but the -1/-1 counter is a counter, not a duration effect, so it stays. Memnite is now 1/1 with a -1/-1 counter, i.e. 0/0.
5. Normally no player gets priority in the cleanup step, but because a state-based action is now waiting, the game checks state-based actions [514.3a]: a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard [704.5f]. Memnite dies.
6. That death happens during the cleanup step, which is still the same turn Virulent Wound resolved, so the delayed trigger triggers and is put on the stack, and players receive priority [514.3a, 603.7b]. It resolves and Natalee gets a poison counter. Since players got priority, another cleanup step then begins after the stack empties and all players pass [514.3a].

This matches the Virulent Wound ruling: the controller misses the poison counter only if the creature isn't put into a graveyard on the turn Virulent Wound resolved — here it is, just barely, in that turn's cleanup step [Virulent Wound ruling #1].

Timing note: I'm assuming Resounding Roar was cast (for {1}{G}, +3/+3), not cycled. If it had been cycled instead, the trigger would give +6/+6 until end of turn — the result at end of turn is the same, since that bonus also ends in cleanup and Memnite still becomes 0/0 [Resounding Roar]. Also, if Virulent Wound had somehow resolved first and Resounding Roar second, nothing changes: the counter and the pump don't interact, and the same cleanup-step death occurs.

Only Addison and Natalee are named here, and the rules provided don't include any multiplayer-specific rules; nothing about this interaction depends on the number of players, since it's just Natalee's own creature dying and Natalee getting the poison counter.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Resounding Roar wears off, but the -1/-1 counter remains. Memnite dies.
