The delayed triggered ability created by Virulent Wound is not a continuous effect, so it still exists during the cleanup step, and will trigger due to Memnite dying. Natalee gets a poison counter.

entries.question: Amaris, Blaine, and Clyde begin a multiplayer game. In Amaris's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Blaine. Does Amaris draw a card for the turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Amaris draws during their draw step because the game began with more than two players (so the first-turn draw skip doesn’t apply), and killing Blaine doesn’t end the game.
entries.answer:
Yes — Amaris draws a card. In a multiplayer game (a game that begins with more than two players, which this three-player game is), the starting player does not skip the draw step of their first turn; that skip only applies in two-player games and to the team that plays first in Two-Headed Giant [100.1b, 800.1, 800.7, 103.8c]. So after Amaris's upkeep, Amaris's draw step happens normally and Amaris draws a card.

Details and assumptions:

- I'm assuming this is Amaris's first turn of the game (they started with Leyline of Anticipation on the battlefield from their opening hand, which is the hand after all mulligans; such "begin the game with it on the battlefield" actions are taken before the first turn begins) [Leyline of Anticipation ruling #1]. If it's any later turn, Amaris obviously draws too — the first-turn draw skip is the only relevant exception, and it doesn't apply here anyway.

- Killing Blaine during Amaris's upkeep with Goblin Charbelcher (fueled by Simian Spirit Guide and Desperate Ritual mana) doesn't end the game, because Clyde is still in it. The turn simply proceeds from the upkeep step to Amaris's draw step, and Amaris draws.

- Contrast with a two-player game: if Amaris and Blaine were the only players and Amaris went first, Amaris would skip the draw step of that first turn, so no card would be drawn — and killing the only opponent would end the game before a draw step mattered [103.8c, 800.7].

- Two-Headed Giant is the one multiplayer exception where the first team does skip its first draw step [800.7]; that format isn't what's described here with three individual players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The game began with more than 2 players, so it is a multiplayer game, regardless of the current number of players remaining.. Amaris will draw a card during their draw step.

entries.question: Allyson controls [Ice Cauldron]. Nico controls [Suppression Field]. Allyson activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Allyson's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly counts the {2} from Suppression Field as mana noted by Ice Cauldron's first ability — the only activation cost of that ability is "{X}, {T}" so only the mana spent to pay X is noted; the extra {2} is not.
entries.answer:
Allyson adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana.

Why: Ice Cauldron's first ability reads "{X}, {T}: ... note the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost." Suppression Field says "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities," and Ice Cauldron's first ability is an activated ability that produces no mana, so the {2} increase applies. Ice Cauldron's activation cost is its analog to a spell's mana cost, and the total cost is that cost plus all cost increases, locked in once determined ([602.1a], [602.2b], [601.2f]). With X=1 that total is {1} + {2} = {3} generic (plus tapping Ice Cauldron), which Allyson paid with {C}{C}{C}.

Ice Cauldron notes the actual mana spent, not the value of X — the ruling that it "counts only mana spent on it. It doesn't see the value of X, so isn't affected by cost reductions" cuts the same way for cost increases. So it noted {C}{C}{C}, and the second ability adds exactly that: {C}{C}{C}. Note that {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic; it can pay generic costs but nothing that demands a color.

Two other points:
- Ice Cauldron's second ability is a mana ability (per its ruling, "Tapping the Cauldron for the mana is a mana ability"), so Suppression Field does not add {2} to activating it. Its cost stays {T} plus removing a charge counter.
- That {C}{C}{C} can only be spent to cast the last card exiled with Ice Cauldron, though Allyson may add other mana from elsewhere to finish paying that spell's cost, including additional costs.

This is the same whether the game has two players or more — Suppression Field affects every player's non-mana activated abilities, including its controller Nico's, so the number of opponents doesn't change the result.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Just {C}. The activation cost of Ice Cauldron's first ability is "{X}, {T}". The additional cost imposed by Suppression Field is not part of the activation cost, and the mana spent on it isn't noted when the ability resolves.
entries.human_note:
Per the Ice Cauldron ruling: The Cauldron counts only mana spent on it. It doesn't see the value of X, so isn't affected by cost reductions. Thus, if you spent {C}{C}{R}{R} on X, you get {C}{C}{R}{R} later even if X was 6. 

This points to an issue we might be seeing in other rulings where we need to make sure that the card is referred to by its full name. would that have effected the answer here?

entries.question: Anya activates [Deceptive Landscape]. Before that resolves Nico casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Anya is resolving Deceptive Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aven Mindcensor merely limits the search to the top four but still counts as "searching your library," so Panglacial Wurm found among those top four can be cast.
entries.answer:
Yes. Anya can cast Panglacial Wurm from their library, as long as they do it before finding (choosing) a card with Deceptive Landscape's search.

Why:

- Aven Mindcensor doesn't stop the search from being a search. It replaces the event of Anya searching their library with searching only the top four cards of that library [614.6]. Both the rules and Aven Mindcensor's own rulings confirm that searching the top four cards still counts as searching that library, and any other instructions tied to the search still apply [701.23f][Aven Mindcensor ruling #1]. Since Aven Mindcensor was on the battlefield before Deceptive Landscape's ability began resolving, the replacement applies to this search.
- Panglacial Wurm says "While you're searching your library, you may cast this card from your library." Deceptive Landscape's ability uses the words "search your library," and Anya is looking through their own library, which is exactly the situation Panglacial Wurm's ability requires [Panglacial Wurm ruling #7]. Panglacial Wurm is among the top four cards Anya can see, so there's no issue of it being hidden.
- Anya must cast Panglacial Wurm before finding any card with the search effect [Panglacial Wurm ruling #2]. Casting follows all normal rules except timing and zone: Panglacial Wurm goes on the stack and Anya pays {5}{G}{G} (plus any additional costs), and may activate mana abilities while casting it [Panglacial Wurm ruling #1]. Note that Deceptive Landscape itself was already sacrificed as part of its own activation cost, so its "{T}: Add {C}" is not available to help pay.
- While searching, Anya must keep the library in its current order until the shuffle [Panglacial Wurm ruling #3]. After casting, Anya resumes the search where they left off, finds a basic Plains, Swamp, or Forest among the top four (if there is one) and puts it onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffles the entire library, not just the top four [Aven Mindcensor ruling #2][701.23f]. When Deceptive Landscape's ability finishes resolving, the active player gets priority with Panglacial Wurm on the stack [Panglacial Wurm ruling #4]. Panglacial Wurm can't be one of the cards found by the search anyway [Panglacial Wurm ruling #5], and it wouldn't qualify as a basic land regardless.

One caveat the provided material doesn't settle: whether Panglacial Wurm could be cast if it were below the top four. Aven Mindcensor's rulings say cards outside the top four can't be *found* and can't be looked at [Aven Mindcensor ruling #3], but they don't address casting from the library specifically. Here it's moot, since the question states Panglacial Wurm is in the top four.

Player count doesn't change anything: Aven Mindcensor applies to each of Nico's opponents, so with more than two players any opponent searching would be limited to their top four the same way, and each such player could still cast their own Panglacial Wurm during their own search.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Aven Mindcensor's ability is a replacement effect that replaces searching a library with searching only the top four cards of that library. However for the purposes of Panglacial Wurm's effect, it still qualifies as "searching a library".

entries.question: Aimee controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Noah casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Aimee turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly says Wayward Angel keeps flying and vigilance (and its printed abilities), whereas the correct ruling is that Turn to Frog removes those, leaving only the threshold-granted trample and the upkeep-sacrifice trigger.
entries.answer:
**Wayward Angel ends up as a face-up, black 4/4 Creature — Frog named Wayward Angel with flying, vigilance, trample, and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature," plus its Threshold ability.**

Why each characteristic comes out that way:

**Timestamps are the key.** Turn to Frog's continuous effect got its timestamp when Turn to Frog resolved [613.7b]. When Aimee then turns Wayward Angel face up, the permanent receives a *new* timestamp at that moment [613.7f]. Since effects within a layer are applied in timestamp order [613.3, 613.7], everything generated by Wayward Angel's own printed abilities is applied *after* Turn to Frog's effects.

- **Abilities (layer 6):** Turn to Frog's "loses all abilities" is applied in layer 6 [613.1f], but Wayward Angel's printed abilities now carry the later face-up timestamp, so they are applied after the removal and Wayward Angel has flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability again [613.3, 613.7, 613.7f]. Compare Turn to Frog ruling: abilities that start applying after Turn to Frog are kept [Turn to Frog ruling #4].
- **Threshold is active:** Aimee has seven cards in their graveyard, so Threshold grants +3/+3, black, trample, and the upkeep sacrifice trigger.
- **Color (layer 5):** Turn to Frog makes it blue [613.1e]; Threshold's "is black" is applied later in the same layer, so Wayward Angel is black only — not blue, and not white-and-black [Wayward Angel ruling #1].
- **Creature type (layer 4):** Turn to Frog sets the creature type to Frog and removes other creature types; nothing later changes that, so it's a Frog, not an Angel Horror. It keeps other card types and supertypes it may have [Turn to Frog ruling #2].
- **Power/toughness:** Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b [Turn to Frog ruling #1], and Threshold's +3/+3 is a modification applied in layer 7c, which applies regardless of when it started [Turn to Frog ruling #3, 613.6]. 1/1 + 3/+3 = **4/4**.
- Because it's face up, it's no longer a 2/2 colorless nameless manifest — it's Wayward Angel with mana cost {4}{W}{W} (mana value 6), even though its current color is black.

**Timing assumption:** I'm reading the sequence exactly as stated — Turn to Frog fully resolved first, then Wayward Angel was turned face up. If instead Wayward Angel had been turned face up *before* Turn to Frog resolved, Turn to Frog would hold the later timestamp: it would strip flying, vigilance, and Threshold entirely, leaving a blue 1/1 Frog with no abilities (still named Wayward Angel).

**Player count:** none of this depends on the number of players — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 black Frog with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature", but no other abilities. Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".
entries.human_note: both answers are saying the same thing.

entries.question: Bobbie has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Angel of Sanctions] that exiled Conrad's [Rotted Hystrix]. Alana casts [Lava Axe], targeting Bobbie. What happens as Bobbie loses the game?
entries.reason: Both answers state that Bobbie's phased-out Angel leaves the game when Bobbie does but that leaving doesn't trigger zone-change abilities (702.26k), so Rotted Hystrix remains in exile.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Bobbie's phased-out Angel of Sanctions token leaves the game along with Bobbie, and per rule 702.26k that departure does not cause zone-change abilities to trigger — so Conrad's Rotted Hystrix stays in exile and does not come back to the battlefield.

Assumed timing: Lava Axe resolves and deals 5 damage to Bobbie, dropping Bobbie from 1 life to -4, and Bobbie loses the game the next time state-based actions are checked. Nothing about the outcome below changes if Bobbie instead lost the game some other way at that moment.

Step by step:

1. "Phased out" means the permanent is still on the battlefield but, except for rules and effects that specifically mention phased-out permanents, it's treated as though it doesn't exist and can't affect or be affected by anything else in the game (702.26b). So Angel of Sanctions being phased out doesn't stop it from being owned by Bobbie.

2. When Bobbie leaves the game, all objects owned by Bobbie leave the game, any effects giving Bobbie control of objects or players end, and any objects still controlled by Bobbie that Bobbie doesn't own are exiled — all immediately, not as a state-based action (800.4a). Rule 702.26k adds the piece that matters here: phased-out permanents owned by a departing player also leave the game, and this doesn't cause zone-change abilities to trigger. Angel of Sanctions is a token owned by Bobbie, so it leaves the game.

3. The only thing that would give Rotted Hystrix back to Conrad is Angel of Sanctions' own text, "exile target nonland permanent an opponent controls until Angel of Sanctions leaves the battlefield." Because 702.26k expressly shuts off zone-change abilities when a phased-out permanent leaves the game this way, that return doesn't happen. Rotted Hystrix simply remains in the exile zone.

4. Rotted Hystrix itself is untouched by 800.4a: it's owned by Conrad, it's in exile rather than on the battlefield, and Bobbie doesn't control it, so it is neither "an object owned by Bobbie" that leaves the game nor "an object controlled by Bobbie" that gets exiled.

Multiplayer vs. two players: this scenario only arises at a multiplayer table (Alana, Bobbie, and Conrad), since 800.4a is the rule that lets a game continue after a player leaves. In a two-player game, Bobbie losing would end the game outright and the fate of the exiled card would be moot.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: All objects owned by Bobbie leave the game. However the game treats phased-out permanents as nonexistent, and does not see the leaves-the-battlefield event happen. Rotted Hystrix will not return to the battlefield.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Natalia controls [Watchwolf] enchanted with [Favorable Destiny]. Aubrey casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Favorable Destiny. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Favorable Destiny is put into its owner's graveyard after Aubrey gains control, while the reference concludes it remains attached to Watchwolf, so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Favorable Destiny is put into Natalia's graveyard as a state-based action, and Aubrey never gets any use out of it.

Here's the chain:

1. **Mycosynth Lattice** says "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types," so Favorable Destiny is an artifact Enchantment — Aura while it's on the battlefield. That makes it a legal choice for Opportunistic Dragon's trigger, which chooses "target Human or artifact an opponent controls."

2. When Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves, Aubrey gains control of Favorable Destiny, **it loses all abilities**, and it can't attack or block. Losing all abilities includes losing its enchant keyword ability ("Enchant creature"), which is a static ability that defines what that Aura is allowed to be attached to [702.5a].

3. Favorable Destiny doesn't move — it stays physically attached to Watchwolf — but with no enchant ability there is nothing it can legally be attached to. An Aura attached to an illegal object is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [303.4c] [704.5m]. This is the same principle as the Mycosynth Lattice ruling about Auras that become creatures via March of the Machines: an Aura that can't enchant anything becomes unattached and is then put into its owner's graveyard by state-based actions [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4].

4. State-based actions are checked the next time a player would receive priority after Opportunistic Dragon's ability finishes resolving, so Favorable Destiny hits the graveyard immediately, before anyone can respond. It goes to its **owner's** graveyard (Natalia's, assuming she owns the card), not to Aubrey's, even though Aubrey controlled it for that instant.

Side note: Favorable Destiny's bonus was already dead weight — Mycosynth Lattice's second ability makes everything colorless, so Watchwolf isn't white and wouldn't have gotten +1/+2 anyway. But the abilities are gone regardless.

Assumed timing: Opportunistic Dragon is still on the battlefield when its trigger resolves. If Opportunistic Dragon had left the battlefield before the trigger resolved, Aubrey would gain nothing — Natalia would keep Favorable Destiny, it wouldn't lose its abilities, and it would stay attached to Watchwolf.

Player count doesn't change any of this: Opportunistic Dragon only requires that the chosen permanent be controlled by an opponent, so the result is the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer one (Aubrey just gets to pick which opponent's artifact to take).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Favorable Destiny will continue to be attached to Watchwolf indefinitely. The "enchant" keyword is a restriction on what an Aura can enchant- without it Favorable Destiny is legally able to enchant anything.
entries.human_note: Enchant restricts what the aura can enchant. without the restriction, it can enchant anything. our answer applied it as allowing it to enchant something rather than restricting it to only things listed in its enchant (whatever) ability. major corner case. never would happen in game. not super important to me to get right.

entries.question: Alaia controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Minotaur Warrior] and [Ogre Resister] in their graveyard. They cast [Dance of the Dead] targeting Minotaur Warrior. What happens as it enters the battlefield?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the ability triggers twice and only returns Minotaur Warrior (the second trigger has no additional effect), matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
Dance of the Dead's enters-the-battlefield ability triggers twice, but you only get Minotaur Warrior back — the second trigger does essentially nothing, and Ogre Resister stays in the graveyard.

Step by step:

1. **Dance of the Dead is an artifact as it enters.** Mycosynth Lattice's "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types" is a continuous effect from a static ability, and such effects apply simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield — before the game determines what abilities trigger on that entry [611.3c]. Mycosynth Lattice explicitly makes Auras artifacts [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2] [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4]. So an *artifact* (Dance of the Dead itself) is entering.

2. **Panharmonicon doubles the trigger.** Panharmonicon reads "If an artifact or creature entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time," and it applies to a permanent's own enters-the-battlefield trigger [Panharmonicon ruling #5]. Dance of the Dead's ability begins "When this Aura enters," so the game determines it triggers twice rather than once [603.2d]. This is not a copy — each instance is a separate trigger, and choices are made separately for each [Panharmonicon ruling #9].

3. **Intervening "if" check.** Dance of the Dead reads "When this Aura enters, if it's on the battlefield..." That's an intervening "if" clause: it's checked on trigger and again on resolution [603.4]. Dance of the Dead is on the battlefield both times here, so both instances trigger and both resolve. Alaia puts both on the stack in any order (they're identical).

4. **First instance resolves.** Dance of the Dead loses "enchant creature card in a graveyard" and gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," puts Minotaur Warrior onto the battlefield tapped under Alaia's control, and attaches itself to Minotaur Warrior. Minotaur Warrior is now a 3/4 (2/3 plus the Aura's +1/+1) that doesn't untap during Alaia's untap step.

5. **Second instance resolves and fizzles in practice.** Dance of the Dead is still on the battlefield, so the intervening "if" is satisfied [603.4]. Losing and gaining the enchant abilities is redundant. "Put enchanted creature card onto the battlefield" does nothing: the enchanted object is Minotaur Warrior, which is already a permanent on the battlefield, not a creature card in a graveyard, and an effect does only as much as possible [609.3]. "Attach this Aura to it" also does nothing, because attaching an Aura to the object it's already attached to has no effect [701.3b].

**Ogre Resister is not affected.** The second trigger doesn't let Alaia choose a different graveyard card — Dance of the Dead's target was locked in when it was cast, and once the creature is returned Dance of the Dead can't be attached to anything else [Dance of the Dead ruling #4].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Panharmonicon and Mycosynth Lattice were both already on the battlefield when Dance of the Dead entered. If Mycosynth Lattice weren't on the battlefield at that moment, Dance of the Dead would be a non-artifact Aura entering, nothing artifact-or-creature would be entering, Panharmonicon wouldn't apply, and the ability would simply trigger once with the same net result. (If Mycosynth Lattice or Panharmonicon entered simultaneously with Dance of the Dead, Panharmonicon still applies to things entering at the same time as it [Panharmonicon ruling #2].)

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Dance of the Dead enters the battlefield attached to Minotaur Warrior and triggers twice. The first trigger will return Minotaur Warrior to the battlefield. The second trigger just does the same things again, so it has no relevant result.

entries.question: Adelaide casts a [Keldon Champion]. In response, Nico casts [Hallow], targeting the Keldon Champion. When Adelaide attacks with the Keldon Champion that turn, will the damage be prevented?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Hallow cast while Keldon Champion was a spell prevents the damage the creature would deal after it becomes a permanent, including combat damage (and notes the resulting life gain).
entries.answer:
Yes — the combat damage Keldon Champion deals that turn is prevented, and Nico gains life equal to the damage prevented.

Why: Hallow targeted Keldon Champion while it was still a permanent spell on the stack. Normally an object that changes zones becomes a brand-new object with no memory of its previous existence, but there is an explicit exception: prevention effects that apply to damage from a permanent spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes [400.7c]. The same principle is stated for choosing sources of damage: if the chosen source is a permanent spell, the effect applies to any damage dealt by that spell and to any damage dealt by the permanent it becomes when it resolves [609.7a].

So Hallow's shield follows Keldon Champion onto the battlefield for the rest of the turn:
- Keldon Champion's enters-the-battlefield trigger ("deals 3 damage to target player or planeswalker") is prevented, and Nico gains 3 life from Hallow.
- Keldon Champion has haste, so it can attack that same turn; its 3 combat damage is also prevented, and Nico gains 3 more life. Hallow says "prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn," so it is not a one-shot shield — it lasts through the whole turn.

Note that Hallow prevents damage dealt by Keldon Champion, not damage dealt to it — blockers still damage Keldon Champion normally, and it can be destroyed by lethal damage.

One timing note: this works only because Hallow was cast while Keldon Champion was still a spell on the stack, as described. Hallow can only target a spell, so once Keldon Champion had resolved into a permanent, Hallow could no longer be cast targeting it at all.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle is which player or planeswalker Adelaide chooses as the target of the enters-the-battlefield trigger, and that damage is prevented regardless of who is chosen.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Effects that apply to damage from a spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes.

entries.question: Amelia attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Shivan Meteor]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion to the reference—saying Amelia cannot suspend Shivan Meteor during Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolution when the reference says they can—so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
No. Amelia cannot suspend Shivan Meteor during the resolution of Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability. Exiling a card with suspend is a special action, and a player may take that special action only when they have priority — no player receives priority in the middle of a spell or ability resolving [116.2f, 608.2g, Shivan Meteor ruling #3].

Why: "Suspend N—[cost]" is a static ability of a card in hand that lets you pay the suspend cost and exile the card with N time counters on it; that action doesn't use the stack and isn't casting the card [702.62a, Shivan Meteor ruling #3, Shivan Meteor ruling #12]. Wildfire Eternal's trigger says "you may cast an instant or sorcery spell from your hand without paying its mana cost" — an effect that specifically instructs a player to cast a spell during resolution. That permission covers casting only; it does not grant priority or permission to take special actions [608.2g].

What Amelia can do instead: as Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolves (during the declare blockers step, before combat damage), Amelia may cast Shivan Meteor itself from hand for free, paying neither {3}{R}{R} nor the {1}{R}{R} suspend cost, choosing a target creature for its 13 damage at that time [Wildfire Eternal ruling #1, Shivan Meteor ruling #11]. Note that "without paying its mana cost" also means Amelia couldn't substitute an alternative cost even if one existed [Shivan Meteor ruling #6]. If Amelia wants to suspend Shivan Meteor for {1}{R}{R} instead, she must do it at a time she holds priority — for example, before the trigger goes on the stack or after it finishes resolving, at any point she could begin casting Shivan Meteor from hand [116.2f, 702.62a, Shivan Meteor ruling #12]. Since Shivan Meteor is a sorcery, that means a main phase of her own turn with an empty stack, not during combat.

This answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents (Wildfire Eternal's afflict and "attacks and isn't blocked" ability only care about the one defending player it's attacking).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes. The suspend special action can be taken whenever Shivan Meteor could be cast from Amelia's hand. Normally that's only when Amelia has priority on their turn with an empty stack, but in this case the effect of Wildfire Eternal is letting that happen while the ability resolves.

(They still have to pay the suspend cost, and afterwards they can choose to cast a different spell from hand without paying its mana cost.)
entries.human_note: I legitimately think rulesguru has this one wrong if you apply the rules strictly enough. [116.2f] and [702.62a] state different things. one says you can perform the special action suspend only when you have priority, but the suspend definition says "if you could begin to cast this card by putting it on the stack, you may..." so this question comes down to "which rule takes precedence?" their reading gives it to the definition of suspend's wording, our definition gives it to the 116.2f's wording.  Is there guidance out there from WOTC on which of those to apply over the other, or is that just on the judge?

entries.question: Andrew attacks with [Raiyuu, Storm's Edge], then attacks with it again. Can they activate [Minas Tirith]'s last ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same core ruling: Raiyuu attacking in two separate combats still counts as one creature, so Minas Tirith's ability cannot be activated.
entries.answer:
No. Andrew has attacked with only one creature this turn — Raiyuu, Storm's Edge — so Minas Tirith's last ability can't be activated, no matter how many times Raiyuu, Storm's Edge attacked.

Why: Minas Tirith's ability reads "{1}{W}, {T}: Draw a card. Activate only if you attacked with two or more creatures this turn." That condition counts *creatures declared as attackers*, not the number of attack declarations. A player "has attacked" when they declared one or more creatures as attackers during a declare attackers step [508.6], and each declare attackers step is a turn-based action in which the active player chooses which untapped creatures they control will attack [508.1a]. Andrew declared Raiyuu, Storm's Edge as the sole attacker in the first combat phase, and then declared Raiyuu, Storm's Edge as the sole attacker again in the extra combat phase — that's the same single creature both times, so the set of creatures Andrew attacked with this turn has exactly one member. The look-back rule for effects that ask about creatures you attacked with this turn similarly counts the creatures themselves [608.2i].

Note that this is baked into the situation: Raiyuu, Storm's Edge only untaps and grants the additional combat phase "whenever a Samurai or Warrior you control attacks alone," and a creature attacks alone only if it's the only creature declared as an attacker in that declare attackers step [Raiyuu, Storm's Edge ruling #1]. So the very sequence described guarantees one attacker per combat.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as Raiyuu, Storm's Edge attacking alone in the first combat phase, untapping, and then attacking alone again in the additional combat phase its ability created. If instead Andrew added any other creature to a declared attack this turn (for example, a second attacker in the extra combat, which would mean Raiyuu, Storm's Edge didn't attack alone that time), then two or more creatures would have attacked and Minas Tirith's ability would be activatable, provided Minas Tirith is untapped and Andrew pays {1}{W} plus tapping it.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with more than two players. Minas Tirith's condition doesn't care which player or players were attacked, only how many creatures Andrew attacked with — so even if Raiyuu, Storm's Edge attacked a different opponent in each combat phase, it's still just one creature.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Raiyuu, Storm's Edge is only one creature, regardless of how many times it attacked.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Soul Seizer] (back face [Ghastly Haunting])which has been mutated with [Everquill Phoenix]. Everquill Phoenix is the top component. Naomi controls [Axegrinder Giant]. Ariel then attacks Naomi with the merged permanent. Naomi declared no blockers and the merged permanent deals damage to Naomi. What happens when the transformation trigger resolves if Ariel elects to transform the merged permanent and targets Axegrinder Giant?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: the Soul Seizer component flips, the merged permanent remains a creature (Everquill Phoenix on top) and cannot attach as an Aura to Axegrinder Giant, so it stays unattached on the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Ariel's merged permanent does transform (the Soul Seizer component flips to its Ghastly Haunting face), but the attach fails: the merged permanent stays on the battlefield as a creature, unattached, and Axegrinder Giant is unaffected — Ariel does not gain control of Axegrinder Giant.

Why:

1. The merged permanent is represented by Everquill Phoenix (top) plus Soul Seizer (under). It has all abilities of every component, but all its other characteristics — name, types, power/toughness — come from the topmost component, Everquill Phoenix [702.140e] [730.2a]. So Soul Seizer's combat-damage trigger is on the merged permanent and triggers when it deals combat damage to Naomi.

2. A merged permanent is not itself a double-faced permanent, but transforming it turns over each double-faced component so that component's other face is up [730.2i]. So the Soul Seizer component becomes Ghastly Haunting face up. Everquill Phoenix is not double-faced and does not turn; it is still the topmost component, so the merged permanent is still a 4/4 Creature — Phoenix named Everquill Phoenix with flying. It is not an Aura.

3. The trigger then tries to attach the merged permanent to Axegrinder Giant. Because the merged permanent is not an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification (its characteristics are Everquill Phoenix's), the effect does nothing and the permanent doesn't move [701.3b]. Ghastly Haunting's "You control enchanted creature" does nothing because nothing is enchanted.

4. No state-based action kills it: the Aura-in-the-graveyard state-based action applies only to a permanent that is an Aura [704.5m], and this merged permanent is a creature, not an Aura. (Relatedly, an Aura that's also a creature couldn't enchant anything anyway [303.4d].)

Net effect on abilities: after the transform, the merged permanent has Everquill Phoenix's abilities (mutate, flying, the mutate trigger) plus Ghastly Haunting's abilities (enchant creature; you control enchanted creature) instead of Soul Seizer's — so the combat-damage transform trigger is gone going forward.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the merged permanent is still on the battlefield with Everquill Phoenix on top when the trigger resolves. If the Soul Seizer component had left the battlefield in response, Ariel couldn't transform it at all [Soul Seizer // Ghastly Haunting ruling #1], and if Axegrinder Giant were an illegal target on resolution, the whole ability would be countered and Ariel couldn't transform [Soul Seizer // Ghastly Haunting ruling #2].

Multiplayer: the result is the same. The trigger targets a creature controlled by the player who was dealt the combat damage (Naomi), so with more than two players it simply restricts Ariel to creatures controlled by whichever defending player took the damage; the attach still fails for the same reason.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
The component that consists of Soul Seizer is transformed. The merged permanent is still a creature. It is not attached to anything. The merged permanent has the abilities in the text box of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half.

When Ariel chooses to transform the merged permanent, all double-faced components are transformed. The merged permanent now has the abilities of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half. ([702.140e]) The merged permanent is still a creature as Everquill Phoenix is still the topmost card. When the transformation trigger tries to attach the merged permanent to Axegrinder Giant, it can't attach because the merged permanent is still a creature. It remains on the battlefield because the state-based action that puts auras not attached to anything into the graveyard is looking for the "Aura" subtype, not the "Enchant" keyword.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Back from the Brink] and has [Phyrexian Marauder] in their graveyard. Can Ainsley activate Back from the Brink's ability to create a token of Phyrexian Marauder? Can they pay more than {0} to do so? If so, will it enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Back from the Brink can be activated to create a Phyrexian Marauder token with X treated as 0 (you can't pay more), so the token enters with no +1/+1 counters.
entries.answer:
Yes, Ainsley can activate Back from the Brink targeting — well, exiling — Phyrexian Marauder from their graveyard, but the mana cost they pay is {0}, and the token enters with no +1/+1 counters.

Why: Back from the Brink's ability reads "Exile a creature card from your graveyard and pay its mana cost: Create a token that's a copy of that card." Phyrexian Marauder's mana cost is just {X}. When an effect instructs a player to pay an object's mana cost that includes {X}, X is treated as 0 unless the object is a spell on the stack; Phyrexian Marauder is a card in the graveyard being exiled, not a spell on the stack, so X = 0 [107.3h]. The same principle applies to cards outside the stack generally [107.3g], and Back from the Brink's own ruling confirms it: "If the exiled creature card has {X} in its mana cost, X is considered to be zero" [Back from the Brink ruling #4].

So Ainsley cannot choose a larger value for X. The cost paid is literally zero mana (the exile of Phyrexian Marauder is the rest of the cost), and there's no way to "pay more" to pump the value — X isn't a choice here, it's fixed at 0.

Because Phyrexian Marauder's ability says "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it," and X is 0, the token copy enters with zero +1/+1 counters. Note that this replacement-style "enters with" ability does function for the token — Back from the Brink's ruling states that "as [this creature] enters" and "[this creature] enters with" abilities work — it just gives 0 counters here [Back from the Brink ruling #3].

Also worth noting from Back from the Brink's rulings: Ainsley is not casting Phyrexian Marauder, so cost reducers, additional costs, and alternative costs don't apply [Back from the Brink ruling #2]. And the activation is sorcery-speed only, per the card's text.

Practical caveat: the token is a copy of a 0/0 Phyrexian Marauder with no counters. The rules excerpts provided here don't include the state-based action rules, so I won't assert a rule number for what happens to a 0/0 creature — but you should expect it not to survive on the battlefield.

Player count doesn't matter: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Ainsley may activate the ability of Phyrexian Marauder paying {0}. He does not have the ability to pay more than {0}. The token will not enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters.

entries.question: Nadia has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Ashley controls a [Peacewalker Colossus] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts a [Clever Impersonator], choosing to have it copy Peacewalker Colossus. What happens?
entries.reason: Both explanations conclude Gather Specimens causes Clever Impersonator to enter under Nadia's control so Nadia chooses what it copies, and if she copies Peacewalker Colossus it enters as a noncreature Vehicle under her control.
entries.answer:
Nadia gets the copy. Clever Impersonator enters the battlefield under Nadia's control, and because Gather Specimens is applied first, it's Nadia — not Ashley — who makes the copy choice as it enters. If Nadia chooses Peacewalker Colossus, the permanent enters under Nadia's control as a 6/6 artifact — Vehicle named Peacewalker Colossus that is NOT a creature.

Why, step by step:

1. Gather Specimens says "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." It isn't targeted and applies to creatures entering under any opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #5]. Clever Impersonator is a creature card being cast by Ashley, so as the spell resolves it would enter under an opponent's control and Gather Specimens applies [Gather Specimens ruling #7].

2. Two replacement effects want to modify how Clever Impersonator enters: Gather Specimens (control) and Clever Impersonator's own copy ability. When multiple replacement effects apply, the affected object's controller chooses one at a time, but the ordering steps force control-changing effects first: a replacement effect that modifies under whose control an object would enter must be chosen before a copy-as-it-enters effect [616.1, 616.1b, 616.1c]. This is exactly the Clone example in Gather Specimens' rulings: the Gather Specimens controller chooses what the copy-creature copies as it enters under their control [Gather Specimens ruling #4].

3. So Ashley's stated intention to copy Peacewalker Colossus doesn't bind anyone. The copy choice is made as the permanent enters [614.12a], by its new controller, Nadia [Clever Impersonator ruling #7]. Nadia may copy Ashley's Peacewalker Colossus, copy any other nonland permanent on the battlefield, or copy nothing — in which case it enters as a 0/0 Clever Impersonator and is put into the graveyard immediately [Clever Impersonator ruling #2].

4. If Nadia does copy Peacewalker Colossus: copy effects copy only printed values, not non-copy effects that changed the original's types, so the "becomes an artifact creature until end of turn" animation on Ashley's Peacewalker Colossus is not copied [Clever Impersonator ruling #10]. Specifically, "If a permanent becomes a copy of a Vehicle, the copy won't be a creature, even if the Vehicle it's copying has become an artifact creature" [Peacewalker Colossus ruling #12]. Nadia's new Peacewalker Colossus is an artifact Vehicle with printed 6/6, crew 4, and the {1}{W} activated ability, and it isn't a creature until Nadia crews it or otherwise animates it. Note it still ended up under Nadia's control even though it isn't a creature on the battlefield, because Gather Specimens was already locked in at step 2 before the copy effect was applied [616.1b].

5. Ashley's original Peacewalker Colossus is unaffected — it stays under Ashley's control and remains an artifact creature until end of turn.

Timing assumption: Gather Specimens resolved earlier this turn, before Clever Impersonator was cast, as stated. That's what makes it applicable — Gather Specimens never retroactively changes control of creatures that already entered [Gather Specimens ruling #1]; if instead Clever Impersonator had already resolved and entered under Ashley's control before Gather Specimens resolved, nothing would change and Ashley would keep the copy.

Multiplayer: the result is the same with more than two players, since Gather Specimens affects creatures entering under any opponent's control, not just one named opponent [Gather Specimens ruling #5]. The one difference at a bigger table is if another player also cast a Gather Specimens this turn: then the would-be controller chooses which Gather Specimens to apply, the new would-be controller repeats the process among the remaining ones, and so on [Gather Specimens ruling #6]; with exactly two opposing Gather Specimens the creature ends up back with the first player's opponent as described in that procedure. Also, when several players must make replacement-effect choices simultaneously, they do so in APNAP order [616.1].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. As Clever Impersonator begins to resolve, Nadia gains control of it before any other choices are made. Nadia will make the choice of what to copy as it enters the battlefield.

entries.question: Aubrey controls a [Gaea's Liege], [Rhonas the Indomitable], and 1 [Forest]. Noel controls 5 Forest. Can Aubrey attack with the Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable?
entries.reason: Both conclude Rhonas cannot be declared as an attacker because attacking restrictions are checked during attacker declaration when Gaea's Liege is still a 1/1 (so there is no other creature with power 4 or greater), while Gaea's Liege can be declared as the lone attacker.
entries.answer:
No — Aubrey can attack with Gaea's Liege, but Rhonas the Indomitable can't be declared as an attacker in this situation.

Why:

1. Rhonas the Indomitable's own text reads "Rhonas can't attack or block unless you control another creature with power 4 or greater." That's an attacking restriction, and restrictions are checked as part of declaring attackers [508.1c]. If a restriction is disobeyed, the whole declaration of attackers is illegal and the game rewinds to before the declaration [508.1, 508.1c].

2. The only other creature Aubrey controls is Gaea's Liege. Gaea's Liege's power is defined by its own text: while it isn't attacking, its power and toughness each equal the number of Forests Aubrey controls — that's 1, so Gaea's Liege is 1/1. Its ruling is explicit: "When being declared as an attacker, use the 'not attacking' power and toughness. It only changes after declaration is complete" [Gaea's Liege ruling #1]. So at the moment attackers are declared [508.1a, 508.1k], Gaea's Liege is a 1/1, not a 5/5, and Rhonas the Indomitable's condition of "another creature with power 4 or greater" is not met.

3. Declaring both at the same time doesn't help. The check happens during the declaration, when Gaea's Liege still uses its not-attacking value of 1 [Gaea's Liege ruling #1, 508.1c]. Gaea's Liege only becomes 5/5 (Noel's 5 Forests) after it has actually become an attacking creature [508.1k], which is too late for Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction.

4. Note that Rhonas the Indomitable does not require the other big creature to attack too — it just has to exist [Rhonas the Indomitable ruling #1]. Aubrey simply doesn't control one here.

So the legal attack is Gaea's Liege alone, which will be a 5/5 while attacking Noel. If Aubrey first gets another creature with power 4 or greater onto the battlefield (or, say, pumps one with Rhonas the Indomitable's {2}{G} ability before attackers are declared), Rhonas the Indomitable could then attack. Aubrey could also use Gaea's Liege's {T} ability to turn lands into Forests to raise its own power — but tapping Gaea's Liege means it can't attack [508.1a], and the ability would need to resolve before declaration.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players nothing changes for Rhonas the Indomitable — the restriction is about what Aubrey controls, not who is being attacked. Gaea's Liege's attacking power would depend on which defending player it's attacking (that player's Forest count), but again only after it's already attacking.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming no other effects resolve between now and the declare attackers step. If Aubrey raises another creature's power to 4 or greater before attackers are declared, Rhonas the Indomitable may attack normally.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. All creatures are declared as attackers at the same time. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".

entries.question: Ariyah casts [Stonewood Invocation] targeting [Skeletal Crocodile], and then attacks with the Skeletal Crocodile. Noah blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Phyresis] and indestructible due to their [Valorous Stance]. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Stonewood Invocation ends, Skeletal Crocodile dies due to the -1/-1 counters, and Baron Sengir was dealt damage this turn so its trigger gives it a +2/+2 counter (ending as a 7/7).
entries.answer:
At the cleanup step, Skeletal Crocodile dies and Baron Sengir survives and grows to 7/7.

How it plays out:

**During combat.** Stonewood Invocation made Skeletal Crocodile a 10/6 with shroud until end of turn (base 5/1). Baron Sengir has infect from Phyresis, so the 5 damage Baron Sengir deals to Skeletal Crocodile isn't marked as damage — instead Noah puts five -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile [702.90c]. That leaves Skeletal Crocodile at 10/6 minus five = 5/1, so it survives combat. Skeletal Crocodile deals 10 damage to Baron Sengir, but Valorous Stance gave Baron Sengir indestructible, so lethal damage doesn't destroy it; the 10 damage just sits marked on Baron Sengir.

**Cleanup step, turn-based action.** All damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" effects end simultaneously [514.2]. So the 10 damage leaves Baron Sengir at the exact same moment Valorous Stance's indestructible wears off — there is no window in which a non-indestructible Baron Sengir has lethal damage marked on it, so Baron Sengir is not destroyed. Stonewood Invocation's +5/+5 and shroud also end here.

**Cleanup step, state-based actions.** The -1/-1 counters are counters, not damage, so they are *not* removed. Skeletal Crocodile returns to its base 5/1 with five -1/-1 counters still on it, making it 0/-4. A creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [704.5f], and the cleanup step does check state-based actions when something like this is pending [514.3a]. Skeletal Crocodile's shroud is gone and wouldn't have mattered anyway — state-based actions don't target.

**Baron Sengir's trigger.** Skeletal Crocodile was dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn (infect changes the result of that damage, not the fact that damage was dealt), so when Skeletal Crocodile dies, Baron Sengir's ability triggers: put a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir. Per [514.3a], that state-based action is performed, then the trigger goes on the stack, then the active player gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities; once the stack empties and all players pass, another cleanup step begins. Baron Sengir ends up a 7/7 flyer with the counter. (Split second from Stonewood Invocation is long gone from the stack and restricts nothing here.)

**Timing assumption.** I'm assuming the normal sequence: Stonewood Invocation resolved before blockers, and Valorous Stance's indestructible was active through combat damage. If instead Valorous Stance had not yet resolved when combat damage was dealt, Baron Sengir would have been destroyed by 10 damage as a state-based action right after the combat damage step, and its own trigger would still see Skeletal Crocodile only if Skeletal Crocodile also died — which it wouldn't have until cleanup, so no +2/+2 counter would ever be placed.

**Player count.** Nothing here depends on the number of players; in a multiplayer game the same cleanup-step sequence applies, with the active player receiving priority first under [514.3a].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Stonewood Invocation wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile remain. Skeletal Crocodile dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

entries.question: Ariel casts [Prismari Command], with both modes targeting Nico. Will they be able to copy it with [Chef's Kiss]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the spell is a legal target for Chef's Kiss because it targets only one object/player (counting distinct targets, not target words), so the candidate reaches the same core ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Yes. Because every instance of the word "target" on Ariel's Prismari Command points at the same player, Nico, Prismari Command counts as a spell "that targets only a single permanent or player," so it is a legal target for Chef's Kiss.

Why: rule [115.9c] says an effect looking for a "[spell or ability] that targets only [something]" counts the number of different objects or players chosen as targets when the spell was put on the stack — not the number of "target" words. Since both chosen modes of Prismari Command picked Nico, that number is one, so the requirement is met. The Chef's Kiss ruling covering this says explicitly that a spell with multiple instances of "target" that all point at the same permanent or player is a legal target for Chef's Kiss [Chef's Kiss ruling #6]. (This assumes the two modes Ariel chose are ones that target a player — e.g. the 2-damage mode aimed at Nico plus the draw-two/discard-two or Treasure mode aimed at Nico. If one chosen mode were "Destroy target artifact," that artifact would be a second, different target and Chef's Kiss could not target Prismari Command at all.)

What happens on resolution of Chef's Kiss: the Chef's Kiss controller gains control of Prismari Command, copies it, and then reselects targets at random for both Prismari Command and the copy — a separate random reselection for each instance of the word "target" in the rules text of each [Chef's Kiss ruling #6]. The new targets can't be the Chef's Kiss controller or a permanent they control, and if any legal targets other than those exist, the random reselection is mandatory [Chef's Kiss ruling #5]. If there are no legal choices for a given target, that target simply stays as it was, which does not by itself make it illegal [Chef's Kiss ruling #3]. Copying Prismari Command and reselecting its targets is not casting a spell [Chef's Kiss ruling #4].

Player count matters for the outcome, not the legality: in a two-player game where Nico is the one casting Chef's Kiss, the only available random targets are Ariel and Ariel's permanents (Nico and Nico's permanents are excluded), so the damage and the draw/discard will land on Ariel. With three or more players, the random pool includes every other player and their permanents, so Prismari Command and its copy can scatter onto different players.

Afterward, each of Prismari Command and its copy resolves independently: if at least one of its targets is still legal, it resolves and does as much as it can; if all its targets are illegal, it does nothing [Prismari Command ruling #1, Prismari Command ruling #2].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When the game checks to see if a spell targets a single permanent or player, it doesn't care how many times that object was targeted, only that it was the only object the spell targeted.

entries.question: Alejandra owns a face-down [Progenitus] in exile. Nicolas uses [Ruin Processor] to put Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard. Where does Progenitus move to?
entries.reason: Both conclude Progenitus goes to the graveyard because a face-down card in exile has no characteristics or abilities, so its replacement effect doesn't exist to apply when it moves.
entries.answer:
Progenitus goes to Alejandra's graveyard — it is not shuffled into her library.

Why: a card exiled face down has no characteristics at all ([406.3a]). With no characteristics, the face-down Progenitus has no abilities while it sits in exile, so its replacement ability ("If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead") simply doesn't exist at the moment Ruin Processor's triggered ability moves it. Replacement effects must already exist before the event they would modify; they can't reach back and change something that has already happened ([614.4]). By the time the card is in the graveyard and face up, the move has already occurred, so the ability can't rewind it.

A few practical points:

- Nicolas can't look at face-down cards in exile, so he can't deliberately pick Progenitus (Ruin Processor ruling #1). He must choose a group of face-down cards (grouped by what exiled them and when) and then pick one at random from that group (Ruin Processor ruling #2). So "Nicolas uses Ruin Processor to put Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard" means the random choice happened to hit Progenitus.
- Progenitus's protection from everything doesn't save it either: Ruin Processor's ability doesn't target and doesn't deal damage, and effects that don't target or damage Progenitus still affect it (Progenitus rulings). Again, the face-down card doesn't even have that ability while in exile.
- Nicolas gains 5 life, since he did put a card into an opponent's graveyard.

If instead Progenitus had been exiled face up (or was otherwise a face-up object with its abilities), the replacement effect would exist beforehand and would apply: Progenitus would be revealed and shuffled into Alejandra's library instead of going to her graveyard ([614.4]).

Multiplayer note: this works the same at any player count. With more than two players, Ruin Processor's controller Nicolas may choose a card owned by any opponent, and each chosen card goes to its own owner's graveyard (Ruin Processor ruling #4); the outcome for Alejandra's face-down Progenitus is unchanged.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The graveyard. Replacement effects must exist before the event in question in order to affect it. Progenitus has no abilities in exile, so there is no replacement effect that would apply to it moving to the graveyard.

entries.question: Aurora controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Snow-Covered Forest. Can Aurora attack with the Gaea's Liege?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling and reasoning as the reference: Gaea's Liege is 3/3 when attack legality is checked so Reverence doesn't stop it, and it becomes 1/1 only after attackers are declared.
entries.answer:
Yes — Aurora can legally declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico.

Why: Reverence says "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you," which is an attack restriction checked when attackers are declared [508.1c]. Gaea's Liege says its power and toughness equal the number of Forests you control as long as it isn't attacking, and equal the number of Forests defending player controls as long as it is attacking. Per [Gaea's Liege ruling #1], when Gaea's Liege is being declared as an attacker you use its "not attacking" characteristics — it only switches after the declaration is complete. So at the moment of declaration Gaea's Liege is a 3/3 (Aurora's three Snow-Covered Forests; snow is just a supertype and they are still Forests, per [Snow-Covered Forest ruling #1]). Power 3 is not "2 or less," so Reverence doesn't stop the declaration, and Gaea's Liege becomes an attacking creature [508.1a] [508.1k].

Afterward: once the declaration is complete and Gaea's Liege is attacking, its power and toughness become equal to the number of Forests Nico controls — 1 — so it's a 1/1 attacker. Reverence does not remove it from combat; the restriction is only checked during the declaration of attackers [508.1c] [508.1k]. (Aurora can also tap Gaea's Liege for its {T} ability to turn a land into a Forest, but tapping it means it can't be declared as an attacker that turn, since attackers must be untapped [508.1a].)

More than two players: this answer covers Aurora attacking Nico specifically. If there are other opponents, Reverence only protects Nico, so attacking a different player has no Reverence restriction at all — though Gaea's Liege's attacking power/toughness would then be set by that defending player's Forest count. Also, per [Reverence ruling #1], even a creature with power 2 or less could still attack a planeswalker Nico controls.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".

entries.question: Ari controls [Village Survivors] and [Vodalian Soldiers] and has 6 life. Nyla controls [Norn's Annex]. If Ari attacks with Vodalian Soldiers, paying 2 life, will it become tapped?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference: attackers are tapped before paying Norn's Annex, so Vodalian Soldiers is tapped when declared and gaining vigilance afterward doesn't untap it.
entries.answer:
Yes — Vodalian Soldiers becomes tapped, and it stays tapped for that combat.

Why: declaring attackers is a single turn-based action performed in a fixed order. The active player taps the chosen creatures first [508.1f], and only afterward chooses optional costs [508.1g], determines and locks in the total cost to attack [508.1h], activates mana abilities if needed [508.1i], and pays the costs [508.1j]. Norn's Annex's cost of {W/P} (payable with {W} or 2 life) for each attacking creature is exactly such a cost to attack, and Norn's Annex's ruling states the controller of each attacking creature pays {W} or 2 life as attackers are being declared.

So the sequence is: Ari taps Vodalian Soldiers as it's declared as an attacker (tapping isn't a cost — attacking simply causes creatures to become tapped [508.1f]), then Ari pays 2 life for Norn's Annex, dropping from 6 life to 4. Only at that point does Village Survivors' fateful hour ability turn on ("As long as you have 5 or less life, other creatures you control have vigilance"), granting Vodalian Soldiers vigilance. Vigilance only prevents a creature from tapping when it's declared as an attacker; it doesn't untap something already tapped. Village Survivors' own ruling says this explicitly: if paying such a cost causes your life total to fall below 6, your tapped attackers will have vigilance, but the ability will have no benefit that combat.

Note also that Village Survivors itself has printed vigilance, so if Ari had attacked with Village Survivors too, Village Survivors would not have tapped regardless of life total.

Multiplayer note: the provided rules and card text don't change with player count in a way that affects this — Norn's Annex only taxes creatures attacking Nyla or planeswalkers Nyla controls. In a game with more than two players, if Ari attacked a different opponent (one who doesn't control Norn's Annex), there'd be no {W/P} cost, Ari's life would stay at 6, and Vodalian Soldiers would still be tapped simply because attacking taps it [508.1f].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Tapping creatures to attack is done before paying any costs to attack.

entries.question: Amari has [Phyrexian Hulk] and [The Mimeoplasm] in their graveyard. Amari casts [Rise of the Dark Realms] to return both to the battlefield. Can they have The Mimeoplasm enter the battlefield as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude The Mimeoplasm cannot copy Phyrexian Hulk because its replacement-effect choice is made before it enters and you can't choose an object that is also entering the battlefield at the same time.
entries.answer:
No. The Mimeoplasm can't copy Phyrexian Hulk here, and in fact it can't exile anything at all, so it enters as a 0/0 Ooze.

Why: The Mimeoplasm's ability reads "As The Mimeoplasm enters, you may exile two creature cards from graveyards..." That's a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield, and the choice it requires is made before The Mimeoplasm is actually on the battlefield [614.1c][614.12a]. Rise of the Dark Realms puts all creature cards from all graveyards onto the battlefield at the same time, so Phyrexian Hulk is entering simultaneously with The Mimeoplasm.

Rule 614.13a is exactly on point: when applying an effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield, you can't choose the object that will become that permanent, nor any other object entering the battlefield at the same time as that object. Phyrexian Hulk is entering at the same time as The Mimeoplasm, so Phyrexian Hulk is not a legal choice for the exile [614.13a].

Worse for Amari, Rise of the Dark Realms takes every creature card out of every graveyard at once, so there are no creature cards left in any graveyard that could legally be exiled — and The Mimeoplasm's own text and rulings require exiling exactly two creature cards; you can't choose to exile just one [The Mimeoplasm ruling #4]. With the optional "you may" not (and not able to be) taken, The Mimeoplasm enters as itself: a legendary 0/0 Ooze with no counters. (What happens to a 0-toughness creature afterward is governed by state-based actions, and no such rule was provided in this context, so I won't state it as grounded here.)

Multiplayer note: Rise of the Dark Realms affects all graveyards, so at a table of three or more the same reasoning applies — every opponent's creature cards also enter simultaneously and therefore none of them are legal exile choices either [614.13a]. The answer is the same at two players and at more.

If instead Amari had gotten The Mimeoplasm onto the battlefield by some means that did not move Phyrexian Hulk at the same time (for example, casting The Mimeoplasm from the command zone or hand while Phyrexian Hulk and another creature card sat in graveyards), the copy choice would work normally and The Mimeoplasm could enter as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk with additional +1/+1 counters equal to the other exiled card's power [The Mimeoplasm ruling #1][The Mimeoplasm ruling #2].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The Mimeoplasm has a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield. The game checks for any replacement effects that modify how an object will enter the battlefield before the object has changed zones. So Phyrexian Hulk is still in the graveyard while Amari is making choices for The Mimeoplasm, however they are not allowed to choose an object that is also changing zones at the same time.

entries.question: Autumn casts [Time Stretch]. Can they choose to skip both extra turns with [Time Vault]?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Autumn can skip only one of the two extra turns with a single Time Vault, while the reference states they can skip both, so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
No. With one Time Vault, Autumn can skip only one of the two extra turns Time Stretch gives them.

Why: Time Vault's own text reads "If you would begin your turn while this artifact is tapped, you may skip that turn instead. If you do, untap this artifact." The skip is a replacement effect — "skip [something]" means "instead of doing [something], do nothing" ([614.10], [614.1b]) — but it only offers the choice if Time Vault is tapped at the moment the turn would begin, and using it untaps Time Vault ([Time Vault ruling #1]). That self-untap is exactly why the card no longer chains: [Time Vault ruling #2] states that with this wording you no longer end up skipping multiple turns even if you find a way to activate the ability multiple times.

Step by step, assuming Time Stretch resolves during Autumn's turn and Autumn targets themselves, and that Time Vault is tapped when the first extra turn would begin:

1. Time Stretch's two extra turns are added after the current turn, one at a time ([500.7]).
2. As extra turn #1 would begin, Time Vault is tapped, so Autumn may skip that turn. Doing so untaps Time Vault, and it untaps before anything else happens in the next turn ([Time Vault ruling #1]).
3. Extra turn #2 then begins with Time Vault untapped, so no skip is available. Once that turn has started it can no longer be skipped anyway; any skip effect would have to wait for the next occurrence ([614.10]).

Autumn could, during extra turn #2, activate Time Vault's "{T}: Take an extra turn after this one" — but that tap creates yet another extra turn, and skipping that later turn just untaps Time Vault again. So the count of turns actually taken doesn't shrink; Autumn never gets to skip both Time Stretch turns off a single Time Vault. Two untapped Time Vaults (or another way to tap it before turn #2 begins without granting a turn) would be needed to skip both.

If Time Vault happens to be untapped when the first extra turn begins, Autumn skips neither of the Time Stretch turns.

Note also that a skipped turn produces no priority, so nothing can be done during it; and if a skip effect tells you to take an action, that action is the first thing that happens in the next turn to actually occur ([614.10b]) — which is how Time Vault's untap lands.

This is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that when several players are given extra turns, those turns are added one at a time in APNAP order ([500.7]), which doesn't change Autumn's ability to skip only one.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. As their turn ends, they can apply Time Vault's replacement effect, which means the next turn gets skipped and Time Vault gets untapped as part of the next turn that actually happens. Then, since it's still tapped as Autumn's turn is ending, they can choose to skip the next turn again.
entries.human_note: our reasoning is wrong but this question will never come up because no player would do that. I wouldn't consider this one part of scoring too strongly, even if it is a ruling we technically could use, it shouldn't weight as hard as most others. that's probably true for most of the corner cases. if we're trying to get questions right, its more important that we get the level 3 questions right than it is we get the corner cases right, but we should try for both.

entries.question: Averie attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Averie casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Mob]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Cephalid Snitch removes only the Angel’s protection from black (separately from other colors), that loss lasts until end of turn even after it untaps, and thus Mob (a black instant) can target it.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can target Pristine Angel with Mob, and Mob will destroy it (barring other effects).

Why: Pristine Angel's static ability reads "As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color." "Protection from each color" is shorthand for several independent protection abilities — protection from white, from blue, from black, from red, and from green — each functioning separately [702.16h], just as "protection from artifacts and from each color" behaves as separate protection abilities [702.16g]. Protection is what stops a permanent from being targeted by spells with the stated quality [702.16b], so only Pristine Angel's protection from black is relevant to Mob, which is a black instant.

Cephalid Snitch's ability said "Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn," and it resolved successfully (legal at the time, since a tapped Pristine Angel had no protection at all and so couldn't stop being targeted). That effect lasts until end of turn and doesn't care whether Pristine Angel is tapped or untapped afterward. Ordering the two effects is a timestamp question: the continuous effect from Pristine Angel's static ability has the same timestamp as Pristine Angel itself (the permanent the ability is on) [613.7a], and Pristine Angel was already on the battlefield before Cephalid Snitch's ability resolved. So Cephalid Snitch's effect has the later timestamp and is applied after Pristine Angel's own effect: Pristine Angel untaps and gains protection from artifacts and from each color, then immediately loses protection from black for the rest of the turn.

Result: for the rest of this turn Pristine Angel still has protection from artifacts, white, blue, red, and green, but not from black, so Mob (a black instant) may legally target it. Note that Mob's convoke doesn't change Mob's color or mana value — tapping creatures only helps pay its {4}{B} total cost — so Mob is black no matter how Nico pays for it (Mob rulings: convoke doesn't change a spell's mana cost or mana value; tapping a creature pays for {1} or one mana of that creature's color).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability was activated and resolved while Pristine Angel was tapped, then Averie's spell untapped it. If instead Cephalid Snitch's ability had been activated while Pristine Angel was untapped, the activation would have been illegal in the first place — an untapped Pristine Angel has protection from blue and couldn't be targeted by Cephalid Snitch's ability, since Cephalid Snitch is a blue source [702.16b].

Player count doesn't matter here: the rules provided (timestamps and protection) work identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Yes. "Protection from all colors" is shorthand for protection from each color individually. It loses protection from black, and still has protection from all the other colors.

(The timestamp of Pristine Angel's ability does not change when it becomes untapped.)
